units.canDo: Can recognise, quote and use about twenty frequent French proverbs and a set of B2 fixed expressions, tell a proverb from a fixed expression and a locution, quote a proverb by half, twist it or use it as a hook in the right register, find the equivalent English proverb or explain that there is none, quote La Fontaine accurately, and write an opinion column that opens with a proverb and discusses whether it holds
units.title: Proverbs and Fixed Expressions

units.sub: Faire le point sur sa grammaire
units.canDo: Can audit their own written and spoken production against the C1 accuracy descriptor, sort every B1 and B2 structure into what they must produce, what they need only recognise and their own weak spots, name the lesson that fixes each weak spot, and write a precise learning plan of 250 to 400 words
units.title: Taking Stock of Your Grammar

units.canDo: Can read a 300 to 400 word essay or opinion piece and state its thesis at its exact scope, what it concedes and then restricts, the real object of the disagreement, what a paragraph, an analogy or a closing line is doing, the writer’s stance toward a source, what its grammar presupposes, its irony from a textual cue and the agent its passives hide, and answer TCF and TEF C1 reading items without falling for their distractors
units.title: Reading Between the Lines

units.canDo: Can follow a 90 to 150 second debate or interview between two or three speakers and a moderator, heard once, and say what they agree on, where the real disagreement lies (including a dispute over a word or a definition), exactly what each speaker concedes, how a speaker narrows a claim, how an objection is answered and what an analogy or allusion means in context; can handle the TCF and TEF Canada C1 listening formats and write a 250 to 400 word account of a debate
units.title: Debates and Interviews

units.canDo: Can tell a dispatch, an article, a report, an editorial, a column, a billet, an op-ed and an open letter apart by their signals, read the inverted pyramid and the parts of an article, show how the choice and order of sources, figures, captions and loaded words frame an event, and compare two treatments of one event in writing
units.title: Newspaper Analysis

units.canDo: Can recognise the passé antérieur in unsimplified literary narrative, with avoir and être and in pronominal verbs, tell it from a passive or a simple past of avoir, follow the immediate anteriority it marks after a time hinge, after « à peine… que » and in a main clause with bientôt, contrast it with the plus-que-parfait, say what it does to the pace of a page, map it to today’s French, and recognise the passé surcomposé as its spoken counterpart without using it
units.title: The Passé Antérieur

units.canDo: Can follow the classical sequence of tenses in an unsimplified literary text, under a present, past or conditional main verb, tell simultaneity, posteriority and anteriority apart, read hypothetical and concessive inversion (eût-il su, fût-il roi), recognise a deliberate break in the sequence and say what it means, and explain the register effect (solemnity, irony, pastiche) while mapping each form to today’s usage
units.title: Literary Sequence of Tenses

units.canDo: Can build and decode relative clauses with partitive dont, preposition + quoi, an infinitive, lequel as subject and abstract antecedents, can tell which noun a relative clause hangs on in a long noun group and repair an ambiguous one, can use the comma to change who is concerned, and can lighten a chain of relatives in formal writing
units.title: Complex Relative Clauses

units.canDo: Can follow and build chains of reference across a long text: pick up an adjective or a whole clause with the neutral le, stand in for a verb with faire, leave out a repeated verb or the rest of a question, take up a noun with celui de or celle que, with a broader noun or with a noun that sums up, use ledit and le cas échéant in administrative writing, and repair a pronoun two nouns could answer, in reading (CE « à quoi renvoie… ») as in writing
units.title: Ellipsis and Reference

units.canDo: Can soften, distance and calibrate claims and requests in speech at C1: add a hedging aside where the doubt lies, grade a forecast from a firm bet to no evidence, make a supposition with devoir, approximate a word precisely, make a formal request, contradict and criticise with regard while keeping firm points firm, use and hear litote and understatement, decode the polite brush-off, and set the dose of hedging for the person and the stakes; can leave a two to four minute spoken message that does all of this
units.title: Nuance in Speech

units.canDo: Can steer a long text or talk with expert discourse markers: correct and narrow a statement while moving on, say what a word means here and name the actual case, add the argument that weighs, argue from the stronger case, read dès lors in time or in logic, accept a cost, close with one marker chosen by register, recognise the contested markers of speech and write their safe equivalents
units.title: Reframing and Concluding

units.canDo: Can recognise and use credibility, reasoning, emotion, authority, analogy, framing, the rhetorical question, anaphora, gradation, paralipsis and the pre-empted objection, judge whether each persuasive move is fair, and write a persuasive piece that names its own moves and answers an objection fairly
units.title: Rhetoric and Persuasion

units.canDo: Can deliver a structured spoken exposé of three to five minutes from a dossier of documents, presenting them in synthesis rather than one by one, stating a spoken problématique and a plan and holding to them aloud; can then defend the exposé before a jury: take the floor formally, reformulate a question, buy time without filling the silence, admit what one does not know, concede a point in public without abandoning the thesis, handle questions outside the dossier and close the exchange
units.title: The Exposé and the Jury

units.canDo: Can turn a subject into a real problem question by defining its terms, choose among dialectical, thematic, analytical and comparative plans from that question, link the parts with transitions that sum up and move on, conclude with an earned opening, write a synthesis of documents in their own words without opinion, and write a structured argumentative essay in a real genre from a short dossier
units.title: Essays and Document Synthesis

units.canDo: Can write a report for a reader who must decide: an executive summary first, a sourced constat kept apart from the analysis, causes ranked, options compared on the same criteria, recommendations in the formal register with the right mood; can tell a compte rendu from a procès-verbal and a relevé de décisions, write each in the present and the impersonal, and replace the office anglicisms
units.title: Reports and Minutes

units.canDo: Can define, distinguish and use the epistemic and logical pairs of abstract discussion (expliquer and justifier, cause and raison, croyance and connaissance, nécessaire and contingent, condition nécessaire and suffisante, prémisse and conclusion, valide and vrai, sophisme and paralogisme, a priori and a posteriori, confirmer, infirmer and réfuter) with their collocations, read them precisely in a text, and answer someone who confuses them
units.title: The Vocabulary of Ideas

units.canDo: Can recognise the historical references francophone press and speech take for granted (1789, 1905, the 18th of June, Vichy, Algeria, Mai 68, the Conquest, the Révolution tranquille, 1830, 1291, 1960, the négritude), unfold what each one recalls, explain what invoking it does in a text, tell legend and apocrypha from fact, and report contested readings with their sources and without a verdict
units.title: The References That Count

units.canDo: Can move from a personal reaction to an argued analysis of how a film, a painting, a photograph, a piece of music or a staging produces its effect, naming its means precisely (shot, frame, off-screen space, editing, soundtrack, composition, light, brushwork, orchestration, staging), and can write a critique that weighs strengths against weaknesses before giving a reasoned verdict
units.title: Analysing a Work

units.canDo: Can choose and use the political and social headwords of public debate (égalité and équité, the senses of justice, la liberté and les libertés publiques, fundamental rights and their texts, pouvoir, puissance and autorité, contre-pouvoir, légal and légitime, l’État de droit and l’impunité, identité in its abstract sense, multiculturalisme and interculturalisme) with their collocations, name the weight a loaded word carries without taking it on, and answer someone who confuses them
units.title: Justice, Freedom, Identity, Power

units.canDo: Can choose precisely among the moral, aesthetic and memorial words of abstract discussion (sincère, véridique and vraisemblable; mentir and se tromper; infox, fausse nouvelle and erreur; morale, éthique and déontologie; remords and regret; intègre and intégral; joli, beau and sublime; goût and esthétique; souvenir and mémoire; commémorer and fêter; histoire and mémoire) with their collocations, read them precisely in a text, and answer someone who confuses them
units.title: Memory, Truth, Beauty, Ethics

units.canDo: Can choose among near-synonyms by intensity (agacer, irriter, exaspérer; grimper, flamber, fléchir, s’effondrer), by connotation (économe or avare, persévérant or obstiné, the suffixes -âtre, -asse, -aud, the euphemism), by collocation (the verb and the intensifier a noun expects) and by region and register (Québec labels in Usito and the OQLF), pick the antonym that matches the sense, read these choices precisely in a text, and write a portrait that is fair and exact
units.title: Synonyms and Shades of Meaning

units.canDo: Can recognise the learned semantic anglicisms of educated French (initier, opportunité, alternative, impacter, académique, versatile, juridiction, éligible, digital, faire sens, questionner, canceller, céduler, booker), say which authorities condemn or accept each and where France and Québec differ, and replace each with the precise French word in a text written for others
units.title: Learned False Friends

units.canDo: Can identify a figure or a stylistic choice in a literary or argumentative text (litotes, antiphrasis, gradation, chiasmus, zeugma, hypallage, metonymy and synecdoche, alliteration and assonance, rhythm and cadence, effects of rupture) and write one precise sentence on its effect, proved by the words of the text, and can write a short commentary on an extract
units.title: Figures of Speech and Their Effect

units.canDo: Can convey the meaning, force and argumentative thread of a complex English text in natural French: reformulates at the level of the idea, renders hedging and understatement at the same degree of certainty, turns topic-sentence paragraphs into signposted French ones, makes implicit links explicit and lightens English redundancy, finds cultural equivalents, summarises across languages, adapts register to the audience, and revises for faux sens, contresens, omissions and additions
units.title: Translating Ideas

units.canDo: Can refuse, announce bad news, say no to a superior and escalate a problem in writing with tact and precision, choosing the degree of indirectness that fits the reader and the stakes without blurring the message; can recognise when politeness turns passive-aggressive; can weigh contested office usage by its sources and write for a reader in France or in Québec; can title slides by their message and handle a hostile question at work

lessons.intro: Somebody asks what you do. You answer in four words, correctly, and then the room waits. This lesson is the three sentences that come after the first one, and the question at the end that hands the conversation back.

move.body: Four of them, and they go in order. What you are, for how long, what that means on a normal day, and a question back. Most people have the first one and stop, which is why the room goes quiet.
move.title: One of the four things your answer does

examples.note: Move 1, and on its own it is not an answer.
Move 4, which is the one nobody teaches.

pair.body: Most job words in French have two written forms and you only ever need one of them about yourself. Where the corpus already had a form, this lesson uses that one rather than inventing a rival.
pair.title: The same job, said about a man and about a woman

examples.note: This one the course already had.
And this one it did not, so it was built the ordinary way.

poste.body: A position at work, a television set, and a police station. The work sense is the one this lesson means and it is the one you will meet in an advert. Nothing about the word tells you which; the sentence around it does.
poste.title: One word, three completely different things

examples.note: The work sense, which is the one you want.
And an interviewer using it about you.

anchor.body: It names the job and nothing else. It is short on purpose, and it is finished in under two seconds, which is exactly why it cannot be the whole turn. Lesson 10 in A1 taught you how to say it. This lesson is about what comes next.
anchor.title: The sentence everything else hangs off

examples.note: Two words after the verb, and then a decision.

detail.body: Not the job title again in longer words. One concrete thing you handle, manage, or are responsible for. This is the half of the answer that tells somebody whether they can picture your day.
detail.title: What you actually do between nine and five

examples.note: A thing you can point at.
And a thing you are answerable for.

posting.body: A handful of fixed headings that repeat across every advert in the language. Once you can find the hours, the contract and the start date, you can read one you have never seen in about thirty seconds.
posting.title: What a job advert is made of

examples.note: And the heading everybody reads first.

handback.body: A short question at the end that puts the turn back on the other person. Without it you have made a statement and they have to think of something. With it you have started something that runs by itself.
handback.title: Turning an answer into a conversation

examples.note: Four words, and the other person is now talking.
The interviewer doing it to you, at the end.

repairMove.body: Lesson 24 in A2 authored six, ordered by what each one costs you. The cheapest gives away nothing; the last one concedes that speaking has failed and asks for it in writing. Reach for the lowest one that will actually fix the problem.
repairMove.title: Lesson 24's six ways to say you did not catch it

examples.note: The cheapest thing you can say.
The first one that names what went wrong.

sections.body: The gap after suis belongs to lesson 10 in A1 and depuis belongs to lesson 14 in A2, so neither rule is written out here. What you studied and the paper that proves it are lesson 30 in A2, which comes next. The six ways to ask somebody to repeat themselves are lesson 24's, and the three rungs for getting something fixed are lesson 28's.

overview.introFr: Quatre mouvements, et le dernier rend la parole.

beats.text: A small meeting room in Lyon. Two people, one table, and a folder nobody has opened yet.

beats.en: So, tell me about your background.
beats.fr: Alors, parlez-moi de votre parcours.
beats.stage: She sits back. This is the easy one.
beats.respell: [a-LOR par-lay-MWAH duh vo-truh par-KOOR]
beats.speaker: The interviewer

beats.en: I am an engineer.
beats.fr: Je suis ingénieur.
beats.stage: Correct. Every word of it.
beats.respell: [zhuh swee-zaⁿ-zhay-NYUR]

beats.text: And then nothing. She waits. You have finished and she does not know that yet.

beats.prompt: Four seconds have gone. What do you do?

options.en: Wait for the next question
options.fr: Wait for the next question

options.en: Keep going, without being asked
options.fr: Keep going, without being asked

followUp.works: Nobody asked you a second question. That is the point: you take it.
followUp.breaks: She will ask another one. It will be smaller, and so will the next.

beats.body: You said something true and correct, and then you stopped. She was waiting for a second sentence because in this room an answer is four of them, not one. Nothing you said was wrong.
beats.coach: Two sentences and the room changes. There are two more after that.

cards.fr: Je suis avocate.
cards.body: The commonest shape, and the course already had this pair. You hear the t in the second one and not in the first. The gap after suis is lesson 10 in A1's and it does not move.
cards.head: un avocat · une avocate
cards.label: Add -e

cards.fr: Je suis employée dans une banque.
cards.body: Written differently, said the same. Nobody hears the difference and you still write it.
cards.head: un employé · une employée
cards.label: Add -e

cards.fr: Je suis pharmacienne.
cards.body: Here you do hear it. The nasal opens up and an n arrives at the end.
cards.head: un pharmacien · une pharmacienne
cards.label: -ien becomes -ienne

cards.fr: Je suis infirmière.
cards.body: The ending opens from ee-ay to ee-ehr. Same again for caissier and caissière.
cards.head: un infirmier · une infirmière
cards.label: -ier becomes -ière

cards.fr: Je suis vendeuse.
cards.body: Works when the word came from a verb you can still see: vendre, coiffer, servir.
cards.head: un vendeur · une vendeuse
cards.label: -eur becomes -euse

cards.fr: Je suis agricultrice.
cards.body: The other big one. Directeur and directrice, traducteur and traductrice, acteur and actrice.
cards.head: un agriculteur · une agricultrice
cards.label: -teur becomes -trice

cards.fr: Je suis ingénieure.
cards.body: Said exactly the same. The written e is the whole change, and professeure works the same way.
cards.head: un ingénieur · une ingénieure

sections.text:
BOULANGERIE MARTIN, Lyon 3e

Nous cherchons un vendeur ou une vendeuse pour notre magasin du centre-ville.

Poste : vente et caisse. Vous vous occupez des clients et vous aidez en cuisine le matin.

Horaires : 35 heures par semaine, du mardi au samedi. Pas de travail le dimanche.

Contrat : CDI après trois mois.

Expérience : deux ans minimum dans la vente.

Début : à partir du 15 septembre.

Envoyez votre CV à martin.lyon@exemple.fr

sections.body: Say the four moves out loud, once, for your own job. Nothing here is listening, so this one is on you: the point is to find out whether you can get from the anchor to the question without stopping, not whether a machine agrees that you did. recorded.desc: THE FOUR KINDS, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, IN THE ORDER THE GRID PRINTS THEM AND WITH NO GAP BETWEEN THEM: « Je vais chez le médecin. », « Je vais à Paris. », « Je vais en France. », « Je vais au marché. » The claim the whole grid rests on is that these are four answers to ONE question, and four separate recordings are four performances: a reader who records them apart will give each one its own shape and the learner will hear four different sentences instead of one sentence with four endings. THE FIRST THREE WORDS OF ALL FOUR MUST BE IDENTICAL. « Je vais » is the constant and the only thing allowed to move is what comes after it. KEEP EVERY NASAL CLOSED: France is /fʁɑ̃s/ with no n sound behind the vowel, médecin ends /sɛ̃/ with none either, and a reader who lets an n out of either is teaching a sound the language does not have.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE FOLD DRILL, THREE LINES, ONE TAKE: « Je vais au marché. », « Je vais au Japon. », « Je vais chez le médecin. » The first two are one word where the page had two and the third is two words that stay two, and THE WHOLE VALUE OF THE TAKE IS THAT THE THIRD ONE HAS A GAP THE FIRST TWO DO NOT. Do not exaggerate it and do not close it: read all three at ordinary conversational pace and let the difference be whatever it naturally is, which is a real and audible thing. A reader who separates « chez » and « le » with a pause is teaching that the phrase is hesitant, and a reader who runs them together is teaching that it folds. Neither is true.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE CHEZ TRAP, AND IT IS THE ONLY WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE IN THIS LESSON. « chez la boulangerie » then « à la boulangerie » then « chez le boulanger », one take, in that order. READ THE WRONG ONE PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly: it is perfectly pronounceable, it sounds completely ordinary, and that is exactly why learners keep saying it. A reading that signals the error teaches that the error is audible, and it is not. The two right versions must sound like two ordinary things somebody would say on the same morning, because they are, and because the point of the pair is that they are not alternatives for one slot: they are two different places to be going. Also in this take, each whole: « chez le médecin », « chez la dentiste », « chez Marie », « à l’hôpital ».

THE CORRIDOR IN NANTES. She has a coffee in each hand, she is friendly and slightly in a hurry, and her question is small talk rather than a request for information. THE LEARNER'S OWN LINE IS THE TAKE THAT HAS TO BE RIGHT: « Je vais... euh... à le médecin... au médecin... » is somebody trying two forms of a rule they were taught, hearing that neither of them is what people say, and running out of sentence. It must sound like a correction beginning rather than like a forgotten word, and the difference is audible: the first two attempts should be confident and the stall should come after them, not before. HER RECOVERY LINE IS THE EXPENSIVE ONE. « Ah, chez le médecin. Rien de grave ? » is her supplying the word without noticing she has supplied it, and moving straight on to something else. Any hint of correction, emphasis or kindness-about-a-mistake in that line turns the scene into a telling-off and loses the whole point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong.
clipIds: Je vais... euh... à le médecin... au médecin...
Ah, chez le médecin. Rien de grave ?

recorded.desc: THE MAN AND THE SHOP, ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, AND THEY MUST SOUND EQUALLY ORDINARY. « Je vais chez le boulanger. » then « Je vais à la boulangerie. » then « C'est la même porte. » Both of the first two are things people say every day and neither is more careful or more formal than the other, so any difference in weight between them teaches a distinction the language does not make. The third line is the punchline and should be read flatly, as a fact rather than as a joke. NOTE ON « même »: it is /mɛm/ with a real m and no nasal vowel at all. The app respells it `mem` deliberately rather than `MEHM`, and a reader who nasalises it is saying a different word.

THE SIX PEOPLE AND THE FIVE PHRASES, ONE TAKE, EVEN PACE, READ AS A LIST. le médecin, le dentiste, boulanger, le vétérinaire, le copain, la tante, then chez toi, chez nous, Bienvenue chez moi, passer chez quelqu'un, aller chez le vétérinaire. EVERY ARTICLE IS ATTACHED AND NONE IS SEPARATED BY A PAUSE, because the learner is being asked to notice that chez does NOT take the article away, and a gap between chez and le would suggest the two words are being held apart on purpose. They are simply two words. THE VOWEL AT THE END OF « médecin » IS /ɛ̃/ AND THE APP WRITES IT EHⁿ, matching three published rows in the sons themes. Read it through the nose with no n behind it.

THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to every other take in this lesson: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and any pair-reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. FIVE OF THEM ARE THE SMALL WORD PLUS A PLACE AND NOTHING ELSE, and those five matter most: the learner has to hear where one word ends and the next begins, so do not run « chez le » together into a single syllable and do not put a gap in it either. Say it the way somebody would say it.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS SIX SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same colleague from the corridor a week later, she has more time, and she is enjoying the conversation. « Tu es chez toi ce soir ? » and « On se retrouve chez Marie ? » both use the word the learner has just spent half an hour on, and NEITHER MAY BE STRESSED: she is not testing anybody, and a lift on chez would turn a conversation into an exercise. Read « Et le week-end, tu pars ? » with genuine curiosity, because it is the turn where the learner gets to choose between three kinds of place and any of the three is a real answer.
clipIds: Tu es chez toi ce soir ?

lessons.intro: French has four small words for where somebody is or where they are going, and which one you use is decided by the place rather than by you. A town, a country, a building, a person: ask which of those four you are looking at and the word is already chosen. Three of the four you have met before without being told they were the same question. The fourth is chez, it takes a person and never a place, and English has nothing like it.

chez.body: Chez takes a person and never a place. Chez Marie, chez le médecin, chez moi. Never a building, never a shop, never a town. Out of 283 sentences in this course that use the word, 0 put it in front of a building. Not one. What the sentences put behind it instead: le 59 times, nous 38 times, moi 34 times, mes 16 times, lui 16 times. Every one of those is a person or a word standing in for one, and that is the whole of the rule. There is no English word for it, which is why it is the one of the four you will have to think about.
chez.title: A person, and never a place

notYet.body: En also means how long something takes and dans also means how far ahead something is, and both of those are lesson 14 in A2, which is the very next lesson. Lesson 14 in A2 is the very next lesson and it takes both of those words back and does something else with them, and that is worth knowing now so you do not think you have met them twice. Lesson 27 in A2 is called « Chez le médecin » and it is fourteen lessons ahead of you. Its whole title is this lesson's third card.

fourKinds.body: Four kinds of place and four answers. Three of them you already have, and the fourth is the one English gives you no help with at all. a person takes chez, as in chez Marie, a city takes à, as in à Paris, a country takes en, au, as in en France, a building takes à + le, as in au marché. Ask what the place IS before reaching for the word in front. A person takes chez. Everything else is a place, and its article decides the rest. A learner who asks what they are DOING gets no help from the answer, because going, arriving, staying and living all take the same word. The place decides it, and the place decides it before the verb has finished.
fourKinds.title: Look at the place before you look for the word

examples.note: A city, so nothing to fold with.
A country with a le, so the le is folded in.
And a building with a la, which does not fold.

manOrShop.body: English says the baker's for the man and the bakery for the shop and lets you use either. French will not: the man takes chez and the shop takes à. Say either in English and nobody notices. Say the wrong one in French and you have said something nobody says, and the reason it is hard is that you were never asked to choose before. When the shop has no person behind it, as a bank or a station does, only one of the two is available and the choice disappears.
manOrShop.title: English has one phrase for both of these

noArticle.body: A city has no article and a person's name has no article, so there is nothing for the word in front to do. À Paris, chez Marie. That is why those two rows of the grid look the simplest and it is also why they are the two learners overthink: there is no rule to apply, and applying one anyway produces « à la Paris » and « chez la Marie », which are the two errors nobody warns you about.
noArticle.title: Two places that never had one to begin with

examples.note: And a second city, so it is a rule rather than a fact about Paris.

theArticle.body: À folds the article in. En throws it out. Chez leaves it alone. In front of a le word: à gives au, de gives du, en gives en, chez gives chez le. That is the whole lesson in one sentence and there is nothing else to it. À and de fold, en throws the article away, and chez leaves it alone. Two of these four are not new. Lesson 24 in A1 gave you what à and de do to an article and lesson 25 in A1 gave you what en does to a country's. What nobody has told you is that they are the same question asked four times.
theArticle.title: Three things a word can do to it

questions.a: The baker, and the aunt. Both of them are people. Everything else in the passage is a building, a town or a country, and every one of those takes something else.

sections.body: À folds the article in. En throws it out. Chez leaves it alone. Ask what the place IS before reaching for the word in front. A person takes chez. Everything else is a place, and its article decides the rest.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Four kinds of place and four answers. Three of them you already have, and the fourth is the one English gives you no help with at all. a person takes chez, as in chez Marie, a city takes à, as in à Paris, a country takes en, au, as in en France, a building takes à + le, as in au marché.
À folds the article in. En throws it out. Chez leaves it alone. In front of a le word: à gives au, de gives du, en gives en, chez gives chez le.

Chez takes a person and never a place. Chez Marie, chez le médecin, chez moi. Never a building, never a shop, never a town. Out of 283 sentences in this course that use the word, 0 put it in front of a building. Not one.
English says the baker's for the man and the bakery for the shop and lets you use either. French will not: the man takes chez and the shop takes à.

Two of these four are not new. Lesson 24 in A1 gave you what à and de do to an article and lesson 25 in A1 gave you what en does to a country's. What nobody has told you is that they are the same question asked four times.
Lesson 24 in A1 owns sur, sous, dans, devant and derrière, and this lesson has not touched one of them.

En also means how long something takes and dans also means how far ahead something is, and both of those are lesson 14 in A2, which is the very next lesson. And when you want to ask the way to somewhere rather than say you are going there, that is lesson 26 in A2.
Lesson 27 in A2 is called « Chez le médecin » and it is fourteen lessons ahead of you. Its whole title is this lesson's third card.

errorTriggers.description: Uses à, au or aux in front of a person, because every place the learner has ever been taught took one of those. It is not a slip: it is lesson 24 in A1 working exactly as taught, on the one kind of place lesson 24 in A1 never covered, and it is the error the scene opens on.

Uses chez in front of a building, usually the shop belonging to a person the learner has just met. The corpus has never done it once in 283 rows and learners do it constantly, because English says the baker's for both.
Folds the article after chez, producing chez au or chez du. A learner who does this has lesson 24 in A1's contraction rule and is applying it to the one word in the language that does not take it.

Keeps the article after en, producing en la France. The mirror image of the one above: en is the only one of the four that removes the article rather than doing something to it, and a learner who has learned to fold expects something to be left.

Puts en in front of a town or à in front of a country, which is the two rows of the grid that look alike being swapped. Both have a proper name and only one of them has an article, and that is the only difference between them.

grammarAssumed: The definite article and its four forms, introduced in a1.04
Noun gender, and that the article carries it, introduced in a1.03
The prepositions of place sur, sous, dans, devant and derrière, introduced in a1.21
The contraction of à and de with the definite article, including the two forms that do not contract, introduced in a1.21
en, au and aux with a country name, selected by gender and number, introduced in a1.22
de, du and des with a country name, introduced in a1.22
The partitive du, de la and de l', and the test that separates it from the locative du, introduced in a1.29
aller and venir in the present, introduced in a2.02
grammarIntroduced: chez as a preposition taking an exclusively animate complement, drilled rather than named
That chez is the only locative preposition in the language which neither contracts with nor suppresses a following definite article
The unification of the à-contraction of a1.21 with the au and aux of a1.22 as one operation rather than two rules, so that au Japon is analysed as à plus le Japon
The three-way opposition of article behaviour: contraction under à and de, suppression under en, and preservation under chez
A four-way categorisation of the complement (person, city, country, common noun) as the sole selector of the locative preposition, applied productively to complements not presented in the lesson
The lexical opposition between an agent noun and its place of business, which English neutralises, and the different prepositions the two require
That a bare toponym takes à with no article, and that the absence is lexical rather than the result of a suppression rule

acts.title: The right place, the wrong word
acts.milestone: You have seen both sets of words in the same position and know that only the words are new.

acts.title: Two words, and one question
acts.milestone: You can pick between lui and leur, and you know the ear will not settle the trap that is coming.

acts.title: The verbs that put a person behind à

acts.title: Three ways it goes wrong

recorded.desc: The two rows of words. Read le, la, les and then lui, lui, leur as SIX SEPARATE WORDS at an even pace, with no extra weight on any of them. The two sentences on the later cards are ONE TAKE each, both halves in it, so the learner hears one sentence becoming another rather than two being compared.

The à disappearing. ONE TAKE PER CARD holding both sentences. The à must be read at its natural weight, which is almost none, because a reader who leans on it teaches that the learner will hear it coming and the whole point is that they will not.
Six verb frames and six short sentences, read separately at a steady pace. Each frame ends « à quelqu'un » and the à must sound exactly as unstressed there as it does inside the sentence beside it.

The possessive against the pronoun. ONE TAKE PER CARD. « Je leur parle » and « Voici leurs clés » must be read with IDENTICAL treatment of the word leur: no lengthening, no s, nothing that would let a listener tell them apart, because the entire card says the difference is not there to hear.

The four trap cards, in order: « Je leurs parle. », « Je leur parle. », « Voici leurs clés. », « Voici leur maison. » The FIRST TWO MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE from one another. A reader who separates them makes the exercise measure something that is not in the language, and the learner will hear the performance rather than the trap.

lui in both jobs. ONE TAKE per card holding both sentences. In « Je parle avec lui » the lui carries the phrase stress and in « Je lui parle » it carries none, and that difference IS real and should be audible; it is the one contrast in this lesson a reader may lean into.

The wrap. ONE TAKE per card holding both sentences. Ne must NOT be given extra length: it is unstressed in speech and often barely there, and a recording that pronounces it carefully teaches a register nobody uses.
audioFirst. Four lines, ONE TAKE, one voice, no gaps that let the learner rehearse between them. Lines 1 and 2 differ by one word and that difference is the whole first question.

Thirteen lines, ONE VOICE, read at dictation pace with the same interval before each. « Voici leurs clés. » must be read with NO audible s, exactly as « Voici leur maison. » is: the whole point of the pair is that the letter is not there to hear, and a reader who distinguishes them makes the exercise measure something that is not there.

lessons.intro: Last lesson you learned where a small word goes: in front of the verb, never after it. That has not changed and it is not what today is about. There is a second set of small words that goes in exactly the same place, and which one a sentence wants is decided by the verb rather than by the meaning. Ten verbs put the person behind à, and six of them do it without English giving you the slightest warning: you phone someone, you answer someone, you ask someone, and French quietly insists on a word your own language never says.

behindA.body: Say the verb, then say à, then the person. Je parle à Marie. Je réponds à Paul. If the sentence takes that shape, the person behind à is what lui and leur stand in for. If the person sits behind à, the pronoun is lui or leur. The hard part is not the pronoun, it is knowing that the à is there at all, because English says nothing in that position for half these verbs. « I phone my mother » has no little word in it anywhere, and French insists on one. So this is not a rule you can work out from the meaning. It is a property of the verb, and the only way to hold it is to have met the verbs.
behindA.title: How to find the word this lesson is about

examples.note: The person is named, and the little word in front of them is the whole signal.
English answers Paul with nothing in between. French does not, and nothing in the English warned you.

theWrap.body: « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » is the line you have carried since the near future, and there is one verb in these sentences so the question of which verb never arises. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. That sentence is lesson 21's, word for word, and it holds here for the same reason: the pronoun belongs to the verb, so it goes where the verb goes. Ne outside both, pas after both. Nothing about this is new and it is on a screen because the sentence is longer now and a longer sentence is where a learner starts wondering whether the rule still applies.
theWrap.title: What ne and pas go round, and it has not changed

examples.note: Ne outside, then the pronoun and the verb together, then pas.
And with a two-word verb: ne, pronoun, first word, pas, second word.

noEnding.body: The second word never answers to lui or leur. Nothing is added. You met an ending on the second word last lesson, when the thing acted on came before the verb: Je l'ai vue, with an e on the end. That rule is about the thing acted on, and lui and leur are never the thing acted on. They are the person it is done TO, which is a different job, and the second word does not respond to them at all. Je lui ai parlé. Je leur ai parlé. Nothing goes on either one, ever, and there is nothing to remember beyond that. It is the one place in these two lessons where the answer is always the same.
noEnding.title: Why nothing is ever added after lui or leur

examples.note: One person, and parlé is bare.
Several people, and parlé is still bare. Nothing was ever going to change it.

onItsOwn.body: « what comes next decides » is lesson 5's line for this pattern and you have met it five times. Here it is again on lui. After a little word like avec, sans or pour, lui stands on its own and stays where English puts it. Je lui parle has a verb straight after it, so it is this lesson's word. Je parle avec lui has avec straight before it, so it is the other one, and it sits where English would put it rather than in front of the verb. Same three letters, two jobs, and the thing beside it settles which. Lesson 21 in A2 had exactly this one lesson ago, on le and la against the article.
onItsOwn.title: The sixth time this shape has come round, and lesson 5 in A2 named it

examples.note: A verb after it, so it belongs to the verb and goes in front of it.
Avec before it, so it stands alone and stays at the end, where English puts it.

sameSlot.body: « The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. » is lesson 21's line and it is true of these two words without a word changed. Je le vois. Je lui parle. Same position, same distance from the subject, and the only difference is which set of words you reached into. That is worth saying out loud rather than leaving you to notice, because a learner who thinks each new pair of pronouns has its own placement rule ends up with three rules where there is one. There is one, it was learned last lesson, and this lesson spends it.
sameSlot.title: The one thing you do not have to learn, and lesson 21 in A2 taught it

examples.note: Subject, word, verb, exactly as last lesson.
And in front of BOTH words when the verb arrives as two, which is also last lesson's.

twoWords.body: À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. One person takes lui and more than one takes leur, and that is the entire choice. The word lui is him or her. Going from one set to the other you lose the gender, which is one less thing to get right. Everything up to now has taught you that French cares about gender more as you go, not less, so this is worth stopping on: le and la told you which kind of person you meant and lui does not. It is a real loss of information and it is also a real saving. Nothing else about these two words changes for anything: not the subject, not the verb, not the tense.
twoWords.title: Two words, and the only question is how many people

examples.note: One person, so lui, and the sentence does not say whether it is a man or a woman.
More than one, so leur, and it never takes an s in this position.

theTarget.body: Six of these ten verbs put a person behind à and English puts nothing at all: phone someone, answer someone, ask someone, tell someone, show someone, give someone. Four of them put a person behind à and English says to, so you get those right without trying. There is no meaning that separates the two groups and no test you can run on the situation; it is a property of each verb, one at a time, and French speakers learned it the same way you are about to. That is the fair description and it is better than a rule that works six times out of ten, because a rule that nearly works is the one you keep applying.
theTarget.term: the person you are talking to
theTarget.title: Ten verbs, and there is no rule behind them

examples.note: Phone someone. Nothing in the English tells you an à is coming.
Write to them. English does tell you, and this is one of the four you already get right.

theirWord.body: You have had leur since lesson 20 in A1 and it meant their. That word is still there and this is a different one, spelled the same. The leur in front of a verb never takes an s. Ever. The possessive counts things and takes an s when there are several of them; this one counts nothing and never takes one, no matter how many people you are talking to. Lesson 20 in A1 handed you the test on the last card of its own lesson and it still works: a possessive has a thing behind it. Leur maison has a thing behind it. Je leur parle has a verb. That is the whole difference and you can see it without knowing a single term.
theirWord.title: The word lesson 20 in A1 gave you, doing something else

examples.note: A thing behind it, so it is the possessive, and it would take an s if there were several houses.
Both jobs in one sentence. The first has a verb behind it and can never take an s; the second has a house behind it.

theLittleWord.body: Lesson 13 in A2 spent a whole lesson on à in front of a place. That à stays in the sentence and folds itself into whatever follows. This one marks a person instead, and it does not stay at all. À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. Je parle à Marie becomes Je lui parle, and there is no à left anywhere. Learners keep it and write Je parle à lui, which is real French and means something else.
theLittleWord.title: Not the à lesson 13 in A2 taught you

beats.text: A Tuesday, the shared kitchen at work, and the kettle taking its time. You have been in this job three months and you have stopped rehearsing sentences before you say them, which is mostly a good thing.

Your colleague is waiting for the same kettle. Somebody from the other team has been off for a fortnight and everybody has been asking after him, and she asks you the question everybody has been asking.

beats.stage: She is not correcting you. What you said was a complete French sentence in which the thing phoned was an it, so she heard you phone an object and is asking which one. Nothing has broken. You are now in a conversation about a telephone.

sections.setting: The same kitchen, a week later, and this time the sentences mean what you meant. Every question is about somebody who is not in the room, which is the only situation this whole lesson is for.

cards.say: Je parle à Marie.
cards.back: If the person sits behind à, the pronoun is lui or leur. And there is no rule behind the list of verbs, which is why the list is the lesson.
cards.front: Which word tells you a person is behind à?

cards.say: Je lui parle.
cards.back: Je lui parle. À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it.
cards.front: « Je parle à Marie. » Say it without the name.

cards.say: Je leur parle.
cards.back: Leur. The leur in front of a verb never takes an s. Ever.

cards.say: Je lui parle.
cards.back: The word lui is him or her. Going from one set to the other you lose the gender, which is one less thing to get right.
cards.front: Is lui a man or a woman?

cards.say: Je lui parle.
cards.back: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Lesson 21's line, unchanged.

cards.say: Je ne lui parle pas.
cards.back: Je ne lui parle pas. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together.

cards.say: Voici leurs clés.
cards.back: « a possessive has a thing behind it ». Voici leurs clés counts keys. Je leur parle counts nothing and never could.
cards.front: Which leur can take an s?

cards.back: Yes, and lesson 5's test settles it: After a little word like avec, sans or pour, lui stands on its own and stays where English puts it.

sections.body: The exam has six rounds and much of it is typed or corrected rather than picked, because the one thing this lesson turns on is a letter you write and never say.

stats.v: 1. If the person sits behind à, the pronoun is lui or leur.
10, and six of them give you no warning in English at all.
0. All ten were already in your corpus, and four more were never listed.
1 of 2. Lui against leur, yes. Leur against leurs, never.

sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds of five. Much of it asks you to write, because the trap at the centre of this lesson is a letter nobody says.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Five on the one decision the verb makes for you.
rounds.label: Which set of words

questions.q: Fix it: « Je le téléphone. »
questions.why: Téléphoner puts the person behind à, so the word is lui. The place was already right, which is what makes this the hardest kind of mistake to hear yourself make.
accept: Je lui téléphone.

questions.q: « Je parle à Marie. » Type it again without the name.
questions.why: À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. Marie was behind à, so lui, and there is no à left in the sentence at all.
accept: Je lui parle.

questions.q: Which one is French?
questions.why: The first and the fourth use the row of words that stands in for a thing; the second leaves it at the end, where English puts it. Répondre puts the person behind à and the word goes in front of the verb.

questions.q: Fix it: « Je le demande. » You are asking a person, not asking for a thing.
questions.why: Demander à quelqu'un. English asks him with nothing in between, so nothing warned you, and that is precisely why demander is on the list rather than deducible from it.
accept: Je lui demande.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Lwee against luhr. One person against several, and that difference is genuinely audible, unlike the one this lesson actually turns on.

rounds.say: Five on a list rather than a rule.
rounds.label: Which verbs take à

questions.q: Which of these puts the person behind à?
questions.why: Téléphoner à quelqu'un. The other three take the person directly and belong to the row of words you learned last lesson. There is no meaning that separates them; it is a property of each verb.

questions.q: And which of these does NOT?
questions.why: Attendre quelqu'un, with nothing in between, and French agrees with English for once. The other three all want à and only one of them says so in English.

questions.q: The little word here is à with its accent, and the accent is the whole difference between it and the verb form a. Which sentence is right?
questions.why: This has to be a choice rather than something you type, because the app compares typed answers with the accents stripped and would accept the second one. The fourth is real French and means talking ABOUT her.

questions.q: « Je parle à mes parents. » Type it again without the names.
questions.why: Several people behind à, so leur, and no s on it in this position.
accept: Je leur parle.

questions.q: Fix it: « Nous obéissons lui. »
questions.why: A verb this lesson never listed, and the rule runs on it unchanged. English obeys him with nothing in between and French will not accept the direct version at all.
accept: Nous lui obéissons.

rounds.say: Five on a letter you write and never say.
rounds.label: The one that never grows

questions.q: Fix it: « Je leurs parle. »
questions.why: The leur in front of a verb never takes an s. Ever. A verb follows it, so it is this lesson's word: « a possessive has a thing behind it », and parle is not a thing.
accept: Je leur parle.

questions.q: Several friends, several sets of keys. Type: Here are their keys.
questions.why: Lesson 20 in A1's word and lesson 20 in A1's rule. The s counts the keys, never the friends, and there are several of both here.
accept: Voici leurs clés.

questions.q: Why does the leur in « Je leur parle. » never take an s?
questions.why: The test is « a possessive has a thing behind it ». There are several people in that sentence, which is exactly why the first option is tempting and why counting people is wrong.
opts: Because there is only one person
Because a verb follows it, so it is not the possessive
Because the verb is in the present

questions.q: Type: I do not write to them.
questions.why: The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. Ne outside both, pas after both, and still no s on leur.
accept: Je ne leur écris pas.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: The s is silent, which is the whole reason this trap exists. Nothing in the sound will ever tell you whether you got it right, so it is settled in writing or not at all.

rounds.say: Five on what sits beside it.
rounds.label: The same word, alone

questions.q: In which sentence does lui stand on its own rather than belong to the verb?
questions.why: After a little word like avec, sans or pour, lui stands on its own and stays where English puts it. In the other three a verb follows and the word goes in front of it.

questions.q: Fix it: « Je pars lui sans. »
questions.why: After sans the word stays where English puts it, at the end. This is the one place in the lesson where the position rule from last lesson does not apply, and what tells you is the little word in front.
accept: Je pars sans lui.

questions.q: « Je parle à lui. » What is wrong with it?
questions.why: Grammatical, and it is the stressed pronoun doing a different job: it singles the person out, the way English does with « I talk to HIM ». That is why it is the hardest of the three traps: nobody stops you, because there is nothing to stop.
opts: Nothing is wrong with it, and it means something else

questions.q: Type: I talk with him.
questions.why: After a little word like avec, sans or pour, lui stands on its own and stays where English puts it. Avec is in front, so lui goes at the end and nothing moves.
accept: Je parle avec lui.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: One person against several, and two different verbs as well, so there are two things separating these and both are audible.

rounds.say: Five on a tense you already have, and one thing that never happens in it.
rounds.label: In the past

questions.q: Type: I talked to them.
questions.why: The second word never answers to lui or leur. Nothing is added. The word goes in front of both halves of the verb, and parlé stays exactly as it is.
accept: Je leur ai parlé.

questions.q: Why is there no ending on parlé in « Je leur ai parlé. »?
questions.why: The second word never answers to lui or leur. Nothing is added. The first option is nearly a rule and is not this one: lesson 21 in A2 showed an ending appearing with the same first word, when the thing acted on came first.
opts: Because leur is the person it was done to, and the second word never answers to that

questions.q: Fix it: « Je l'ai parlé. » You are talking about a person.
questions.why: The right place and the wrong row of words, in the past. Parler puts the person behind à, so the word is lui.
accept: Je lui ai parlé.

questions.q: Lesson 20 in A2 showed you « Elle s'est lavé les mains. » with no ending on lavé. Why not?
questions.why: « When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending. » is lesson 21's line and it needs the thing acted on to be in front. Les mains comes after, so nothing goes on.
opts: Because the hands are named after the verb

questions.q: Type: I wrote to her.
questions.why: A different verb, and the second word is bare again. It is not a fact about parler.
accept: Je lui ai écrit.

rounds.say: Five that ask for more than one thing at once.
rounds.label: All of it

questions.q: « Je lui parle. » Make it negative. Type the whole sentence.
questions.why: The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. Ne outside, pas after, and the word stays where it was.
accept: Je ne lui parle pas.

questions.q: Fix it: « Je ne leurs écris pas. »
questions.why: The leur in front of a verb never takes an s. Ever. Écris follows it, so it is this lesson's word, and the wrap has nothing to do with it either way.
accept: Je ne leur écris pas.

questions.q: Which one is right?
questions.why: The first adds an ending that never comes; the third uses the row of words for a thing; the fourth splits the verb in half. Every part of the right answer is a rule you already had.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: The ending is silent, which lesson 1 in A2 taught you and this lesson leans on: nothing about the small word in front responds to the subject, and nothing about the verb ending is audible either.

questions.q: Fix it: « Je leurs montre la photo. »
questions.why: The leur in front of a verb never takes an s. Ever. There is a photo in the sentence and it sits after the verb, where things sit. The word in front is the people, and it can never grow an s.
accept: Je leur montre la photo.

sections.body: If the person sits behind à, the pronoun is lui or leur. There is no rule behind which verbs do that, which is why the list was the lesson and the two words were the easy half.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: If the person sits behind à, the pronoun is lui or leur.
À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. Six of the ten verbs give you no warning at all in English, and four of them say "to" and let you off.
« The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. » is lesson 21's line and it was true of these two words without a word changed. One position, two sets of words.
The word lui is him or her. Going from one set to the other you lose the gender, which is one less thing to get right.
The leur in front of a verb never takes an s. Ever. Lesson 20 in A1 gave you the test and it still works: a possessive has a thing behind it.
After a little word like avec, sans or pour, lui stands on its own and stays where English puts it. That is lesson 5's shape for the sixth time, and lesson 21 in A2 had the fifth.
The second word never answers to lui or leur. Nothing is added. Lesson 20 in A2 said the reason was waiting here and it was.

Next: lesson 23 in A2 takes à plus a thing into the same place, which is this lesson's little word with something that is not a person behind it. And two of these small words in one sentence is a question nobody has answered yet.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches into lesson 21 in A2's row of words for a person who sits behind à. « Je l'ai téléphoné. » THE error of this lesson, and it is worse than the one lesson 21 in A2 predicted because the sentence is grammatical: the position rule was applied perfectly and the result means something else, so nobody corrects it.

Keeps the à and writes « Je parle à lui. » Grammatical, and it is the stressed pronoun singling the person out rather than the plain sentence the learner was building. Lesson 13 in A2 taught an à that stays in the sentence and this one does not, so the habit is transferred rather than invented.

Puts lesson 20 in A1's s on a word that can never take one. « Je leurs parle. » The learner has had leur/leurs as an agreeing possessive since lesson 20 in A1 and there are several people in the sentence, so the s looks right and nothing in the sound argues.

Adds an ending to the second word after lui or leur, carrying lesson 21 in A2's preceding-object rule into a place it does not reach. « Je leur ai parlés. » lesson 21 in A2 taught an ending appearing with the same auxiliary one lesson ago, so this is a rule generalising rather than a rule forgotten.

grammarAssumed: The third-person direct object pronouns le, la and les and their obligatory preverbal placement, introduced in a2.06
Past participle agreement with a preceding direct object, introduced in a2.06
The possessive determiners leur and leurs and their agreement with the thing possessed, introduced in a1.17
The preposition à in front of a place, and its contraction with the definite article, introduced in a2.04 and a1.21
The present tense of regular -ER verbs and its silent endings, introduced in a2.01
Standard negation with ne … pas around a finite verb, introduced in a1.18
That ne … pas encloses the verb that changed rather than the one carrying the meaning, introduced in a2.19 and quoted by a2.05, a2.21, a2.22, a2.23 and a2.06
The passé composé as auxiliary plus past participle, introduced in a2.05
The futur proche, introduced in a2.19
The rising-intonation question, introduced in a1.19
grammarIntroduced: The third-person indirect object pronouns lui and leur, as a paradigm distinct from the direct object pronouns of a2.06 and from the homophonous possessive determiner of a1.17

The lexical class of verbs governing a dative complement in à, taught as an enumerated list of ten rather than as a semantic generalisation, with the four that English marks with "to" separated from the six it does not mark at all
That the à of the dative complement is absorbed by the pronoun and does not surface, in explicit contrast with the locative à of a2.04 which does
Neutralisation of the gender contrast in the third-person singular indirect form, so that lui covers both antecedents where le and la did not
That leur as an indirect object pronoun is invariable and never carries the plural -s of the homophonous possessive determiner, a distinction realised orthographically only
The stressed pronoun lui after a preposition, as the sixth instance of the one-form-two-jobs pattern named by a2.02, disambiguated by the element adjacent to it
That the past participle never agrees with an indirect object, which is the reason a2.23 named for the suspended agreement in « Elle s'est lavé les mains » and deferred to this unit
That ne … pas encloses the indirect clitic together with the finite verb, quoting a2.06 unchanged rather than extending it
Pronominal y and en are reserved entirely for a2.25, and the co-occurrence of two object pronouns in one clause is reserved beyond this unit

acts.title: Four seconds apart
acts.milestone: You know that the small word in front of the verb is what decides which first word comes next.

acts.title: Where everything lands
acts.milestone: Six positions in one order, and the six people who fill them.

acts.title: The little word decides
acts.milestone: You can build the whole form, for a verb the lesson never showed you, and put the ending on in writing.

acts.title: The two that go wrong
acts.milestone: One negation rule, five lessons long, and one sentence added to it.

recorded.desc: THE SAME TWO PEOPLE AS lesson 19 in A2's SCENE, A MONTH ON, AND THIS EXCHANGE IS GOING WELL UNTIL IT IS NOT. HIS FIRST LINE « Ce matin, j'ai lavé la voiture. » IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE SCENE AND IT MUST SOUND COMPLETELY ORDINARY. It is fluent, correct and unremarkable, and it is what makes the next one happen. Any weight on it teaches that something was already wrong. HER LINE « Et ce matin ? » IS AN ORDINARY FOLLOW-UP, warm and short. HIS SECOND LINE « Ce matin, je... j'ai... je me... » IS TWO REAL FALSE STARTS. The pauses are actual pauses and he is deciding, not performing hesitation. HIS THIRD LINE « J'ai levé à six heures. » IS SAID FLUENTLY AND WITH CONFIDENCE. This is the single most important instruction in the take: it is a complete, well-formed French sentence and he believes he has said what he meant. Any hesitation on it teaches that the error is audible, and the whole point of the scene is that it is not. HER LAST LINE « Tu as levé quoi ? » IS A GENUINE QUESTION rather than a correction. She is waiting to be told what he lifted. There is no note of doubt in it and nobody is embarrassed.
clipIds: Ce matin, j'ai lavé la voiture.
Ce matin, je... j'ai... je me...
Je me suis levé à six heures.

recorded.desc: THE THREE PAIRS, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, AND THIS IS THE TAKE THE LESSON RESTS ON. Six lines in this order: « J'ai lavé la voiture. » « Je me suis lavé. » « J'ai couché les enfants. » « Je me suis couché. » « J'ai réveillé mon frère. » « Je me suis réveillé. » THE VERB MUST SOUND IDENTICAL IN EACH PAIR. « lavé » is the same syllable in lines one and two and nothing about it may change; the same for « couché » and « réveillé ». The learner is being taught that the verb is not what moved. READ EACH PAIR AT THE SAME PACE AS ITS PARTNER. Slowing the second one hands the learner the answer for the wrong reason. DO NOT LEAN ON « me » OR ON « suis ». They are the two words that carry the whole lesson and a reading that marks them teaches that they are strange. They are not strange; they are simply there. RECORD ALL SIX AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE. Six recordings are six performances.

FOUR SHORT LINES, ONE TAKE, PLAINLY, AND NONE OF THEM IS BEING TAUGHT. « je me · tu te · il se · nous nous · vous vous · ils se » read as a list at an even pace, with a real boundary inside « nous nous » and « vous vous ». Then « levé · levée · levés · levées », WHICH MUST BE FOUR IDENTICAL SOUNDS. Not similar: identical. This is the card that claims the learner already owns the endings and the claim is that they sound the same. Then « Je me suis lavé. » and « Elle s'est souvenue de mon nom. », both entirely ordinary. THE WHOLE TAKE IS A CHECKLIST RATHER THAN A LESSON and should sound like somebody reminding you of something you know.
clipIds: Elle s'est souvenue de mon nom.

recorded.desc: ONE SENTENCE, SIX TIMES, AND IT IS THE SAME SENTENCE EVERY TIME: « Je ne me suis pas levé. » EVERY ROW OF THIS TABLE PLAYS THE WHOLE SENTENCE rather than its own word, because a word said on its own is not the word said in place. READ IT AT ORDINARY CONVERSATIONAL SPEED, ONCE, and let the slow speed do the rest. A reading that separates the six words teaches six words rather than one sentence. THE « ne » MUST BE AUDIBLE AND UNSTRESSED. It is the word whose POSITION the screen is about, so it cannot be swallowed the way ordinary speech swallows it, and it cannot be leaned on either. THERE IS NO PAUSE ANYWHERE INSIDE « ne me suis pas ». Those four words are one run.
clipIds: Je ne me suis pas levé.

recorded.desc: THE SIX PERSONS, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, IN THIS ORDER: « Je me suis levé tôt. » « Tu t'es levé tôt. » « Il s'est levé tôt. » « Nous nous sommes levés tôt. » « Vous vous êtes levés tôt. » « Ils se sont levés tôt. » THE VERB IS THE SAME SOUND IN ALL SIX and so is « tôt ». The only thing that changes is the two or three words at the front. LINES TWO AND THREE ELIDE AND MUST NOT BE BROKEN AT THE APOSTROPHE. « t'es » and « s'est » are each one syllable and a pause there teaches a boundary that is not in the language. THE DOUBLED WORDS IN LINES FOUR AND FIVE MUST NOT BE RUN TOGETHER. « Nous nous » is two words with a real boundary between them, at ordinary pace and with no emphasis on either. « sommes » IS /sɔm/ WITH A REAL M AND NO NASAL IN IT. It does not rhyme with « sont ». RECORD ALL SIX AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE.

THE TAKE THAT HAS TO PROVE A NEGATIVE, ONE VOICE, FOUR LINES: « Il s'est lavé. » « Elle s'est lavée. » « J'ai lavé la voiture. » « Je me suis lavé. » LINES ONE AND TWO MUST BE COMPLETELY IDENTICAL. Same speed, same weight, same length, same everything. The mission asks the learner to hear no difference and it only works if there is none, so these two are recorded in one breath and not spliced. LINES THREE AND FOUR ARE THE OPPOSITE INSTRUCTION AND THEY ARE IN THE SAME TAKE DELIBERATELY. They differ by a whole word and should be read at the same pace so that word is the only difference. DO NOT COMPENSATE. The temptation on line two is to help the learner by lengthening the ending. That is the exact thing the lesson says is impossible and doing it teaches a sound that is not in French.

THE EXCEPTION, ONE TAKE, FOUR LINES, AND NOTHING IN THE READING MAY MARK ANY OF THEM AS UNUSUAL: « Elle s'est lavée. » « Elle s'est lavé les mains. » « Elle s'est levée. » « Elle s'est brossé les dents. » ALL FOUR ARE ORDINARY, CORRECT FRENCH and the card's whole claim is that the second and fourth are not mistakes. A reading that hesitates on them argues the opposite. LINES ONE AND TWO ARE ONE SOUND UP TO « lavé » and then one of them continues. That is the only difference and it is the difference the learner is being asked to notice. THERE IS NO PAUSE BEFORE « les mains » OR « les dents ». The sentence runs straight through.

FOUR LINES, ONE TAKE, ENTIRELY PLAINLY: « Nous nous sommes dépêchés. » « Vous vous êtes reposés. » « Elle a lavé la voiture. » « Elle s'est lavée. » THE FIRST TWO CARRY NO TEACHING INTENT AT ALL. They are two ordinary sentences and the card's point is that nothing about them is special. LINES THREE AND FOUR ARE THE PAIR and they must be read at the same pace. The difference is « a lavé » against « s'est lavée » and the learner is meant to hear the first half change and the second half not. THE ENDING ON « lavée » IS SILENT AND MUST STAY SILENT. Line four ends on exactly the same sound as line three.

THE NEGATIVE, ONE TAKE, FOUR LINES: « Je me suis levé. » « Je ne me suis pas levé. » « Il ne s'est pas levé. » « Nous ne nous sommes pas levés. » NOT A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. All four are correct French. THE « ne » MUST BE AUDIBLE AND UNSTRESSED IN ALL THREE NEGATIVES. It is the word whose position the mission is about, so it cannot be swallowed and it cannot be leaned on. THERE IS NO PAUSE BETWEEN « ne » AND THE LITTLE WORD. « ne me » is one run and « ne s'est » is one run. A break there is exactly the reading that makes the error sound plausible. « pas » CLOSES STRAIGHT AFTER THE FIRST WORD and the second word follows it without a gap. The learner has to hear that the sentence does not stop at « pas ».
clipIds: Je ne me suis pas levé.
Nous ne nous sommes pas levés.

recorded.desc: THE AUDIO STEP OF THE TRAP, AND IT IS A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. Four lines, one take, in this order: « Je m'ai levé. » then « Je me suis levé tôt. », then « Je me suis lavé. » then « J'ai lavé la voiture. » READ THE FIRST LINE PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly. It is perfectly pronounceable and it is what a careful learner produces from a correct sentence they said four seconds earlier; a reading that signals the error teaches that the error announces itself, and it does not. DO NOT SEPARATE THE FIRST TWO LINES WITH A LONG PAUSE. The pair is the teaching and it works when the two sit against each other. LINES THREE AND FOUR ARE THE SECOND PAIR and the verb « lavé » is the same syllable in both. Nothing about it may change.

THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to rec-a2-23-silent: there the learner is comparing and here they are spelling, and a paired reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. MANY OF THESE END ON THE SAME SYLLABLE AND SEVERAL PAIRS ARE ONE SOUND END TO END. That is correct and must not be corrected for. « Il s'est lavé. » and « Ils se sont lavés. » differ in writing only, and the learner works out which from the two or three words at the front. THE FRONT OF THE SENTENCE IS WHERE ALL THE INFORMATION IS. « Il s'est », « Ils se sont », « Elle s'est », « Je me suis », « Tu t'es »: these must be clearly and evenly said, because they are the only thing distinguishing most of the thirteen. THE ELIDED FORMS ARE ONE SYLLABLE. « t'es » and « s'est » are not broken at the apostrophe. SAY IT THE WAY SOMEBODY WOULD SAY IT, at the pace of somebody dictating an address to a friend.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS FIVE SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same binôme from the opening scene and this time the exchange works. EVERY QUESTION IS ASKED WITHOUT INVERSION and should sound completely ordinary: « Tu t'es couché tard hier ? » is a statement with a question mark on it, which is what people say. HER OWN LINES CARRY THE STRUCTURE TWICE and neither may be marked or slowed. She is using it, not demonstrating it. THERE IS NO PAUSE INSIDE « t'es réveillé » OR « t'es couché ». The little word and the first word are one run.

Et tes collègues, ils sont arrivés à l'heure ?

lessons.intro: You can already say what you did yesterday, and you can already say what you do every morning with a small word in front of the verb. Putting those two together needs one fact and it is not the one people expect: the small word decides which of the two past helpers you reach for. Laver takes avoir and se laver takes être, and nothing about the meaning or the movement has a say in it. This is that fact, the order the words go in, and the ending that nobody can hear.

later.body: The same little words do a second job later, standing in for a thing rather than pointing back at the person. That is lesson 21 in A2 and lesson 22 in A2, and the reason the ending disappears on this screen is waiting there too. This is the only past you need for now. Lesson 17 in A2 gave you the second words and lesson 18 in A2 gave you the endings, and nothing after this changes either of them.
later.title: What is waiting after this

silent.body: « Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person. » is lesson 1's line, from the first lesson of this level, and lesson 18 in A2 quoted it for the same reason. Levé, levée, levés and levées are one sound. You cannot check this one by listening. All four spellings are the same sound, on every verb here, and lesson 18 in A2 had one verb where you could hear it. This lesson has none.
silent.title: Nothing here can be checked by ear

afterIt.body: When something is named straight after the second word, the ending goes away again. You will meet this and you are not being asked to produce it. Elle s'est lavée has nothing after it and takes the ending. Elle s'est lavé les mains names something, and it does not. You will read both and only the first one is being asked of you today.
afterIt.title: Something named after the second word

theWrap.body: Lesson 21 in A1 gave you two words either side of the verb: « Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. » lesson 15 in A2 said which verb: « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » lesson 19 in A2 added the little word: « Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. » And now there is a third word. The wrap goes round the little word and the first word. The second word sits outside it.
theWrap.title: It closes after the first word

onlyPast.body: In the present nothing on the end of the verb knows who the subject is. Only the extra word changes. That is lesson 19's sentence, and it is exactly what stops being true here: in the past there is a second word, and it does know. Lesson 28 in A1 gave you these verbs and neither of those lessons put an ending on one.
onlyPast.title: What the present did not do

firstWord.body: Lesson 16 in A2 gave you a past made of two words and lesson 18 in A2 gave you the choice between them. Every verb that carries the little word takes être, including the ones that take avoir without it. Laver takes avoir on its own and se laver takes être, and the only thing that changed is the little word in front.
firstWord.title: It is être, and nothing else decides it

theEnding.body: Add nothing for a man on his own, e for a woman, s for more than one, and es for more than one woman. You cannot check this one by listening. All four spellings are the same sound, on every verb here, and lesson 18 in A2 had one verb where you could hear it. This lesson has none. So this is the one thing in the lesson you can only get right in writing, and it is the reason the dictée is the longest part.
theEnding.title: Four spellings, one sound

littleWord.body: Lesson 19 in A2 taught you that about half the verbs in a day carry a small word between the person and the verb, and that it is the person said a second time: « The pronoun changes with the subject, because it is the subject. » In the past it does one more thing. If the little word is there, the first word is être. It is the only part of the sentence you have to look at.
littleWord.title: The one that decides everything else

secondWord.body: « After être, the second word ends like a describing word. » is lesson 18's line and it has not changed here. Add nothing for a man on his own, e for a woman, s for more than one, and es for more than one woman. Lesson 17 in A2 gave you the second words themselves, group by group: « Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in. »

sections.body: If the little word is there, the first word is être. Every verb that carries the little word takes être, including the ones that take avoir without it. Laver takes avoir and se laver takes être; coucher takes avoir and se coucher takes être. The verb does not decide it, the meaning does not decide it, and whether anybody moved does not decide it.
sections.title: The rule, in one line

sections.body: Add nothing for a man on his own, e for a woman, s for more than one, and es for more than one woman. You cannot check this one by listening. All four spellings are the same sound, on every verb here, and lesson 18 in A2 had one verb where you could hear it. This lesson has none. And after avoir nothing goes on at all, in any person, which is lesson 18's rule and has not changed. When something is named straight after the second word, the ending goes away again. You will meet this and you are not being asked to produce it.

sections.body: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. The wrap goes round the little word and the first word. The second word sits outside it. Je me suis lavé becomes Je ne me suis pas levé. And ne never shortens here, in any person, because every form of the little word starts on a consonant.

beats.text: The same language exchange, a month on. You can tell her what you did yesterday now, and you have been doing it all evening without a single stumble.

beats.en: This morning, I washed the car.

beats.speaker: Ton binôme

beats.en: I lifted at six.
beats.fr: J'ai levé à six heures.
beats.stage: And it lands on the one he has just used. It worked four seconds ago on the same kind of sentence, so there is no reason in his head for it not to work now.

cards.fr: Elle s'est cassé le bras en tombant du vélo.
cards.sub: She broke her arm falling off her bike.

sections.title: When The Ending Goes Away

sections.say: Three cards on why the rule is about the small word and not about what the sentence is saying.
sections.hint: Nobody hurries themselves, and it still takes être.

cards.fr: Nous nous sommes dépêchés
cards.body: Lesson 19 in A2 taught that some of these point at nothing at all. The action does not come back to anybody and the little word is obligatory anyway, and it still means être.
cards.head: Nobody hurries themselves
cards.label: se dépêcher

cards.fr: Vous vous êtes reposés
cards.body: Lesson 18 in A2 gave you fifteen verbs that take être and twelve of them move. Resting is not one of them, and it does not need to be: the little word decided this before the meaning got a vote.
cards.head: And nothing here moves
cards.label: se reposer

cards.fr: Elle a lavé la voiture · Elle s'est lavée
