whatComesNext.body: Lesson 5 in A2 gave this pattern its name on venir de: one form, two jobs, and the word after it settles which. Here it is three words instead of two. « Il y a » with a thing behind it says that thing exists. « Il y a » with a measurement behind it, and nothing after the measurement, says how far back. Nothing about the three words changes and nothing ever will, so there is no spelling to learn and no sound to catch. There is only the next word.
whatComesNext.title: You have had this shape before

examples.note: A measurement, and then a full stop. So it is a distance back.

presentNotPerfect.body: English says I have lived here. French says I live here, and adds depuis to say since when. The verb never moves. That is the whole of it, and it is the single place at this level where translating word for word produces something a French listener cannot decode. « J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans » does not sound like a mistake to them; it sounds like you moved out three years ago, which is the opposite of what you meant. Across every published French sentence in this app, 560 hold depuis and 31 of those sit beside a past tense. 447 hold pendant and 97 do.
presentNotPerfect.title: The verb does not move

measurementThenStop.body: A measurement and then a full stop means ago. A time word still being described is a thing. That last clause is not a decoration. « Il y a une heure » is an hour ago and « il y a une heure de retard » is an hour of delay, and the first four words are identical. In this app's published French, 33 sentences use it for ago and 130 use it for there is, and only two put anything at all after the measurement.

sections.text: Je suis à Lyon depuis six mois. J’habite dans le quartier de la Guillotière, et je travaille dans une école depuis le mois de mars. Le matin, je prends le tram : il passe toutes les six minutes, alors je ne pars jamais plus de dix minutes avant le cours. Le soir, je lis pendant une heure, toujours à la même table du même café. Il y a un homme qui vient tous les jours à la même heure, et il ne parle à personne. Ma voisine me demande souvent depuis quand je suis ici. Je réponds « depuis six mois », et elle dit toujours la même chose : « Déjà ? »
sections.title: Six Months In Lyon

glossary.note: A part of a city. Nothing about it is this lesson.
How often, rather than how long. That is the frequency system and it belongs to another lesson.
Joins a fact to what follows from it.
From lesson 21 in A1, the negation lesson, and it is here so the passage has one sentence that is not about time.
What people say when six months sounds short to them and long to you.

questions.a: Being in Lyon since six months ago, and working at a school since March. Both are still true, so French keeps the verb in the present. English would use "have been" for both and move the verb; French does not.
questions.q: Every verb in this passage is in the present tense, and two of the sentences are about things that started in the past. Which two, and what makes the present tense correct in both?

questions.a: The hour of reading has both ends on it. It starts, it finishes, and it happens again the next evening. Everything the passage uses depuis for is still going.
questions.q: The passage uses depuis three times and pendant once. What is different about the sentence with pendant in it?

questions.a: It exists. The word after it is un, which is an article and not a measurement, and that settles it before you get to the noun.
questions.q: « Il y a un homme qui vient tous les jours. » Which of the two jobs is il y a doing here, and how can you tell without reading the rest?

questions.a: That she expects the thing to still be true. Depuis quand can only be asked about something that is still running, so the answer will be in the present tense whatever it turns out to be.
questions.q: The neighbour asks « depuis quand ». What does that question tell you about the answer she is expecting?

sections.body: Before you pick the word, ask whether the thing is still running, finished, ahead of you or behind you. The word follows from the answer and never from the English. The clock and the calendar gave you when on a dial and when on a page. These five give you when measured from right now, forwards and backwards, and how wide a stretch was.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: depuis, pendant, il y a, dans, en. Five words, and every one of them wants a different shape of time behind it. Pick the shape first and the word picks itself.
If it is still happening, French keeps it in the present. English says I have lived here. French says I live here, and adds depuis to say since when. The verb never moves.
Both of these come out as "for" in English and they are not interchangeable in French. Pendant closes the stretch. Depuis leaves it open.

You have had this shape before. Lesson 5 in A2 called it what comes next decides, on venir de, and it is the same job here. A measurement and then a full stop means ago. A time word still being described is a thing.
Dans says when it starts. En says how long it took. One of them is a point and the other is a length, and English uses "in" for both.

Il y a for "ago" wants a past tense, and you do not have one yet. It arrives in lesson 16 in A2, and this is the phrase it will arrive holding. French says « je pars dans dix minutes » with a present tense, and that is correct as it stands. The other way of saying it is lesson 15 in A2, which is next.

Lesson 15 in A1 gave you the clock and lesson 13 in A1 gave you the calendar. Lesson 13 in A2 gave you en and dans in front of a place yesterday, and its own line was: À folds the article in. En throws it out. Chez leaves it alone.

errorTriggers.description: Picks the wrong one of the five, usually by translating the English preposition rather than by looking at what the time is doing. "For" gives depuis or pendant, "in" gives dans or en, and English does not distinguish either pair.
Puts the verb in a past tense after depuis, which is the English perfect being translated word for word. The single biggest interference point at this level and the reason this lesson exists.
Swaps the two words that both come out as "for". Pendant closes the stretch and depuis leaves it open, and a learner working from the English has nothing to decide on.

Reads il y a as "there is" where it means ago, or the other way round. The two jobs share all three words and only the next one settles it, which is doctrine §B.7's shape and the second of its four instances.
Merges the two that both come out as "in". Dans is when it starts and en is how long it takes, and learners produce the wrong one about half the time.

grammarIntroduced: depuis with a present-tense verb to express a situation begun in the past and still obtaining, against the English present perfect which the learner will otherwise calque
depuis taking either a point of origin or a span, with no change to the verb in either case
The opposition between depuis and pendant as open and closed duration, and that English neutralises it under a single preposition
pendant as a bounded span compatible with any tense
il y a plus a completed measurement of time as a deictic point in the past, against il y a plus a nominal as an existential, and that the following constituent is the sole disambiguator
That the existential reading survives a temporal noun where that noun is itself modified, which bounds the rule
dans plus a span as a future point, expressed with a present-tense verb at this trail position
en plus a span as the time taken to complete an action, against dans as the time until it begins
The temporal senses of en and dans as distinct from the locative senses introduced in a2.04

lessons.intro: A screen tells you to do something and there is nobody to ask. Then you have to explain what it said to a person who cannot see it. This lesson is both halves, and the one thing that runs through them: every tech word in French has more than one name, and which one you use says who you think is listening.

menu.body: A list of options read out by a machine, each one ending in a number to press. It plays once at its own speed and there is nobody to ask. Listen for the number and for the one word that tells you which option is yours, not for the whole sentence.
menu.title: The recorded menu

examples.note: The word is connexion. The number is 1.
The word is technicien. The number is 3.

wifi.body: French took the word and not the pronunciation. It is two clean syllables, wee then fee, with the stress on the second. Say it the English way to a French technician and the sentence stops there, which is a strange way to lose a conversation about a router.
wifi.title: Said weefee, not why-fye

examples.note: The respelling is the whole lesson.

voice.body: One object, more than one name, and the name you pick says who you think you are speaking to. A screen, a support agent and a friend do not use the same word for the same thing. Nothing here is more polite than anything else; two of the three are simply wrong for the person in front of you.
voice.title: Who the word is talking to

examples.note: What an agent says, and what Canada writes.
What a friend in France says.

screen.body: An interface tells you to do things. It does not ask, it does not explain, and it will not say it again differently if you did not follow. These are fixed strings: learn each one whole, with what it means you should do next, the way you learned bonjour.
screen.title: What a screen says to you

examples.note: It wants the code, now, in that box.

borrowed.body: French borrows an English tech word, official French translates it, and Quebec resists hardest. Some words go one way only. Some have both a borrowed and a translated form, and then which one you use is a regional signal rather than a matter of being right.
borrowed.title: Taken, translated, or both

examples.note: Translated, and the English word is not used.

invisible.body: In a shop you can point. On a support line the other person has nothing but what you say, so you have to give four things nobody asks you for: what happened, when it started, what you already tried, and what the message said. That is the whole call.
invisible.title: They cannot see your screen

beats.text: Nine at night. A bank site, a laptop, and a password that worked yesterday. Third attempt. The page reloads and something small and grey appears under the box.

beats.en: Try again later
beats.fr: Réessayez plus tard
beats.stage: It does not say why. It does not say how much later.
beats.respell: [ray-ay-say-YAY plü TAR]
beats.speaker: The screen

beats.text: He calls the number at the bottom of the page. A woman answers on the fourth ring. She has his account open. She cannot see his screen.

beats.en: What exactly is showing on the screen?
beats.fr: Qu'est-ce qui s'affiche exactement à l'écran ?
beats.respell: [kess kee sa-FEESH eg-zak-tuh-MAHⁿ ah lay-KRAHⁿ]
beats.speaker: The agent

beats.prompt: He has one sentence. Which one does he give her?

options.en: It is not working.
options.fr: Ça ne marche pas.
options.respell: [sa nuh MARSH PAH]

options.en: The site is rejecting my password.
options.fr: Le site refuse mon mot de passe.
options.respell: [luh SEET ruh-FÜZ mohⁿ moh duh PASS]

followUp.works: She types for four seconds and tells him the account locked after three attempts. Twenty minutes.
followUp.breaks: What is not working? She has to ask four more questions to get where one sentence would have taken her.

beats.body: In a shop you can point at the thing. On a support line there is nothing to point at, so the sentence has to carry the whole screen. Both are true. Only one is any use to her.
beats.coach: Say what the screen said, and say what you did before it said it. That is the call.

sections.say: L'écran vous donne un ordre, l'agent vous pose une question, l'ami vous parle. Trois voix, un seul appareil.

rows.say: Saisissez votre code

detail.say: Saisissez votre code

rows.say: Appuyez sur Entrée

detail.say: Appuyez sur Entrée
detail.body: Appuyer sur is to press a key or a button. Entrée is the return key, and French keyboards print the word rather than an arrow.
detail.title: Appuyez sur Entrée

rows.say: Veuillez patienter

detail.say: Veuillez patienter
detail.body: The politest thing a machine says, and the one that asks for the least. It is working. Pressing anything now starts it again.
detail.title: Veuillez patienter

rows.say: Sélectionnez une option

detail.say: Sélectionnez une option

detail.title: Sélectionnez une option

rows.say: Cliquez sur le lien

detail.say: Cliquez sur le lien
detail.body: Usually the link is in a message rather than on the page you are reading. Look at your mail before you look for it here.

rows.say: Réessayez plus tard

detail.body: The one from the scene. It never says how much later, and it usually means something at their end is busy or your account is locked for a while.

sections.title: Six things a screen says

sections.say: L'écran vous donne un ordre, l'agent vous pose une question, l'ami vous parle. Trois voix, un seul appareil.
sections.hint: Six strings. Each one is one thing to do.

cards.fr: Saisissez votre code
cards.body: Literally: take in your code. What it wants: the six digits, in the box, now.
cards.head: Saisissez votre code
cards.label: the box is waiting

cards.fr: Appuyez sur Entrée
cards.body: Literally: press on Enter. What it wants: that key, not the button on screen.
cards.head: Appuyez sur Entrée
cards.label: the key with the word on it

cards.fr: Veuillez patienter
cards.body: Literally: be so good as to be patient. What it wants: nothing at all from you.
cards.head: Veuillez patienter
cards.label: the politest one

cards.fr: Sélectionnez une option
cards.body: Literally: select an option. What it wants: one of them, before it will go on.
cards.head: Sélectionnez une option
cards.label: a list, none of it chosen

cards.fr: Cliquez sur le lien
cards.body: Literally: click on the link. What it wants: the one it just sent you.
cards.head: Cliquez sur le lien
cards.label: usually in a message

cards.fr: Réessayez plus tard
cards.body: Literally: try again later. What it wants: you, gone, for an amount of time it will not name.
cards.head: Réessayez plus tard
cards.label: no number given

sections.title: Four prompts, once each

questions.q: Which one is telling you to do nothing?
questions.why: Patienter is to wait. It is the only one of the four that asks nothing of you at all.

questions.q: Which one wants something typed?
questions.why: Saisir is what a form does with a value it takes in. There is a box and it is empty.

questions.q: You heard the third one. What is on the screen?
questions.why: An option is one of several. If you are being asked to choose one, several of them are showing.

questions.q: The fourth one gives you a number of minutes.
questions.why: It never does, and that is the complaint people have about it. Plus tard is as precise as it gets.

lines.fr: Pour un problème de connexion, tapez 1.

sections.title: The recorded menu

questions.q: Your password is refused. Which number?
questions.why: Oublié is the word to listen for. A refused password and a forgotten one go to the same place.

questions.q: You want a person, not a machine. Which number?
questions.why: Parler à is the giveaway. It is the only option with a human being at the end of it.

questions.q: You missed it. What do you press?
questions.why: Réécouter is re plus écouter, to listen again. Nine is where menus usually put it.

questions.q: The wifi is down at your flat. Which number?
questions.why: Connexion. Not a technician yet: option 3 is for when the first one has not fixed it.

questions.q: How many times will it say all this?
questions.why: Once. That is why option 9 exists, and it is exactly what a listening exam does to you.

sections.say: L'écran vous donne un ordre, l'agent vous pose une question, l'ami vous parle. Trois voix, un seul appareil.
sections.text: AVIS AUX USAGERS. En raison d'une maintenance, le service de demande en ligne est indisponible du vendredi 18 h au lundi 8 h. Pendant cette période, il n'est pas possible de créer un compte ni de déposer un dossier. Les dossiers déjà déposés sont conservés et seront traités normalement. Si vous avez reçu un code de vérification avant le vendredi 18 h, ce code reste valable pendant sept jours. Pour toute question urgente, veuillez appeler le 3939 du lundi au vendredi. Nous vous remercions de votre compréhension.
sections.title: The notice on the portal

glossary.note: The word a French service uses instead of down. It says nothing about why.
Borrowed straight from English, and pronounced the French way: [mehⁿ-tuh-NAHⁿSS].
Literally to put down. It is the verb every French administration uses for handing in a file.
The whole bundle of papers about you. Not a folder on a computer, in this sentence.
Nothing you already sent has been lost. This is the sentence people miss.
Still good, still usable. A ticket, a code and a passport are all valable.
What a public service calls the people who use it. A shop would say clients.
The closing formula. It means the notice is over, not that anything will be explained.

questions.a: Yes. Les dossiers déjà déposés sont conservés, and they will be processed as normal.
questions.q: You started an application on Thursday. Is it still there?

questions.a: No. The outage runs from Friday 18h to Monday 8h, and creating an account is named as one of the two things you cannot do.
questions.q: It is Saturday afternoon. Can you create an account?

questions.a: No. A code received before Friday 18h stays valid for seven days.
questions.q: Your verification code arrived on Thursday evening. Is it dead?

questions.a: The 3939 number, but only Monday to Friday. So on a Saturday the notice offers nothing at all, which it does not say out loud.
questions.q: It is genuinely urgent and it is Saturday. What does the notice offer?

sections.hint: Top line to the agent. Bottom line to your friend. Same screen both times.

cards.fr: FRIEND Ça bugue depuis hier.
cards.body: Bugue is fine with a friend and wrong with an agent. Marcher is safe with both.
cards.head: AGENT Ça ne marche plus depuis hier.

cards.fr: FRIEND Mon ordi rame.
cards.body: Two words shorter and two registers down. Ordi is ordinateur with the end bitten off.
cards.head: AGENT Mon ordinateur est très lent.
cards.label: it is slow

cards.fr: FRIEND Je te l'envoie par mail.
cards.body: Vous and courriel travel together. Tu and mail travel together. Mixing them is the error.
cards.head: AGENT Je vous envoie ça par courriel.
cards.label: I will send it

cards.fr: FRIEND T'as essayé de le redémarrer ?
cards.body: T'as is tu as, said fast. Write it out to an agent and it reads as a text message.
cards.head: AGENT Vous avez essayé de redémarrer ?
cards.label: have you tried restarting

cards.fr: FRIEND Tu peux m'envoyer une capture ?
cards.body: The words barely change. The pronoun does all the work, and it does all of it.
cards.head: AGENT Pouvez-vous m'envoyer une capture ?

sections.title: Marked in both directions

errors.why: Reasonable, because email is what half the internet says and nobody in France would blink. In Quebec courriel is the ordinary word and the borrowed one reads as careless.
errors.right: Je vous envoie mon courriel.
errors.wrong: Je vous envoie mon email. (to an agent in Montreal)

errors.why: Reasonable, because courriel is the official term and being correct is usually safe. Here it is not: it is the word their bank uses and it lands as a joke.
errors.right: Envoie-moi un mail.
errors.wrong: Envoie-moi un courriel. (to a friend in Paris)

errors.why: Reasonable, because French really did take cliquer, scanner and zoomer the same way. This one it did not: télécharger arrived first and holds the ground completely.
errors.right: Je vais télécharger le fichier.
errors.wrong: Je vais downloader le fichier.

errors.why: Reasonable, because so many device words came straight across. Ordinateur is the one French built itself, and it is the borrowing that never happened.
errors.right: Mon ordinateur ne marche pas.
errors.wrong: Mon computer ne marche pas.

errors.why: Reasonable, because everybody drops the ne out loud and you will hear it dropped all day. On the phone to somebody official it is the one place the missing word is heard.
errors.right: Ça ne marche pas.
errors.wrong: Ça marche pas. (to a support agent)

errors.why: Reasonable, because mél is printed on French forms next to Tél. It is an abbreviation for writing, not a word for saying, and said aloud it is the same sound as mail anyway.
errors.right: Mon mail ne marche pas.
errors.wrong: Mon mél ne marche pas. (to anybody, out loud)

turns.ai: Service technique, bonjour. Quel est le problème ?
turns.en: Technical support, hello. What is the problem?

alts.en: Hello. I cannot log in.
alts.fr: Bonjour. Je n'arrive pas à me connecter.

alts.en: Hello. My account is locked, I think.
alts.fr: Bonjour. Mon compte est bloqué, je crois.

turns.user: Bonjour. Le site refuse mon mot de passe.
turns.userEn: Hello. The site is rejecting my password. (What happened, in one sentence)

turns.ai: Depuis quand est-ce que ça ne marche plus ?
turns.en: How long has it not been working?

alts.en: It has not worked for two days.
alts.fr: Ça fait deux jours que ça ne marche plus.

alts.en: Since last night, around ten.
alts.fr: Depuis hier soir, vers vingt-deux heures.

turns.user: Ça s'est bloqué ce matin.
turns.userEn: It froze this morning. (When)

turns.ai: Qu'est-ce qui s'affiche exactement à l'écran ?
turns.en: What exactly is showing on the screen?

alts.en: The screen is showing an error message.
alts.fr: L'écran affiche un message d'erreur.

alts.en: It says "Try again later".
alts.fr: Il y a écrit « Réessayez plus tard ».

turns.user: Le message dit que le code a expiré.
turns.userEn: The message says the code has expired. (What the screen said, in its words)

turns.ai: Vous avez essayé de redémarrer l'appareil ?
turns.en: Have you tried restarting the device?

alts.en: Yes, twice, and it is the same.
alts.fr: Oui, deux fois, et c'est pareil.

alts.en: No, not yet. Shall I do it now?
alts.fr: Non, pas encore. Je le fais maintenant ?

turns.user: J'ai déjà essayé de redémarrer.
turns.userEn: I have already tried restarting it. (What you tried, before she suggests it again)

turns.ai: Je vais vérifier votre compte, ne quittez pas.
turns.en: I am going to check your account, please hold.

alts.en: All right. How long does that take?
alts.fr: D'accord. Ça prend combien de temps ?

alts.en: Fine. Can I stay on the line?
alts.fr: Très bien. Je peux rester en ligne ?

turns.user: D'accord. C'est quoi, le délai ?
turns.userEn: All right. How long will it take? (Now you ask. This is the turn the exam scores)

turns.ai: Votre code arrive dans deux minutes par courriel.
turns.en: Your code will arrive in two minutes by email.

alts.en: Thank you. And if I do not get it?
alts.fr: Merci. Et si je ne le reçois pas ?

alts.en: Thank you. Where exactly do I enter it?
alts.fr: Merci beaucoup. Je le saisis où, exactement ?

turns.user: Merci. Je dois faire quoi maintenant ?
turns.userEn: Thank you. What do I need to do now? (Ask again. Never leave with only half of it)

turns.ai: Cliquez sur le lien dans le courriel, puis saisissez le code.
turns.en: Click the link in the email, then enter the code.

alts.en: Perfect, thank you very much. Have a good evening.
alts.fr: Parfait, merci beaucoup. Bonne soirée.

alts.en: All right, got it. Thank you, goodbye.
alts.fr: D'accord, c'est noté. Merci, au revoir.

turns.user: Très bien. Merci de votre aide, bonne soirée.

turns.ai: Salut, ça va ? Tu as l'air énervé.
turns.en: Hi, you all right? You seem annoyed.

alts.en: Hi. My account is locked, it is driving me mad.
alts.fr: Salut. Mon compte est bloqué, ça me rend fou.

alts.en: I am fine. Well, the bank site is not working.
alts.fr: Ça va. Enfin, le site de la banque marche pas.

turns.user: Salut. Le site de la banque, ça bugue depuis ce matin.
turns.userEn: Hi. The bank site has been playing up since this morning. (Same fault, other voice)

turns.ai: T'as essayé de le redémarrer ?
turns.en: Have you tried restarting it?

alts.en: Yes, obviously. It makes no difference.
alts.fr: Oui, évidemment. Ça change rien.

alts.en: Not yet. You think that might work?
alts.fr: Pas encore. Tu crois que ça peut marcher ?

turns.user: Ouais, deux fois. Mon ordi rame aussi, en plus.
turns.userEn: Yeah, twice. My computer is crawling as well, on top of that.

turns.ai: Ça me le fait aussi depuis hier. Ils ont une panne, je pense.

alts.en: Seriously? Right, it is not me then.

alts.en: Oh yeah? They said nothing on the phone.

turns.user: Ah, tu vois. J'ai appelé, ils m'ont rien dit.

alts.en: OK, I will do that right now.
alts.fr: Ok, je te fais ça tout de suite.

alts.en: Hang on, I am sending it now.
alts.fr: Attends, je te l'envoie là.

turns.user: Ouais, je te l'envoie par mail.
turns.userEn: Yeah, I will send it to you by email. (mail, not courriel. He is not your bank)

turns.ai: Ok. Et ils t'ont dit quoi, au téléphone ?
turns.en: OK. And what did they tell you, on the phone?

alts.en: Nothing useful. Just to wait.
alts.fr: Rien d'utile. Juste d'attendre.

alts.en: That the code had expired. Great.
alts.fr: Que le code avait expiré. Super.

turns.user: De réessayer plus tard. Ça m'avance pas beaucoup.

sections.say: L'écran vous donne un ordre, l'agent vous pose une question, l'ami vous parle. Trois voix, un seul appareil.
sections.body: You can do what a French screen tells you without translating it first, you can hear a recorded menu once and know which number to press, and you can describe a fault to somebody who has nothing to look at. The last thing is the one to check: when you said it to the agent and then said it again to your friend, did the words change? If they did not, the lesson has not landed yet, and the two conversations in act 5 are the place to go back to.
sections.title: Where you stand

questions.q: A French friend, out loud, in a café. Which one?
questions.why: Mail is what is said in France. The other two are correct French and both sound like paperwork here.

questions.q: A support agent in Montreal, on the phone. Which one?
questions.why: Courriel is the ordinary word in Quebec and it is never wrong with an agent anywhere.

questions.q: A government form, printed, with a box next to it. Which one?
questions.why: What something written calls it. Nobody says the four syllables out loud unless they are reading them.

questions.q: Which of these is wrong in BOTH directions?
questions.why: Mail in Montreal is marked, and courriel to a Paris friend is marked the other way. Most of the lexicon carries no voice at all.

questions.q: « Mon ordi rame. » Who are you talking to?
questions.why: Ordi is a clipped word and ramer is familiar. Both are fine with a friend and neither belongs on a support line.
opts: a technician you have never met

questions.q: Listen. Who is speaking?
questions.say: Votre code arrive dans deux minutes par courriel.
questions.why: A person, using vous and the official word. A machine would not say votre code arrive, and a friend would have said mail.

questions.q: Listen. Who is speaking?
questions.say: Veuillez patienter
questions.why: Veuillez is the politest opening in French and almost nobody uses it out loud. On a screen it is ordinary.

questions.q: You are texting a French friend about an email. Write the word, with its article.
questions.why: The France-standard spoken form, and the one this lesson scores. Courriel would be correct French and the wrong voice.
accept: un mail
le mail
mail
questions.answer: un mail

questions.q: « Veuillez patienter ». What do you do?
questions.why: It is working and it is asking you for nothing. Pressing anything now starts it over.

questions.q: « Sélectionnez une option ». What is on the screen?
questions.why: An option is one of several, so several are showing. That is usually why the page will not go on.

questions.q: « Cliquez sur le lien ». Where is the link, usually?
questions.why: Almost always in the mail or the text that arrived a second ago, not on the page you are reading.
opts: at the top of this page
in a message it just sent you

questions.q: Which of these is the screen reporting rather than asking?
questions.why: It has already happened and there is nothing to press. The other two are jobs with something waiting.

questions.q: « Réessayez plus tard ». How much later?
questions.why: It never says, and that is the complaint everybody has about it. Plus tard is as precise as it gets.

questions.q: Listen. What does it want you to do?
questions.say: Saisissez votre code
questions.why: Saisir is what a form does with a value it takes in. There is a box and it is empty.

questions.q: The screen wants you to wait. Write the two words it uses.
questions.why: The politest thing a machine says, and the one that asks for the least.
accept: veuillez patienter
questions.answer: Veuillez patienter

questions.q: The screen wants your code. Write the three words it uses.
questions.why: Saisir belongs to forms and to almost nothing else. It is why the string is worth learning whole.
accept: saisissez votre code
questions.answer: Saisissez votre code

questions.q: The agent cannot see your screen. Which sentence is worth saying?
questions.why: All three are true. Only one of them tells somebody with nothing to look at what actually happened.
opts: Le site refuse mon mot de passe.

questions.q: She asks « Depuis quand ? ». What is she after?
questions.why: Depuis is a starting point. She wants the time, and it is one of the four things a support call always needs.

questions.q: Which of these four does a support call always need?
questions.why: What happened, when, what you already tried, and what the screen said. The exact wording of the message is the one people leave out.

questions.q: You have already restarted it. When do you say so?
questions.why: Say it up front and you save the two minutes she was going to spend asking. It is one of the four.
opts: when she asks you to restart it

questions.q: Listen. Which number do you press?
questions.say: Pour parler à un technicien, tapez 3.
questions.why: Parler à is the giveaway. It is the only option on that menu with a person at the end of it.

questions.q: It stopped working this morning. Write it, starting with Ça.
questions.why: Bloqué is what people actually say about a screen that stopped. It is more use to her than ne marche pas.
accept: Ça s'est bloqué ce matin
Ca sest bloque ce matin
ça s'est bloqué ce matin.
questions.answer: Ça s'est bloqué ce matin

questions.q: Too vague for somebody who cannot see it. Write a sentence she can use.
questions.why: Name the thing and name what it did. The correction is not grammar, it is how much of the screen the sentence carries.
accept: Le site refuse mon mot de passe.
Le site refuse mon mot de passe
questions.answer: Le site refuse mon mot de passe.
questions.prompt: Ça ne marche pas.

questions.q: She needs the words on the screen, not your reading of them. Write it out.
questions.why: Cassé is a guess about the cause. What the message said is a fact, and it is the one she can act on.
accept: Le message dit que le code a expiré.
Le message dit que le code a expiré
questions.answer: Le message dit que le code a expiré.
questions.prompt: L'ordinateur est cassé.

questions.q: Right words, wrong person. This went to a Paris friend. Write it out.
questions.why: Tu and mail travel together. Courriel with tu is the word their bank would have used.
accept: Je t'envoie ça par mail.
Je t'envoie ça par mail
questions.answer: Je t'envoie ça par mail.
questions.prompt: Je t'envoie ça par courriel.

questions.q: This went to a support agent. Write it out.
questions.why: Bugue is fine with a friend and reads as a text message on a support line. Marcher is safe with both.
accept: Ça ne marche plus depuis hier.
Ça ne marche plus depuis hier
questions.answer: Ça ne marche plus depuis hier.
questions.prompt: Ça bugue depuis hier.

questions.q: On the phone to somebody official. One word is missing. Write it out.
questions.why: Everybody drops the ne out loud. On a call to somebody official it is the one place it is heard missing.
accept: Ça ne marche pas.
Ça ne marche pas
questions.answer: Ça ne marche pas.
questions.prompt: Ça marche pas.

questions.q: Which pair belongs together?
questions.why: The pronoun and the word for email move as a set. Getting one right and the other wrong is the whole error.

questions.q: You wrote « Je vais downloader le fichier ». What is wrong with it?
questions.why: It was a reasonable guess: French really did take cliquer, scanner and zoomer. Télécharger got there first and holds the ground.
opts: French took cliquer but not this one
downloader is not a real word anywhere

questions.q: A French form has a box marked « Mél ». Out loud, people call that
questions.why: Mél is an abbreviation for writing, the one printed next to Tél. Nobody says it, and said aloud it is the same sound as mail anyway.

questions.q: Listen. Is this for an agent or a friend?
questions.say: Salut, je te l'envoie par mail.
questions.why: Salut, tu and mail all point the same way. Any one of the three would have settled it.

questions.q: Your computer is slow. Say it to a FRIEND, in three words.
questions.why: Two words shorter than mon ordinateur est lent, and two registers down. To an agent you would use the long one.
accept: mon ordi rame
Mon ordi rame
questions.answer: mon ordi rame

sections.say: L'écran vous donne un ordre, l'agent vous pose une question, l'ami vous parle. Trois voix, un seul appareil.
sections.body: L'écran vous donne un ordre, l'agent vous pose une question, l'ami vous parle. Trois voix, un seul appareil. Every tech object in French has more than one name, and the name you pick says who you think is listening. That is the whole unit, and it is the one thing here that no other unit teaches. Next comes lesson 36 in A2, where eight different situations arrive in one sitting and the only question that runs through all of them is the one this lesson asked: which voice does this one want?
sections.title: One appareil, three voices
points: The screen orders, the agent asks, the friend talks. Same device.
Six screen strings, learned whole. You never build one.
They cannot see it: what happened, when, what you tried, what it said.
Being too formal is safe everywhere else in this course. Here it is not.

errorTriggers.description: Uses a form from the wrong voice: courriel to a friend, or mail to an agent in Quebec.
Treats an instruction as a report, or a report as an instruction, and waits or presses wrongly.
Says ça ne marche pas to somebody who cannot see the screen, and leaves out three of the four things they need.
Starts with vous and finishes with tu vocabulary, or the reverse, inside one exchange.

grammarIntroduced: choosing between three names for one referent by who is listening
fixed interface strings, learned whole

acts.title: The second word
acts.milestone: You can build the past of any regular verb out of two words, and you know which of the two you already had.

acts.title: What goes in the gap
acts.milestone: You can make any of it negative, in any person, and put both halves where French puts them rather than where the end of the sentence feels like it wants them.

acts.title: Two words, and one you already had
acts.milestone: You can put any regular verb into the past from its group alone, and you know that the second word never changes for anybody.

acts.title: A plan, or a memory
acts.milestone: You can tell a plan from something that is over by the shortest word in the sentence, and you answered for five verbs the lesson never showed you.

acts.title: What the last two lessons left here
acts.milestone: You closed lesson 12's question about where a short adverb goes in a two-word verb, and lesson 14's about how to say how long ago something happened.

acts.title: Out loud
acts.milestone: You held the conversation the kettle lost, and you spelled the difference the ear cannot hear.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: You built past forms for verbs this lesson never listed, which is the half of it a list could never have taught you.

recorded.desc: THE SIX PERSONS, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, IN THE ORDER THE SHEET PRINTS THEM AND AT AN EVEN PACE: « J'ai mangé. » « Tu as mangé. » « Il a mangé. » « Nous avons mangé. » « Vous avez mangé. » « Ils ont mangé. » THE LAST WORD OF ALL SIX MUST BE IDENTICAL. `mangé` is the constant and the entire claim of the screen is that it does not move, so a reader who lengthens it in the plural is teaching the opposite of what the table says. THE LIAISONS IN nous avons AND vous avez ARE OBLIGATORY: /nu.za.vɔ̃/ and /vu.za.ve/, one word each, and so is the one in ils ont, /il.zɔ̃/. KEEP THE NASALS CLOSED: avons is /a.vɔ̃/ and ont is /ɔ̃/, with no n sound behind either vowel.

THE AFFIRMATIVE AND THE NEGATIVE, ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, THREE PAIRS, AND THE BRIEF NAMES THIS TAKE SPECIFICALLY: « J'ai mangé. » then « Je n'ai pas mangé. », « Il a mangé. » then « Il n'a pas mangé. », « Ils ont mangé. » then « Ils n'ont pas mangé. » RECORDED APART, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO SMALL WORDS AND THE ENTIRE TEACHING IS LOST. THE `ai` IS SWALLOWED IN THE NEGATIVE AND MUST STAY SWALLOWED. « je n'ai pas » is /ʒə ne pa/ at ordinary speed and the learner is being asked to catch the n' and the pas around something they can barely hear. Do not lean on « pas » and do not pause before it: it is an ordinary unstressed word sitting in a gap. NOTHING MAY BE STRESSED IN THE NEGATIVE THAT IS NOT STRESSED IN THE AFFIRMATIVE.

THE FUTUR PROCHE AGAINST THE PASSÉ COMPOSÉ, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, RECORDED ADJACENTLY, AND THE BRIEF NAMES THIS TAKE SPECIFICALLY. Four lines in this order: « Je vais manger. » « J'ai mangé. » « Je vais manger avec des amis. » « J'ai mangé avec des amis. » APART, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO AUXILIARIES. THE LAST WORD OF ALL FOUR IS THE SAME SOUND AND MUST BE THE SAME SOUND. /mɑ̃.ʒe/ every time, with no lengthening, no extra breath and no difference of any kind between the naming form and the past form. A reader who distinguishes them is teaching something that is not true and the whole lesson rests on it not being true. THE DIFFERENCE IS ENTIRELY IN /vɛ/ AGAINST /ʒe/, and both are one short unstressed syllable. Do not lift either of them: the learner has to learn to catch an unstressed syllable, and a take that stresses it teaches them to listen for something that will not be there in the wild.
clipIds: Je vais manger avec des amis.

recorded.desc: THE AUDIO STEP OF THE GAP TRAP, AND IT IS A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. Four lines, one take, in this order: « Je n'ai mangé pas. » then « Je n'ai pas mangé. », then « J'ai mangé bien. » then « J'ai bien mangé. » READ THE WRONG ONES PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly. They are perfectly pronounceable and they are what a fluent English speaker produces on their first attempt; a reading that signals the error teaches that the error is audible. IT IS NOT AUDIBLE. Both wrong lines hold exactly the same words as the right one beside them, in a different order. DO NOT PAUSE AT THE SEAM. A break before « pas » or before « bien » in the wrong lines would mark them, and the learner would learn to listen for a pause that is not there.

THE THREE GROUPS, ONE TAKE, AS THREE PAIRS: « parler » then « J'ai parlé. », « finir » then « Il a fini. », « vendre » then « Il a vendu. » THE FIRST PAIR IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS AND IT IS THE EASIEST ONE TO FAKE: « parler » and « parlé » ARE THE SAME SOUND and the take has to prove it rather than hide it. Read them identically. Any difference at all between the two teaches the learner that there is one, and the entire dictée in this lesson exists because there is not. THE OTHER TWO PAIRS DO DIFFER, and audibly: /fi.niʁ/ against /fi.ni/, /vɑ̃dʁ/ against /vɑ̃.dy/. Let them. The contrast between a pair you can hear and a pair you cannot is the point of putting all three in one take.

THE KETTLE ON A MONDAY. She is waiting for it too and has decided to be friendly about it; the question is small talk rather than an enquiry. THE LEARNER'S OWN LINE IS THE TAKE THAT HAS TO BE RIGHT: « Hier soir, j'ai... j'ai... » is somebody who has committed to a tense out loud and cannot produce the word that finishes it. The repeat is not a stammer and it is not embarrassment: it is somebody holding a sentence open while they look for something. Leave a real gap after the second « j'ai » and let it be uncomfortable. HER LAST LINE IS THE EXPENSIVE ONE. « Ah, ce soir alors ! » is cheerful and completely unremarkable: she has heard a correct sentence and believed it. Any hint of doubt, checking or kindness-about-a-mistake turns the scene into a correction and loses the whole point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong.

THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to rec-a2-05-pair and rec-a2-05-tense: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and a paired reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. THE FOUR NEGATIVES ARE THE ONES THAT MATTER. The learner has to hear the n' and the pas as two separate small words between the subject and the second word, and « n'ai » and « n'ont » are very short. Do not run « je n'ai » together into one syllable and do not run « pas mangé » together either. SAY IT THE WAY SOMEBODY WOULD SAY IT, at the pace of somebody dictating a phone number to a friend.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS SIX SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same colleague, later in the week, with more time. EVERY QUESTION IS ASKED WITHOUT INVERSION and should sound completely ordinary: « Tu as travaillé samedi ? » is a statement with a question mark on it, which is what people say, and reading it as a careful sentence would make it sound like a lesson. NEITHER « as » NOR « a » MAY BE STRESSED anywhere in the take. They are the words carrying the tense and the learner has to get used to catching them unstressed, because that is the only way they will ever hear them.
clipIds: Et toi, tu as travaillé samedi ?
Et Camille, elle a répondu à ton message ?
On mange ensemble ce soir, alors ?

lessons.intro: Somebody is going to ask you about yesterday, and to answer you need a verb that is suddenly two words long. The first one is avoir, which you have had for fifteen lessons and do not have to learn again. The second is built off the verb you mean, and its ending comes straight off the group you already put that verb in. What is new is the space between the two, because it turns out to be a real place: some words go in it, one of them is the negative, and the thing you actually ate does not.

endings.body: -ER goes to -é, -IR goes to -i, -RE goes to -u. Three groups you have had since lesson 1 in A2, and the past form runs one ending per group with no exceptions inside the regular set. Give it a verb you have never met and you can still build it: if it ends in -er the past form ends in -é, and that is the whole of the decision.
endings.title: Three groups, three endings

examples.note: -RE, so -u. Lesson 4's own verb, and the group where the ending is furthest from the naming form.
-IR, so -i, on a verb the endings grid does not use.

laterOn.body: Two things are deliberately not in this lesson. About forty verbs have a past form you could not have guessed, and they are lesson 17 in A2, which is next. A short list of verbs uses être rather than avoir for the first word, and their past form does change to match the person, and that is lesson 18 in A2. Neither of them changes anything you have learned here: the shape stays two words with a gap in it. You will need all of this again at lesson 30 in A2, where the whole conversation is about what you studied and how it went.
laterOn.title: What is still coming

examples.note: The shape. It survives both of the next two lessons unchanged.
And the gap, which survives them too.

noAgree.body: After avoir the past form is one shape and it stays that shape. Not mangée for a woman, not mangés for a group, not mangées for a group of women. Elle a mangé, ils ont mangé, elles ont mangé. This is worth saying plainly because lesson 18 in A2, two lessons from here, says the opposite for a short list of verbs that use être instead, and the contrast only works if you have this side of it cleanly first. There is one case where a past form does agree with avoir and it needs object pronouns, which is lesson 21 in A2, five lessons after this one.
noAgree.title: It does not change for anybody

examples.note: A feminine subject, a feminine object, and not a letter has moved.
And elle again, with something in the gap. Répondu is still répondu.

oneSound.body: Manger and mangé are one sound. There is no listening exercise anywhere that can tell you which one you heard, and anybody who says otherwise is selling you something. What you listen for is the little word in front. Manger and mangé are /mɑ̃.ʒe/, parler and parlé are /paʁ.le/, travailler and travaillé are /tʁa.va.je/. The difference is real and it is entirely on paper, which is why this lesson has a dictée and why the ear questions in it are about the little word in front instead.
oneSound.title: Manger and mangé

examples.note: Lesson 15's construction. The last word is the naming form.
This lesson. The last word is the past form, and it is the same sound.

pastForm.body: The second word is built off the naming form and the group decides how. An -ER verb ends in -é, an -IR verb ends in -i, an -RE verb loses its ending and takes -u. That is the whole regular system and it is the same three groups lesson 1 in A2, lesson 3 in A2 and lesson 4 in A2 taught you. It never changes for the person: the same five letters sit in all six rows of the table.
pastForm.title: The second word, and where it comes from

examples.note: -IR, so -i. Lesson 3's own verb, one tense later.

twoWords.body: Every verb you have met so far has been one word: je parle, il finit, nous vendons. From here on the past is TWO: a form of avoir for whoever you are talking about, and then the past form of the verb that carries the meaning. Lesson 11 in A1 already gave you all six forms of avoir, so there is nothing new to learn about the first word. Everything that is hard about this tense comes from the fact that there are two of them and there is a gap in between.
twoWords.title: The verb is two words now

examples.note: Avoir for je, then the past form. Two words and a finished evening.
Avoir moved for ils. The second word did not.

whenWord.body: French does not need the time word to tell you the thing is over. You do, for a while, because English keeps two different pasts and French is handing you one. Put a time on it until you stop needing to. English keeps two pasts apart, "I ate" and "I have eaten", and French runs both of them through this one form, so for a while your ear will want a signal that French is not sending. Hier, avant-hier, la semaine dernière, il y a trois jours. Lesson 14 in A2 gave you « il y a » for a length of time behind you and could not finish the job, because saying how long ago something happened needs this tense.
whenWord.title: Say when, and it settles

examples.note: Yesterday, and there is nothing left to work out.
Lesson 14's own card, and it already holds this tense.

inBetween.body: The two words are a pair with a gap in the middle, and the gap is where the small words live. Pas goes in it, bien and déjà go in it, and the thing you ate does not. Ne in front of avoir, pas straight after it, and the past form outside both. The gap is one word wide and nothing longer goes in it. A short adverb goes there too: bien, mal, déjà, beaucoup, encore. What does NOT go there is the thing the sentence is about. « J'ai mangé une pomme », never « j'ai une pomme mangé », because the gap is one word wide and an object is not a small word.
inBetween.title: The gap, and what lives in it

examples.note: Pas in the gap, and mangé outside it.
And the apple, which stays outside because it is not a small word.

whichVerb.body: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. That is lesson 15's line, from one lesson ago, and it was about « je ne vais pas partir ». It is exactly as true here: avoir is the word that changed when you picked the person, so both halves go round avoir, and the past form is left where it is. Nothing about this rule is new. What is new is that the word it aims at is now the FIRST of two rather than the only one there is.

sections.say: One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between. Three pairs. Read each one down rather than across, and watch the two extra words land in the same place every time.

cards.body: English has the same shape and puts the "not" in the same gap: have, not, eaten. You already do this in your own language, which is why it feels wrong rather than difficult when it comes out backwards.
cards.head: I have not eaten.

cards.body: The pas has gone past the gap and landed behind the past form. English puts "not" beside the word carrying the meaning, and French puts it in the gap, and those are two different places as soon as the verb is two words.
cards.head: Je n'ai mangé pas.
cards.label: what you produce

cards.body: Ne in front of avoir, pas straight after it, and mangé outside both. One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between.
cards.head: Je n'ai pas mangé.

cards.body: Avoir has gone missing altogether. Both halves went round the past form, which is the word that did not change for anybody, and a past form on its own is not a sentence in any person.
cards.head: Je ne mangé pas.
cards.label: and the other one

cards.body: Lesson 15 in A2 said it one lesson ago: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. Here the one that changed is avoir, so both halves go round avoir and the past form stays outside them.

errors.why: The pas has gone past the gap and landed behind the past form. English puts "not" beside the word carrying the meaning, and French puts it in the gap, and those are two different places as soon as the verb is two words.

sections.say: Lesson 12 in A2 taught you where a short adverb goes and then said this: « In a past tense the short ones move, and that rule arrives with the tense in lesson 16 in A2. » This is the tense, and this is the rule. Lesson 12 in A2 put the short ones straight after the verb when there was one verb. There are two now, so "straight after the verb" has become "in the gap", and it is the same instruction.

sections.say: Lesson 14 in A2 taught « il y a » as a length of time behind you and then had to hand the sentence forward, because saying how long ago something happened needs a past tense and that tense is this one. Its own card is on the left and it already holds this lesson's tense. French does not need the time word to tell you the thing is over. You do, for a while, because English keeps two different pasts and French is handing you one. Put a time on it until you stop needing to.

sections.text: Hier, j'ai travaillé jusqu'à sept heures. Après, j'ai mangé avec des amis dans un petit restaurant près du bureau. Nous avons beaucoup parlé et nous avons choisi le menu ensemble. Je n'ai pas payé, parce que Camille a insisté. Ensuite, j'ai cherché mes clés pendant dix minutes. Je n'ai pas trouvé mon parapluie. Ce matin, je n'ai pas encore fini le rapport. J'ai commencé il y a trois jours, et je vais finir ce soir.
sections.title: Monday, At The Kettle

glossary.note: A point in time you stop at. Nothing about it is this lesson.
The word that puts one finished thing after another, which is what this tense is for.
Two words, and the verb after it behaves exactly as it would anywhere else.
From insister, an -ER verb, so its past form ends in -é. You could have built it without being told.
The thing that was not found. It sits after the past form, where objects sit.

questions.a: The ne has shortened to n' every time, because every form of avoir starts on a vowel, and the pas is in the gap every time: n'ai pas payé, n'ai pas trouvé, n'ai pas encore fini, and the encore is in the gap with it. Four verbs, four gaps, one position.
questions.q: The passage holds four negatives. What do all four have in common?

questions.a: Yes. The gap takes small words and pas encore is two of them, sitting together in front of the past form. What it does not take is the report, which is what the sentence is about and which sits after fini where it belongs.
questions.q: « Je n'ai pas encore fini le rapport. » There are two words in the gap. Is that allowed?

questions.a: Three, and they are the three you have: travaillé, mangé, parlé, payé, cherché, trouvé, commencé and insisté are all -ER verbs ending in -é; choisi and fini are -IR verbs ending in -i; and there is no -RE verb in it at all. Eight of the ten are the commonest group in the language.
questions.q: Count the groups. How many different endings are in the passage?

questions.a: « J'ai commencé » is over and « je vais finir » has not happened. The two constructions are the same shape: a little word that changes for the person, then a word that does not. The little word is the entire difference. Ai against vais.
questions.q: The last sentence has two tenses in it. What are they and what is the difference?

rounds.label: Where the small words go

questions.q: You did not eat. Which one is French?
questions.why: Ne in front of avoir, pas straight after it, and the past form outside both. The gap is one word wide and nothing longer goes in it. One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between.

questions.q: Make this negative. Il a mangé.
questions.why: Ne in front of a, pas straight after it, and mangé untouched. The ne shortens because a is a vowel, and it does that in front of every form of avoir.
accept: Il n'a pas mangé.
Il n'a pas mangé

questions.q: Fix this. You mean that they did not eat.
questions.why: The pas went past the gap and landed behind the past form. It belongs straight after ont, which is the word that changed for ils.
accept: Ils n'ont pas mangé.
Ils n'ont pas mangé

questions.prompt: Ils n'ont mangé pas.

questions.q: Which of these can go in the gap?
questions.why: Only small words go in the gap: pas, bien, mal, déjà, encore, beaucoup. Everything the sentence is about goes after the past form.

questions.q: Make this negative. Nous avons fini.
questions.why: The ne shortens in front of avons and the liaison z goes with it, which changes the sound and not the spelling of anything else.
accept: Nous n'avons pas fini.
Nous n'avons pas fini
Nous n avons pas fini
questions.answer: Nous n'avons pas fini.

questions.q: Fix this. Avoir has gone missing.
questions.why: Avoir has gone missing altogether. Both halves went round the past form, which is the word that did not change for anybody, and a past form on its own is not a sentence in any person.
accept: Je n'ai pas mangé.
Je n'ai pas mangé

questions.prompt: Je ne mangé pas.

parle

questions.q: Grandir. Elle a ___.   (a verb this lesson never showed you)

questions.answer: grandi

questions.q: Which group does a past form ending in -u come from?
questions.why: Three groups, three endings, and they are the same three groups you already have. An -ER verb ends in -é, an -IR verb ends in -i, an -RE verb ends in -u, and there is nothing else to learn about a regular one.

questions.q: Perdre. Which is the past form?

Tu as mangé
Tu as mange
Tu as mange.

questions.q: Fix this. It sounds exactly right and it is not.

accept: J'ai mangé.
J'ai mangé
J'ai mange

questions.answer: manger

questions.q: Fix this. The second word is in the wrong tense.

Nous avons parlé ensemble
Nous avons parle ensemble

J'ai mangé une pomme

questions.q: Where does the apple go?
questions.why: Ne in front of avoir, pas straight after it, and the past form outside both. The gap is one word wide and nothing longer goes in it. An apple is not a small word.

Elle a bien repondu

Elle a bien mangé
Elle a bien mange

rounds.say: Six on the little word in front, and one of them is the only listening question in the lesson.
rounds.label: A plan or a memory

questions.q: Listen. Which one did you hear?
questions.say: J'ai mangé.
questions.why: Ai, so it is over. Vais would have made it a plan, and the last word of the two sentences is the same sound either way.

questions.q: Il va manger. When is this?
questions.why: Va, so it has not happened. Lesson 15 in A2 taught this one lesson ago and the two constructions are the same shape.

questions.q: Il a mangé. When is this?
questions.why: A, so it is finished. The a and the va are both one short unstressed syllable and they are the entire difference.

questions.q: Which word tells you the tense?
questions.why: Je vais manger and j'ai mangé end on exactly the same sound. Vais against ai is the whole difference between something that has not happened and something that is over, and both of them are one short unstressed syllable.

questions.q: Write it as something that is over. Je vais travailler.
questions.why: Swap the little word in front and put the second one in the past form. Nothing else about the sentence moves.
accept: J'ai travaillé.
J'ai travaillé
J'ai travaille
questions.answer: J'ai travaillé.

questions.q: Hier, ___ mangé au restaurant.
questions.why: Hier fixes it as over, so the little word in front has to be a form of avoir. « Hier, je vais manger » says something that cannot be true.

J'ai bien mangé

Il a deja fini

questions.answer: il y a

questions.q: Which of these is NOT allowed in the gap?
questions.why: The gap takes small words. A report is the thing the sentence is about and it goes after the past form.

questions.q: Fix this. Both halves have travelled together.
questions.why: They are not a unit that moves. The ne goes in front of avoir and shortens against it, and the pas goes in the gap behind it.

Il n a pas fini

sections.body: Put avoir in front for whoever you are talking about, then the past form of the verb, and leave a gap between them. Everything small goes in that gap and nothing else does. Lesson 11 in A1 gave you all six forms of avoir and you do not learn one new one here. Lesson 1 in A2, lesson 3 in A2 and lesson 4 in A2 gave you the three groups, and the three past endings run one per group. Lesson 21 in A1 gave you the two halves of the negative and lesson 15 in A2 told you which verb they go round. The only new thing in this lesson is that there is now a gap between two words, and what is allowed to sit in it.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between. The two words are a pair with a gap in the middle, and the gap is where the small words live. Pas goes in it, bien and déjà go in it, and the thing you ate does not.
Ne in front of avoir, pas straight after it, and the past form outside both. The gap is one word wide and nothing longer goes in it.
Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. That is lesson 15's line and it is exactly as true with avoir in front as it was with aller.

Three groups, three endings, and they are the same three groups you already have. An -ER verb ends in -é, an -IR verb ends in -i, an -RE verb ends in -u, and there is nothing else to learn about a regular one.
After avoir the past form does not agree with anybody, in any person and any gender.

Lesson 12 in A2 put the short ones straight after the verb when there was one verb. There are two now, so "straight after the verb" has become "in the gap", and it is the same instruction. In a past tense the short ones move, and that rule arrives with the tense in lesson 16 in A2.

Lesson 14 in A2 taught « il y a » as a length of time behind you and then had to hand the sentence forward, because saying how long ago something happened needs a past tense and that tense is this one. Its own card is on the left and it already holds this lesson's tense.

Some verbs have a past form you could not have guessed from the naming form, and there are about forty of them. They are the next lesson, lesson 17 in A2, and not one of them is in this one. A short list of verbs uses être instead of avoir for the first word, and their past form does change to match the person. That is lesson 18 in A2, and it is the opposite of this rule. Learn this one cleanly first. You will want all of it again at lesson 30 in A2, where the whole conversation is about what you studied and how it went.

errorTriggers.description: Puts the pas behind the past form: « je n'ai mangé pas ». The error this lesson exists to prevent, and the one an English speaker makes first, because the end of the sentence is where the thought finished.
Gives the past form the wrong group's ending: « j'ai finu », « il a vendi ». It comes from treating the ending as a property of the verb rather than of the class the verb is in.

Writes the naming form where the past form belongs: « j'ai manger ». THE ONE NOBODY HEARS THEMSELVES MAKE, because the two are one sound, so it survives every amount of speaking practice and shows up the first time the learner writes anything down.

Agrees the past form with the subject or the object: « elle a mangée ». It comes from lesson 10 in A2 and lesson 11 in A2, where agreeing everything was the correct instinct, and it is about to come back as the correct instinct again at lesson 18 in A2.

Hears « je vais manger » as something that happened, or « j'ai mangé » as a plan. Costs comprehension rather than accuracy, and the learner has no way of finding out: both sentences are correct and both end on the same sound.

Puts a short adverb on the end rather than in the gap: « j'ai mangé bien ». It is the same error as the pas one and the learner does not usually notice they are the same, which is why the gap is taught as a place rather than as two separate rules.

grammarAssumed: The full present of avoir, in six persons, introduced in a1.07
The regular -ER conjugation and its silent endings, introduced in a2.01
The regular -IR conjugation, introduced in a2.10
The regular -RE conjugation, introduced in a2.11
ne … pas round a single finite verb, introduced in a1.18
That ne … pas encloses the finite verb rather than the infinitive in a two-verb predicate, introduced in a2.19
The placement of short adverbs after a simple-tense verb, introduced in a2.17
il y a plus a duration, introduced in a2.18 for reception and deferred here for production
The nine subject pronouns, and that on takes the il form, introduced in a1.05
grammarIntroduced: The passé composé with avoir as auxiliary, for a completed past event, covering both the English simple past and present perfect
The regular past participle: -er to -é, -ir to -i, -re to -u, one ending per conjugation class
That the participle is invariable after avoir, with no agreement for the subject in any person or gender
That ne … pas encloses the auxiliary and not the participle, extending a2.19's rule from a periphrastic future to a compound tense
The elision of ne to n' before every form of avoir, and the loss of the liaison in n'avons and n'avez
The placement of short adverbs between auxiliary and participle, closing the deferral a2.17 made explicit
il y a plus a duration as "ago", in production, closing the deferral a2.18 made and for which its canDo was reworded
The homophony of the -er infinitive and the -é participle, as an orthographic distinction with no phonetic exponent
The auxiliary as the sole exponent of tense in the futur proche / passé composé opposition
Irregular past participles and être as auxiliary are named and reserved for a2.20 and a2.21 respectively

recorded.desc: IL FINIT AND ILS FINISSENT, ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, ONE VOICE, RECORDED ADJACENTLY AND IN THAT ORDER, WITH NO TEACHING PAUSE BETWEEN THEM. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. The two are one sound apart and that sound is a final S, not a syllable: eel fee-NEE, then eel fee-NEES. Do not lengthen the plural, do not lean on the ending, do not add the faintest vowel after the S, and do not slow down for the second one. The difference must be exactly the size it is in ordinary speech, because the whole claim of the lesson is that a learner can catch it at conversational pace. RECORDED APART, IN TWO SESSIONS, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO FORMS and the teaching is lost: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between the halves will be heard as the difference, and the real difference will not be. The same instruction applies to every pair in this clip list, and each pair is one take.

All six forms as one continuous take, in the order the table shows them (je, tu, il, ils, nous, vous), by one voice at one speed, then the six full sentences in the same take. The first three must be INDISTINGUISHABLE from each other, because they are: three spellings and one sound. The fourth adds one S and nothing else. The last two add a whole syllable each and should sound ordinary rather than emphasised: -issons ends on a nasal vowel with no N sound on the end of it. Do not stress the verb anywhere; the weight belongs at the end of the phrase.

THE SINGULAR TRIPLE, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. je finis, tu finis, il finit, then je remplis, tu remplis, il remplit. This is the opposite instruction from the usual one and it is the same instruction the contrast clip carries from the other side: do not help. Do not differentiate them, do not touch the final letter, do not let the t of finit surface. If a listener can tell any of these three apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Read them at conversational pace, one after another, with no pause for teaching.

The three number pairs, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE BACK TO BACK, singular then plural: Elle choisit / Elles choisissent, Il réussit toujours / Ils réussissent toujours, Elle grandit vite / Elles grandissent vite. In every pair the PRONOUN must sound identical on both sides, because it is: elle and elles are one sound and so are il and ils. The only difference the learner may hear is the S at the end of the verb. Any difference in the pronoun, in pace or in emphasis destroys the pair, because the learner will use it instead of the S.

The ten naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice. Every one of them ends in the same EER sound and that sameness is the teaching: the learner should come away hearing -ir as one ending rather than ten word-endings. Do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, one man in his forties at an ordinary shift-desk pace, mildly hurried and entirely unbothered. The last line (« D'accord. Une place à six heures. ») must be brisk and final rather than pointed: the whole scene turns on nobody minding and nobody checking, so any hint of doubt or of correction in his voice would destroy it. He is writing while he speaks and he has already moved on.

Alors, qui finit à six heures ce soir ?
D'accord. Une place à six heures.

lessons.intro: The second of the three regular patterns, and the first verb in this course whose ending tells your ear something. Six endings, three of which arrive as a sound, and one of those three is the difference between one person and several.

stem.body: finir gives fin-. choisir gives chois-. remplir gives rempl-. Take the last two letters off the naming form and what is left does not move, whoever is speaking. That is the same machine lesson 1 in A2 gave you for -er verbs, and nothing about it has changed. What has changed is the six things you put on the end of it.
stem.title: What is left when -ir comes off

examples.note: fin- with the je ending on it.
The same fin-, with the nous ending, which is longer than you expect.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on an -ir verb means on finit and never on finissons: the spoken we takes the short form and puts no sound on the end at all. That is the one place this lesson's rule will not help you, and it is the form you will hear most.
nousOn.title: The we that sounds singular

examples.note: The written one, with the ending you can hear.
The spoken one, taking the il form, and sounding like one person.

theSound.body: The three plural forms all have -iss- in the spelling and all three reach the ear, but not in the same way. ils finissent adds one sound, an S, right at the end of the verb: fee-NEE becomes fee-NEES and the word is still two syllables. nous finissons and vous finissez add a whole syllable each. What matters at the moment of listening is not which of those you got, it is that you got something at all, because the singular gives you nothing.
theSound.title: What the plural puts on the end

examples.note: One sound more than the singular, and nothing else.
A whole syllable more, and you would not mistake it for anything.

notThisFamily.body: partir, sortir, dormir, servir, sentir, venir, tenir, ouvrir, offrir and courir all end in -ir and not one of them takes -iss- anywhere. Several are more common than any verb in this lesson, so you will meet them early and often. They are not exceptions to this pattern; they are a different pattern, and running the machine on them produces something no French speaker says. Recognising that a verb is not in this family is worth as much as building the ones that are.
notThisFamily.title: Ending in -ir is not enough

examples.note: This one is in the family, and the plural says so out loud.
And this one is too, even though on makes it sound singular.

singularThree.body: Three spellings and one sound. -is, -is and -it all arrive as nothing, exactly the way -e, -es and -ent did on an -er verb in lesson 1 in A2, so in the singular the pronoun is still carrying the person on its own. This half of lesson 1 in A2 has not been taken back and it never will be. What is new is that the plural no longer joins them.
singularThree.title: je finis, tu finis, il finit

examples.note: Ends in -it, and is said exactly the same way.

sections.body: The singular hides the person. The plural announces itself. In the singular, je finis, tu finis and il finit are three spellings and one sound, exactly as je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent were four spellings and one sound in lesson 1. Nothing there has been withdrawn: out loud the singular of an -ir verb still tells you nothing about who is speaking, and the pronoun in front is still carrying it. What has changed is that the plural stopped joining them. ils finissent puts one S at the end of the verb, and the word is still two syllables, so it is a consonant that arrives rather than a beat. nous finissons and vous finissez each add a whole syllable, which nobody could miss. So three of the six now reach the ear, and one of those three is the first singular against plural pair in this course that a learner can settle without reading the page. The one place this does not hold is on. It means we, it takes the il form, and it is what almost every French speaker actually says, so the commonest spoken plural in the language sounds exactly like one person. That is not an exception to the rule so much as a reminder of what the rule is about: the rule is about the FORM, and on is grammatically singular.
sections.title: The two halves, and where the line falls

sections.body: The method has not changed since the last unit and it will not change in the next one: find the stem, add the person. What each unit gives you is a different short set of endings to add. The one after this takes the third and last regular pattern, and after it there is no regular set left to learn, only verbs that had to be memorised outright. The habit worth carrying out of this lesson is a listening habit rather than a spelling one. You have now met a verb whose ending tells you something, so from here on the question at the end of a French verb is not whether you heard anything, it is what you heard. And you have met the reason that question has a limit: the naming form of a verb does not tell you which family it is in, so ten of the commonest verbs in the language end in -ir and take none of this.
sections.title: What carries forward

sheets.title: The ten verbs
contains: The ten that end in -ir and are not here

sections.body: Every verb here builds all six of its present-tense forms from one stem plus the six endings on the other sheet, so one pattern gives you ten verbs and sixty forms, and it keeps working on verbs nobody has shown you: rougir, punir, salir, bâtir, agir and vieillir all behave identically. That is not true of every verb ending in -ir, and the exceptions are not rare ones. partir, sortir, dormir, servir, sentir, venir, tenir, ouvrir, offrir, courir all end in -ir and not one of them takes the extra sound anywhere in its present tense. Several of them are more frequent than anything on the list above, which is the awkward part: you will meet the exceptions before you have finished practising the rule. Nothing in the naming form separates the two groups, so this is the one thing in the lesson that is learnt verb by verb rather than worked out. venir and tenir have a unit of their own at lesson 5 in A2. The others are worth treating as individual words for now: recognising that a verb is not in this family is most of the benefit, because it stops you producing a form that does not exist.

sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that finishes the set.
sections.body: You can build the present tense of any regular -ir verb, including ones nobody has shown you. More than that, you can do something with your ears that lesson 1 could not ask of you: hear one person against several from the verb alone, with no pronoun to help. The half of that lesson that still holds is the singular, where three spellings are one sound and the page is the only place they differ. The singular hides the person. The plural announces itself. The next unit takes the third and last set of endings, and after it there is no regular pattern left to learn.
