sections.setting: Jeudi matin. Sophie revient de trois jours de congé. Elle pose son sac et te demande ce qui s'est passé pendant son absence. Madame Diallo a appelé mardi.

sections.say: Le message reste, le point de vue change.
sections.brief: Hier, ton collègue Marc était absent. Isabelle Morin lui a laissé ce message sur la boîte vocale du bureau : « Bonjour Marc, c'est Isabelle Morin, de la mairie de Laval. Je vous appelle pour le projet de la bibliothèque. Nous avons bien reçu vos plans, merci. Le conseil se réunit jeudi et je vous donnerai sa réponse vendredi. Est-ce que vous pouvez m'envoyer le budget avant mercredi ? Et qu'est-ce que vous pensez d'une visite du terrain la semaine prochaine ? Rappelez-moi demain matin, je suis au bureau jusqu'à midi. Merci. » Aujourd'hui, Marc est de retour. Écris-lui un message pour lui transmettre l'appel.
sections.title: Transmets le message de la boîte vocale

criteria.label: Les bonnes personnes
descriptors: 3 : Isabelle Morin devient elle, Marc devient tu, et vos plans devient tes plans. Aucun je du message ne reste.
2 : Une ou deux personnes restent comme dans le message, mais on comprend qui parle.
1 : Le message est recopié avec je et vous : Marc ne sait plus qui dit quoi.

criteria.label: Les temps qui reculent
descriptors: 4 : Après a dit ou a demandé, chaque présent passe à l'imparfait, chaque passé composé au plus-que-parfait et chaque futur au conditionnel, sans erreur de forme.
3 : Presque tous les temps reculent. Une forme hésite : un futur resté, ou un auxiliaire mal choisi.
2 : Plusieurs temps restent comme dans le message, ou le verbe qui rapporte change sans cesse de temps.
1 : Les temps du message sont gardés partout.

criteria.label: Questions et demande
descriptors: 3 : La question oui ou non avec si, la question avec ce que, la demande avec de + infinitif, sans est-ce que.
2 : Une des trois garde sa forme de question, ou la demande passe par que.
1 : Les questions sont recopiées avec est-ce que et un point d'interrogation.

criteria.label: La mission complète
descriptors: 2 : Qui a appelé, ce qu'elle veut, ce que Marc doit faire, demain matin écrit ce matin, et entre 90 et 130 mots.
1 : Il manque un élément, ou demain matin est resté demain matin.

sections.briefEn: Yesterday your colleague Marc was away. Isabelle Morin left the message above on the office voicemail. Marc is back today: write him a message passing on the call.
sections.produce: Écris un message de 90 à 130 mots à Marc, avec un verbe au passé pour rapporter, une question avec si, une question avec ce que ou un mot de question, une demande avec de + infinitif, et les bons mots du temps pour aujourd'hui.
scaffold: Elle a aussi demandé ce que...

watchFor.pattern: The voicemail copied in the first person, so je and vous stay (je vous donnerai ma réponse).
watchFor.feedback: Ce n'est pas Isabelle qui écrit, c'est toi. Son je devient elle et son vous devient tu : elle te donnerait sa réponse.

watchFor.pattern: vos plans kept as vos, or turned into ses plans, although the plans are Marc’s and the learner is writing to Marc.
watchFor.feedback: Les plans sont à Marc, et tu lui écris : tes plans.

watchFor.pattern: A present kept after a past reporting verb in more than one place (elle a dit que le conseil se réunit jeudi et qu’elle est au bureau).
watchFor.feedback: Après elle a dit, le présent passe à l'imparfait : le conseil se réunissait jeudi.

watchFor.pattern: A future kept after a past reporting verb (elle a dit qu'elle te donnera sa réponse).
watchFor.feedback: Après a dit, le futur devient conditionnel : elle te donnerait sa réponse.

watchFor.pattern: A passé composé kept instead of the pluperfect (elle a dit qu'ils ont reçu tes plans).
watchFor.feedback: Ils ont reçu, rapporté au passé, devient ils avaient reçu.

watchFor.pattern: A pluperfect with the wrong auxiliary or a missing agreement after être.
watchFor.feedback: Avait ou était, comme au passé composé, et l'accord après être.

watchFor.pattern: est-ce que or a question mark kept in a reported question (elle a demandé est-ce que tu peux envoyer le budget ?).
watchFor.feedback: Une question rapportée perd est-ce que et son point d'interrogation : elle voulait savoir si tu pouvais...

watchFor.pattern: qu'est-ce que kept, or que alone (elle a demandé qu'est-ce que tu penses, elle a demandé que tu penses).
watchFor.feedback: Qu'est-ce que devient ce que : elle a demandé ce que tu pensais.

watchFor.pattern: The request reported with the imperative kept (elle a dit rappelez-moi demain matin) or without de.
watchFor.feedback: Une demande passe avec de et l'infinitif : elle t'a demandé de la rappeler.

watchFor.pattern: demain matin kept although the message is relayed the next day, or turned into le lendemain matin, which points to tomorrow for Marc.
watchFor.feedback: Le message date d'hier. Son demain matin, pour Marc, c'est ce matin.

watchFor.pattern: Missing who called, what she wants, or what Marc has to do; or under 90 words.
watchFor.feedback: Relis la mission : qui a appelé, ce qu'elle veut, et ce que Marc doit faire.

graderNotes: The greeting (Salut Marc) and the sign-off do NOT count toward the word budget. Count the body only, with 10% tolerance (81 to 143) before criterion « tache » loses its point.

The shift after a past reporting verb is expected (level 4 of « temps »). A present or future kept for something still true or still ahead today (le conseil se réunit jeudi, since Thursday has not come yet) is ordinary speech: it may cost at most one point on « temps », and feedback calls it spoken, never wrong.

« Hier » for the day of the call and « ce matin » for the voicemail’s « demain matin » are CORRECT, because the learner writes the next day. « le lendemain matin » is a real error here: for Marc it points to tomorrow.
The conditionnel passé (elle a dit qu’elle t’aurait répondu) is B2 and not taught; do not require it, and do not mark a correct one as an error.
The subjunctive (lessons 14 to 16 in B1) is not needed here. A correct one is not an error; an incorrect one is not marked under this lesson.
Accept « elle voulait savoir », « elle a demandé » and « elle se demandait » interchangeably for the reported questions, and any reporting verb from act 10 with its correct construction.
The learner’s own gender is unknown: judge agreement for internal consistency only. « elle t’a remercié » agrees with Marc and is correct.
Accept regional vocabulary (courriel and email, boîte vocale and messagerie, cellulaire and portable).
Feedback language: simple French (B1), addressed as « tu », with one short English gloss allowed per comment.
sections.modelAnswer: Salut Marc, hier après-midi, Isabelle Morin, de la mairie de Laval, t'a laissé un message pour le projet de la bibliothèque. Elle a dit qu'ils avaient bien reçu tes plans, et elle t'a remercié. Elle a expliqué que le conseil se réunissait jeudi et qu'elle te donnerait sa réponse vendredi. Elle voulait savoir si tu pouvais lui envoyer le budget avant mercredi. Elle a aussi demandé ce que tu pensais d'une visite du terrain la semaine prochaine. Enfin, elle t'a demandé de la rappeler ce matin, parce qu'elle était au bureau jusqu'à midi. Il est déjà dix heures, alors appelle-la vite. Bonne journée !
sections.modelAnswerEn: Hi Marc, yesterday afternoon Isabelle Morin, from Laval town hall, left you a message about the library project. She said they had received your plans and she thanked you. She explained that the council was meeting on Thursday and that she would give you its answer on Friday. She wanted to know whether you could send her the budget before Wednesday. She also asked what you thought of a site visit next week. Finally, she asked you to call her back this morning, because she was in the office until noon. It is already ten, so call her quickly. Have a good day!

sections.say: Le message reste, le point de vue change.
sections.body: Tu passes un message au présent et au passé, tu rapportes une question et une demande, tu fais reculer les temps et tu sais quand les mots du temps bougent. Le piège qui reste est le plus discret : un seul je ou un seul futur oublié dans un long message. Avant l'examen, relis ton message pour Marc et souligne chaque verbe après que, si ou ce que. À côté, écris le temps que la personne a vraiment dit. Si les deux sont pareils après a dit, cherche pourquoi. EN: Underline every verb after que, si or ce que and write the tense originally said next to it; if nothing moved after a dit, find out why.

sections.body: Le message reste, le point de vue change. Tu passes un message au présent et au passé, avec les bonnes personnes, les bons temps et les bons repères, et tu sais rapporter une question et une demande. La prochaine leçon change de sujet et va plus loin avec la négation : ne... plus, ne... jamais, ne... que, personne, rien. EN: Next lesson: advanced negation.
sections.title: Le discours indirect, en résumé
points: Dire que : que ne tombe jamais, et les personnes suivent qui parle.
Si pour oui ou non, ce que pour qu’est-ce que, de pour une demande.
Après a dit : imparfait, plus-que-parfait, conditionnel.
Les mots du temps bougent seulement si le jour a changé.

errorTriggers.description: Repeats the original words when passing a message on, keeping the speaker’s je and mon, or drops que after dire the way English drops that.
Leaves pronouns and possessives where the original speaker put them instead of moving them to the new speaker and listener.
Keeps est-ce que, inversion or the question mark in a reported yes/no question, uses que instead of si, or elides si before elle.
Keeps qu'est-ce que or est-ce que after a question word, inverts a pronoun subject, or confuses ce que and ce qui.
Reports an order with que and a conjugated verb or keeps the imperative, instead of de plus the infinitive, or splits ne pas.
Keeps the present after a past reporting verb in writing, or pushes an imparfait further back that should stay put.
Keeps the passé composé after a past reporting verb, uses the imparfait for a finished event, or builds the pluperfect with the wrong auxiliary or no agreement.
Keeps the future (or va + infinitive) after a past reporting verb, or builds the conditional on the infinitive instead of the future stem.
Keeps demain, hier or ici when the day or place has changed, or shifts them when the message is passed on the same day.
Uses only dire, or gives a reporting verb the wrong construction (promettre que + infinitive, conseiller que), or forgets that every past reporting verb shifts the tense.
Writes a relayed message that leaves out who called, what they want or what has to be done, or mixes direct and reported speech.

grammarIntroduced: Indirect (reported) speech with dire que and other reporting verbs, with que never omitted, and the person and possessive shift to the new speaker

Reported yes/no questions with si (s’il, s’ils; the future allowed after this si) and reported wh-questions, with qu’est-ce que becoming ce que, qu’est-ce qui becoming ce qui, and no est-ce que or subject-pronoun inversion
Reported commands with dire, demander or conseiller à quelqu’un de + infinitive, including de ne pas + infinitive

The sequence of tenses after a past reporting verb: présent to imparfait, passé composé to plus-que-parfait, futur to conditionnel présent, aller + infinitive to allait + infinitive; imparfait and conditionnel unchanged
The plus-que-parfait, produced for the first time in B1, as the reported form of a passé composé (imparfait of avoir or être plus the participle, with agreement after être)
Time and place expressions in reported speech (le lendemain, la veille, ce jour-là, la semaine suivante, là), shifted only when the day has changed

recorded.desc: IL PART AND ILS PARTENT, ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, ONE VOICE, RECORDED ADJACENTLY AND IN THAT ORDER. The two are one consonant apart: eel par, then eel part. The T at the end of the plural must be ORDINARY: a final consonant released the way any French speaker releases it, not a taught, lengthened or emphasised one. RECORDED APART THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO FORMS, and any drift in pace or pitch between the halves will be heard as the difference instead of the T. The same instruction covers every pair in this clip list, and each pair is one take. The wrong-then-right pass for the trap drill goes in the same session: the wrong version is a competent learner saying eel par-TEES, which is confident and fluent and not a word, and it must not be caricatured.

THE COUVRIR QUARTET, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE FOUR MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. je couvre, tu couvres, il couvre, ils couvrent. This is the opposite instruction from the shedder clip and it is just as important: do not help, do not differentiate them, do not let the final -ent surface as anything at all. If a listener can tell any of these four apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Then nous couvrons and vous couvrez in the same take, ordinary and unemphasised, because they are the only two the ear is supposed to get.

THE WAKING S, and the pair must differ ONLY in the link. « Il ouvre à huit heures. » then « Ils ouvrent à huit heures. », one take, back to back. In the first the l of il runs onto the vowel as one word, ee-loovr. In the second the s of ils arrives as a z, eel-zoovr. THE VERB ITSELF IS IDENTICAL IN BOTH and must sound it: the whole teaching is that what changed is in front of the verb and not inside it. Do not separate the pronoun from the verb with a pause in either half, because the pause is exactly what destroys a liaison.

The mixed listening pairs, each pair one take back to back, singular then plural: il part / ils partent, il couvre / ils couvrent, il court / ils courent. Two of those three pairs are AUDIBLY DIFFERENT and one is IDENTICAL, and the learner is being asked to notice which is which, so the recording must not flatten the difference in the first two or invent one in the third. il court and ils courent in particular must be the same sound: courir has no consonant to give back and a helpful reading that hints at one would make the hardest question in the lesson unanswerable.

The twelve naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice, in the order the lesson groups them: the six shedders, then the five that take -er endings, then courir. Every one ends in the same EER sound and that sameness is the point, and the learner should come away hearing that the infinitive tells them nothing, which is exactly what the lesson claims. Do not vary the intonation between the groups; the grouping is on the screen and must not be given away by the reading. About a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, one woman in her twenties at an ordinary hostel-desk pace, friendly and unhurried. The « Pardon ? » is the whole scene and it is the hardest line to get right: it is a genuine, mild, unbothered request for a repeat, from somebody who simply did not catch a word. NOT a correction, not surprise, not amusement, and above all not pointed. She has no idea anything went wrong; there was just no word there. If it sounds at all like a raised eyebrow the scene stops being about the language and starts being about her.

lessons.intro: Twelve verbs end in -ir and take none of the pattern you just learned. They split into two families, and each one runs a rule you already have, so the only new skill here is deciding which before you build.

wakingS.body: ouvrir and offrir begin with a vowel, and the silent s of ils wakes up in front of a vowel. So il ouvre is ee-loovr and ils ouvrent is eel-zoovr: the verb is identical and the little word in front is not. The plural is audible after all, and it is the link doing it rather than the ending. These two are the most common verbs of their group, so this is the version you will meet first.
wakingS.title: When the plural is audible anyway

examples.note: The l of il links onto the vowel.
The s of ils arrives as a z, and that is the whole difference.

shedding.body: Take the last two letters off partir and you have part-. In the singular the t goes too, so je pars, tu pars and il part are all just par. In the plural it returns: ils partent ends on a t you can hear, and nous partons and vous partez bring a whole syllable. That is the same shape as finir from the last lesson, arriving by a different route: finir puts an -iss- in, and these give back a letter they already had.
shedding.title: partir, sortir, dormir

examples.note: One consonant more, and it is the only thing saying several.

erEndings.body: These five end in -ir and take the endings of an -er verb: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. So je couvre, tu couvres, il couvre and ils couvrent are four spellings and one sound, exactly as je parle and ils parlent were. Their infinitives all end in -vrir or -frir, and no verb from the last lesson does, so this is the one group you can spot from the spelling alone.
erEndings.title: ouvrir, offrir, couvrir

examples.note: Several, and not one sound has changed.

endingLies.body: ralentir takes the -iss- and sentir does not, and both end in -tir. guerir takes it and courir does not, and both end in -rir. So the infinitive cannot be read off for the answer, and the six that shed have to be held as a list rather than worked out. Six is not many, and they are worth it: partir, sortir and dormir are among the first verbs anybody needs.
endingLies.title: The last four letters decide nothing

examples.note: sentir, and the t comes back.
courir, where nothing comes back at all.

theFamilies.body: Every verb ending in -ir is in one of three groups. The ones from the last lesson add -iss- in the plural. Six shed a consonant in the singular and give it back in the plural: partir, sortir, dormir, servir, sentir, mentir. Five take the endings of an -er verb outright: ouvrir, offrir, couvrir, decouvrir, souffrir. Knowing which group a verb is in is the whole job, because each group runs a rule you already have.
theFamilies.title: Which rule this verb runs

examples.note: A shedder: the t comes back and you hear it.
An -er-ending verb: nothing comes back and nothing is heard.

sections.title: couvrir, all nine pronouns

sections.body: Put the two side by side and the shedders have five different sounds across nine pronouns while the -er-ending family has three. That is the whole of the difference, and neither of them is new. The plural puts a sound on the end. is what the first table does: par in the singular and part in the plural, and the t was in the naming form the whole time. Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person. is what the second table does, unchanged from the very first verb lesson, because these five simply are -er verbs wearing an -ir infinitive. The only genuinely new thing in this lesson is deciding which table a verb belongs to before you start, and the naming form tells you only when it ends in -vrir or -frir. There is one wrinkle in the second table and it matters because it covers the two commonest verbs in that family. ouvrir and offrir begin with a vowel, so the silent s of ils wakes up in front of them: ils ouvrent is eel-zoovr and il ouvre is ee-loovr, and the plural is audible after all. The verb has not changed. The link in front of it has. A consonant blocks that, which is why couvrir and not ouvrir is the verb this lesson used to state the four-spellings-one-sound claim.
sections.title: Why the two tables look so different

sections.body: The shedding mechanism is the one that keeps coming back. Lesson 5 teaches venir and tenir, which shed a consonant and change the vowel of the stem as well: je viens against ils viennent is the same movement with more happening. Lesson 4 teaches the regular -RE verbs, and il vend against ils vendent is exactly this lesson's first table with a different letter. So the six verbs you held as a list here are the entry price for three later units rather than a dead end. What does NOT carry forward is the -iss- of the previous lesson: it belongs to that family and to no other, and knowing where it stops is worth as much as knowing where it applies.
sections.title: What carries forward

sheets.title: The twelve, sorted
contains: Which verb is in which family
The one ending that gives it away

sections.body: Five of the twelve are free. ouvrir, offrir, couvrir, découvrir, souffrir all end in -vrir or -frir, and no verb that takes the -iss- ends either way, so the spelling settles them before you have to think. The other six are the price of the lesson: partir, sortir, dormir, servir, sentir, mentir have to be held as a list, because ralentir takes the -iss- and sentir does not and both end in -tir, and guérir takes it and courir does not and both end in -rir. Six is not many, and they are six you need early: partir, sortir and dormir turn up in the first week of anybody's French. courir is the odd one out and is worth a sentence of its own. It uses the endings of the shedders, so it looks like them on the page, but its stem has no consonant to shed, so it never gives one back and il court and ils courent are one sound. Filed with the shedders it will mislead you; filed on its own it costs nothing.

questions.a: Yes, but not from the verb. ouvre and ouvrent are one sound; what you hear is the silent s of ils waking up as a z in front of the vowel.
questions.q: The speaker says « Ils ouvrent à sept heures ». Could you hear that it was plural?

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have taken twelve verbs that all end in -ir and split them into two groups, and neither group asked you to learn a new sound. One gives a consonant back in the plural and one gives nothing, and the naming form only tells you which when it ends in -vrir or -frir. What is left is the part that says whether the sort has stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

rounds.say: Sort it before you build it.
rounds.label: Which family

questions.q: Which of these four takes the endings of an -er verb?
questions.why: offrir ends in -frir. Every -vrir and -frir verb takes -er endings, and it is the only ending in this area that decides the answer.

questions.q: Which of these four sheds a consonant in the singular?
questions.why: dormir gives je dors and ils dorment. The other three end in -vrir or -frir and never move a letter.

questions.q: Both ralentir and sentir end in -tir. Which one takes the -iss-?
questions.why: ralentir, from the last lesson. sentir gives elles sentent with a t. The last four letters decide nothing, which is why six verbs have to be held as a list.

questions.q: Ils ___ à huit heures. (partir)
questions.why: partir sheds its t in the singular and gives it back here. No -iss- anywhere in this verb.
accept: partent
questions.answer: partent

questions.q: Fix this. Three friends, at the desk: « Ils partissent à huit heures. »
questions.why: That is the last lesson’s rule on a verb that does not take it. The t was in partir all along.
accept: Ils partent à huit heures
partent
questions.answer: Ils partent à huit heures.

questions.q: Nous ___ tout. (couvrir)
questions.why: couvrir takes -er endings, so nous takes -ons exactly as it does on parler.
accept: couvrons
questions.answer: couvrons

rounds.say: These six are all shedders. Land the letter.
rounds.label: The consonant that comes back

questions.q: Listen. How many people?
questions.say: Ils partent tôt.
questions.why: A t arrived at the end of the verb, and on a shedder the singular never has one.
opts: It is not a real form

questions.q: Ils ___ encore. (dormir)
questions.why: The m of dormir comes back in the plural. je dors is just dor; ils dorment ends on the m.
accept: dorment
questions.answer: dorment

questions.q: Which form of sortir has NO consonant at the end of the sound?
questions.why: il sort is just sor. The t is written and never said, which is true of all three singular forms.

questions.q: Fix this. Two colleagues: « Ils part à huit heures. »
questions.why: The singular form on a plural subject. This is the commoner of the two mistakes, and out loud it says one person.
accept: Ils partent à huit heures
partent
questions.answer: Ils partent à huit heures.

questions.q: Elles ___ le café. (sentir)
questions.why: sentir sheds its t in the singular and restores it here, exactly like partir. Both end in -tir and neither takes the -iss-.
accept: sentent
questions.answer: sentent

questions.q: Listen. Which is on the page?
questions.say: Il part tôt.
questions.why: No consonant arrived, so it is the singular. On a shedder the ear really does settle this, which is the whole reason the family is worth naming.
opts: Both are said exactly like this

rounds.say: These are the -er endings. The recording will not help you.
rounds.label: Where nothing comes back

questions.q: Listen. How many people?
questions.say: Ils couvrent tout.
questions.why: couvrir takes -er endings, so il couvre and ils couvrent are one sound. Nothing in the recording can settle it.
opts: One or several, the sound does not say
It is not a real form

questions.q: Tu ___ tout. (couvrir)
questions.why: The -es of an -er verb. Silent, only tu takes it, and nothing you can hear will ever catch it.
accept: couvres
questions.answer: couvres

questions.q: je couvre, tu couvres, il couvre, ils couvrent. How many different sounds?
questions.why: One, and that is the same claim the very first verb lesson made about parler. This family never left it.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: The whole ending, exactly as on an -er verb. Nothing comes back in this family because nothing ever left.

questions.q: Fix this. One person: « Il couvrent tout. »
questions.why: Both spellings are said identically, so this survives being read back aloud. Only the pronoun on the page decides it.
accept: Il couvre tout
couvre
questions.answer: Il couvre tout.

questions.q: Ils ___ un cadeau. (offrir)
questions.why: offrir ends in -frir, so -ent, silent. What you would actually hear is the z of ils in front of the vowel.
accept: offrent
questions.answer: offrent

rounds.say: Two of this family start with a vowel, and they are the two you will meet.
rounds.label: The s that wakes up

questions.q: Listen. How many people?
questions.say: Ils ouvrent à huit heures.
questions.why: A z arrived in front of the verb. That is the silent s of ils waking up before a vowel, and the verb itself is unchanged.
opts: It is not a real form

questions.q: So what is different between il ouvre and ils ouvrent, out loud?
questions.why: ee-loovr against eel-zoovr. The verb is identical in both; the s of ils is what arrives.
opts: The link in front of the verb

questions.q: Why can you NOT hear the difference in ils couvrent?
questions.why: A liaison needs a vowel to land on. couvrir begins with a c, so the s of ils stays silent and the pair stays identical.
opts: couvrir starts with a consonant, so nothing links
couvrent is not a real form

questions.q: Vous ___ à sept heures ? (ouvrir)
questions.why: -ez, an -er ending. And the s of vous wakes up in front of the vowel too: voo-zoo-vray.
accept: ouvrez
questions.answer: ouvrez

questions.q: Say it: they open at eight.
questions.why: Land the z between ils and ouvrent as one movement. The verb itself stops after oovr.

questions.q: Fix this. A shop, several staff: « Il ouvrent à huit heures. »
questions.why: The verb is right and the pronoun is not. Out loud this one IS catchable, because the missing s is a missing z.
accept: Ils ouvrent à huit heures
Ils
questions.answer: Ils ouvrent à huit heures.

rounds.say: No warning which family. Decide, then build.
rounds.label: Both families at once

questions.q: Nous ___ ce soir. (sortir)
questions.why: A shedder, so the t comes back and brings a syllable. No -iss-, because sortir is not that family.
accept: sortons
questions.answer: sortons

questions.q: Tu ___ la ville. (découvrir)
questions.why: -vrir, so -er endings, so -es and silent. The accent is on the stem and is not what is being asked.
accept: découvres
decouvres
questions.answer: découvres

questions.q: Which pair sounds IDENTICAL?
questions.why: courir uses the shedders’ endings and has no consonant to shed, so it gives none back. The other three all restore one.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.say: Ils dorment encore.
questions.why: The m landed, so it is the plural. The other three all stop at dor, which is what a shedder does when only one person is doing it.
opts: Both the first and the third

questions.q: Fix this. A group, still asleep: « Ils dormissent encore. »
questions.why: dormir sheds its m and gives it back. It never takes an -iss-, and nor do the other five in its family.
accept: Ils dorment encore
dorment
questions.answer: Ils dorment encore.

questions.q: One verb ends in -rir and takes the -iss-. Which?
questions.why: guérir, from the last lesson. courir does not, and ouvrir and offrir end in -vrir and -frir and take -er endings instead.

sections.say: Four things, and then the unit that picks this up.
sections.body: You can take any verb ending in -ir and place it before you build it, which is the only new skill in this lesson: everything after the decision is a rule you already had. Two families, and you already know both rules. Six shed a consonant and give it back, five take the endings of an -er verb, and one is neither. The next unit on the trail teaches lesson 5’s venir and tenir, which run the shedding mechanism with a vowel change on top, and lesson 4 does the same thing with a whole different ending.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Check the family before you build.
6 shed a consonant in the singular and give it back in the plural.
5 end in -vrir or -frir and take the endings of an -er verb.
In front of a vowel the s of ils wakes up, so the plural is audible after all.

errorTriggers.description: Sorts a verb into the wrong family, usually by reading the last four letters of the naming form.
Leaves the consonant off a shedder’s plural: ils part, ils dorm. Says one person out loud.
Expects the plural of an -er-ending verb to be audible, and hears a difference that is not there.
Misses the z of ils in front of a vowel, or adds one where a consonant blocks it.
Puts the -iss- of the last lesson on a verb that never takes it: ils partissent, ils dormissent.

grammarAssumed: The present tense of regular -er verbs, introduced in a2.01
That -e, -es and -ent are silent and -ons and -ez are not, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -ir verbs and the -iss- of the plural, introduced in a2.10
That the plural of a regular -ir verb is audible where the singular is not, introduced in a2.10
Liaison, and that a silent final consonant links onto a following vowel, introduced in sons.10
grammarIntroduced: That a verb ending in -ir belongs to one of three families, decided verb by verb
The present tense of the verbs whose stem sheds a consonant in the singular
That -vrir and -frir verbs take the endings of a regular -er verb
That the infinitive ending does not predict which family a verb is in
That liaison makes the plural of a vowel-initial verb audible when the ending cannot

sections.say: The number comes once. Asking again is part of the script. Seven moves, and by the end of this deck you can predict which one is next.

cards.fr: Bonjour.
cards.body: In a French shop this is not a pleasantry, it is the price of entry, and it comes before the noun rather than after it. Skipping it is the one thing that reliably changes the room.
cards.head: Move 1
cards.label: you, and only here

cards.fr: Vous désirez ?
cards.body: She starts. From here to the end of the transaction you are answering, and the initiative never comes back to you.
cards.head: Move 2
cards.label: she asks

cards.fr: Je voudrais...
cards.body: Your request, and the only long sentence you get to build. At a market stall a quantity goes in here; at a clothes shop a size does.
cards.head: Move 3
cards.label: you answer

cards.fr: Et avec ceci ?
cards.body: The upsell, and it has no verb and no noun in it. Ce sera tout ? is the same move at a supermarket till. Saying nothing gets you asked twice.
cards.head: Move 4
cards.label: she asks

cards.fr: Ça fait...
cards.body: The frame, and the number is directly behind it. This is the one move in the seven that you cannot recover from by guessing, and act 3 is about nothing else.
cards.head: Move 5
cards.label: the figure lands

cards.fr: Par carte, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: You pay. Three words is the whole answer to Vous réglez comment ?, and lesson 24 in A2 taught the same exchange at a restaurant table.
cards.head: Move 6
cards.label: you answer

cards.fr: Je vous rends...
cards.body: The change, and a second figure. It is said faster than the first because she has already moved on to the person behind you.
cards.head: Move 7
cards.label: the second figure

sections.title: Seven Moves, In This Order

sections.say: Two hundred and thirty rows in this corpus are about shopping. Not one of them was in her voice until this lesson.

rows.say: Vous désirez ?

detail.title: She asks a quantity

rows.say: Et avec ceci ?

detail.say: Ce sera tout ?
detail.body: No verb and no noun in the whole question. Ce sera tout ? is the same move at a supermarket till, and silence gets you asked again rather than nothing.
detail.title: She upsells

rows.say: Ça fait quinze euros soixante, s'il vous plaît.

detail.say: Ça vous fait vingt-trois euros quarante.
detail.body: The frame is two syllables and the number is directly behind it. Nothing pauses between them, and the s'il vous plaît on the end means she has finished.

rows.say: C'est pour offrir ?

rows.say: Je vous rends deux euros soixante.

sections.title: What She Says, And Nobody Taught You

sections.say: Four, against her nine. You are not short of French. You are short of turns.

cards.fr: Bonjour.
cards.body: She has nine lines in this lesson and you have four. That is not a gap in your French, it is the shape of a till: she holds the prices, the stock and the initiative. You hold four short formulas, and that is enough.
cards.head: Why four
cards.label: the shape of a till

cards.fr: Bonjour, je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
cards.sub: [bohⁿ-ZHOOR zhuh voo-DREH ün ba-GET seel voo PLEH]
cards.body: Greeting and request in one breath, and the only long sentence you build in the whole transaction. Everything after this is three words or fewer.
cards.head: Move 3
cards.label: the one long one

cards.fr: Ça fait combien ?
cards.body: The most frequent question in a French shop, and it did not exist anywhere in this corpus before this lesson. Quel est le prix ? is published and is what a classroom teaches; this is what is said at a counter. Store it whole.
cards.head: Asking
cards.label: what is actually said

cards.fr: Ça fait quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros trente.
cards.body: Your question and the shape of her answer, together. The same two syllables open both, which is why the frame is worth hearing: it means the same thing whoever says it.
cards.head: The answer
cards.label: the same frame, coming back

cards.fr: Par carte, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: Three words answer the payment question completely. En espèces, s'il vous plaît is the other half. Building a sentence around either marks you out as translating rather than talking.
cards.head: Move 6
cards.label: three words is enough

cards.fr: je veux  /  je voudrais
cards.body: Both are correct and both are understood. Je veux is what a child says about a toy, and across a counter it lands too blunt. Nobody will tell you: nobody corrects a customer. Lesson 7 in A2 taught vouloir; here the choice costs something.
cards.head: One word apart
cards.label: grammatically perfect, socially wrong

lines.en: The total is forty-two euros.
lines.fr: Le total est de quarante-deux euros.

sections.title: Four Totals, Said Once

questions.q: Line 1. What is the total?
questions.why: Quatre-vingt-dix-sept, then trente. The cents are a bare number with no word in front of them, so nothing marks where the euros stop except the word euros itself.

questions.q: Line 2. What is the total?
questions.why: Vingt-trois euros quarante. The frame had vous inside it this time, which adds a syllable and changes nothing you have to do.

questions.q: Line 3. What is the total?
questions.why: Huit euros dix. Ça fera is a future tense doing the job of a present, and the figure sits in exactly the same place behind it.

questions.q: Line 4. How many of these four had cents in them?
questions.why: Only line 4 stopped at the currency word. When nothing follows euros, there are no cents, and that silence is the whole signal.

sections.say: Lesson 4 in A1 taught you the shape of a price. Nothing here is new about the number. What is new is that it lands inside her sentence and stops without warning.

rows.say: Ça fait dix-sept euros trente.

detail.say: Ça fait dix-sept euros trente.
detail.body: Lesson 4 in A1 §15 taught this: no word for centimes, no et joining the halves, and the only clue the price has finished is that she stops. Here the run starts mid-sentence, so there is no pause in front of it either.
detail.title: The bare cents

rows.say: Le total est de quarante-deux euros.

detail.say: Le total est de quarante-deux euros.
detail.body: When the sentence ends on the currency word there are no cents. The silence after euros is information, and it is the only kind of pause the price gives you.
detail.title: No cents at all

rows.say: Ça fait six euros quatre-vingt-quinze.

detail.say: Ça fait six euros quatre-vingt-quinze.
detail.body: Two syllables of euros and five of cents. Lesson 3 in A1 already ran quatre-vingt-quinze against quatre-vingt-dix-neuf at speed; the difference here is that you are past the currency word before it starts.
detail.title: The cents outrun the euros

rows.say: Ça fait cinquante euros pile.

detail.say: Ça fait cinquante euros pile.
detail.body: Pile means on the nose. It is the one word that tells you no cents are coming, so you can stop listening a syllable early.
detail.title: The word that closes it

rows.say: Ça vous fait dix-neuf euros quatre-vingt-dix.

detail.say: Ça vous fait dix-neuf euros quatre-vingt-dix.
detail.body: Dix-neuf and quatre-vingt-dix both end on a form of ten, and the currency word between them is the only thing separating the euros from the cents.
detail.title: Nineteen and ninety in one breath

rows.say: Alors, deux baguettes, ça fait deux euros quarante.

detail.say: Alors, deux baguettes, ça fait deux euros quarante.
detail.body: She lists what you bought before she gives the figure. Alors and the list are your warning that a number is next, and it is the only warning a French counter offers.
detail.title: The order counted back first

sections.title: Where The Cents Hide

sections.say: The number comes once. Asking again is part of the script. Four ways of saying it, and you need all four to know a figure is one syllable away.

cards.fr: Ça fait quinze euros soixante.
cards.body: The plain one, and the one you will hear most. Two syllables of frame and then the number, with nothing in between.
cards.head: Costume 1
cards.label: ça fait

cards.fr: Ça vous fait vingt-trois euros quarante.
cards.body: The same move with vous dropped inside it. One extra syllable, no extra meaning, and it is the version that catches people who learned only the first.
cards.head: Costume 2
cards.label: ça vous fait

cards.fr: Ça fera huit euros dix, s'il vous plaît.
cards.sub: [sa fuh-RA weet eu-ro DEESS seel voo PLEH]
cards.body: A future tense for something that is true right now. Fera and fait are the same verb and the same move; only the ending moved.
cards.head: Costume 3
cards.label: ça fera

cards.fr: Le total est de quarante-deux euros.
cards.body: The supermarket screen version, and the most formal of the four. Note the de before the figure, which none of the others has.
cards.head: Costume 4
cards.label: le total est de

cards.fr: Ça fait deux euros soixante-dix de rendu.
cards.sub: [sa feh deu-z eu-ro swa-sahⁿt-DEESS duh rahⁿ-DÜ]
cards.body: The same frame, carrying the opposite number. This is your change, not your bill. The frame tells you a figure is coming and never tells you which figure, so the word after it is the one to hold on to.
cards.head: The catch
cards.label: the frame lies about which number

sections.frSub: Ça fait, ça vous fait, ça fera
sections.title: One Move, Four Costumes

sections.say: Pairs that differ by one syllable and by a lot of money. You can see the French here, so this is the contrast rather than the test.

rule.body: French numbers build to the right, so two prices can share every sound until the last one. Lesson 3 in A1 taught the pairs. At a till they arrive after a currency word and with no second chance.
rule.title: The syllable at the end is the whole number

cards.ipa: /ka.tʁə.vɛ̃.dis.sɛt/
cards.tip: Quatre-vingt-dix-sept and quatre-vingt-sept share four syllables. The dix in the middle is ten euros, and it is the shortest syllable in the run.
cards.promptSound: Ça fait quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros.

cards.ipa: /swa.sɑ̃t.kɛ̃z/
cards.tip: Soixante-quinze and soixante-cinq both open on soixante. Lesson 3 in A1 owns this pair; here it arrives with euros behind it and no time to reconstruct.
cards.promptSound: Ça fait soixante-quinze euros.

cards.ipa: /dø ø.ʁo dis/
cards.tip: Deux euros dix and douze euros are almost the same mouthful. The currency word sits in the middle of one and at the end of the other, and that is the only clue.
cards.promptLabel: two euros ten against twelve euros
cards.promptSound: Ça fait deux euros dix.

cards.fr: that is your change
cards.ipa: /də ʁɑ̃.dy/
cards.tip: Same frame, same shape, opposite direction. De rendu on the end is the word that tells you this figure is coming back to you rather than out of your pocket.
cards.promptLabel: the frame that is not the price
cards.promptSound: Ça fait deux euros soixante-dix de rendu.

drill.promptSay: Ça fait quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros trente.
Ça fait soixante-cinq euros.
Ça fait douze euros.
Ça fait deux euros dix.
Je vous rends deux euros soixante.
Ça fait six euros quatre-vingt-quinze.

sections.title: Which Number Was It

sections.say: The number comes once. Asking again is part of the script. Lesson 24 in A2 taught the six ways. Nothing new here, except that the thing you missed was a figure.

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: One word, and it gives away nothing about why you missed it. Lesson 24 in A2 put it first because it is what a French speaker says without thinking, and because it costs you nothing at all.
cards.head: Rung 1
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 1

cards.fr: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.body: Asks for the whole thing again. At a till the whole thing is one short sentence, so this costs almost nothing more than rung 1 and is worth reaching for straight away.
cards.head: Rung 2
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 2

cards.fr: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: The first rung that names the fault. Use it when she has already repeated the figure once at exactly the same speed, which is what happens if you asked with rung 1.
cards.head: Rung 3
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 3

cards.fr: Ça fait combien, pardon ?
cards.body: Lesson 24 in A2 teaches you to reach for the lowest rung that will fix the problem. A number is the one case where naming what you missed beats asking for the whole sentence again, because there is only one thing you could have missed.
cards.head: A number is different
cards.label: name the figure, not the sentence

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: Nobody is annoyed. A French speaker repeats a price without a flicker, several times a day, for French people too. The instinct to apologise first is what turns a one-word repair into an incident.
cards.head: The part that goes wrong
cards.label: not an apology

sections.title: You Missed The Number

sections.say: The number comes once. Asking again is part of the script. That goes for the second number too, and it is said faster than the first.

rows.say: Je vous rends deux euros soixante.

detail.say: Je vous rends deux euros soixante.
detail.body: A second number, in the same shape as the first. Rendre is lesson 4 in A2's verb and it is used whole here: the useful part is that a figure follows it immediately.
detail.title: The figure comes back

rows.say: Voilà votre monnaie.

detail.say: Voilà votre monnaie.
detail.body: The coins go into your hand and she says nothing about how many. You are expected to have caught the first figure, which is the whole argument for catching it.
detail.title: No number this time

rows.say: Vous avez la monnaie ?

detail.say: Je n'ai que des billets.
detail.body: It means she is short of coins, and it is a request rather than curiosity. Je n'ai que des billets is the straight answer and it keeps things moving.
detail.title: Asked BEFORE you pay

rows.say: Vous n'avez pas plus petit ?

detail.say: Vous n'avez pas plus petit ?
detail.body: Never a smaller object. Handing over a fifty for a baguette is what triggers it, and it is asked in every bakery in France before nine in the morning.
detail.title: Plus petit is a note

rows.say: Je vous rends la monnaie sur vingt euros.

detail.say: Je vous rends la monnaie sur vingt euros.
detail.body: Not what you get back. The figure inside sur vingt euros is the note, which is the opposite of what an English ear reaches for, and it is the one place in this lesson where the number in the sentence is not yours to keep.
detail.title: Sur names the note you handed over

rows.say: Vous pouvez faire l'appoint ?

detail.say: Désolé, je n'ai pas de monnaie.
detail.body: L'appoint is the exact coins. Being asked for it is being asked to do arithmetic in a queue, which is why recognising the phrase fast matters more than being able to say it.
detail.title: The politest way to say she has no change

sections.title: What Comes Back

sections.say: Two words from you and four instructions from the machine. The last two cards are Quebec, and they are here to be recognised rather than said.

cards.fr: Vous réglez comment ?
cards.body: Comment is how, not how much. Lesson 24 in A2 taught this exact question at a restaurant table and the answer at a till is the same three words.
cards.head: She asks
cards.label: the method, not the amount

cards.fr: Par carte, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: Three words and the transaction moves on. En espèces, s'il vous plaît is the other half. payer par carte and payer en espèces are already published as infinitives; these are the answer forms.
cards.head: You answer
cards.label: three words

cards.fr: Insérez votre carte et tapez votre code.
cards.sub: [aⁿ-say-RAY votr KART ay ta-PAY votr KOD]
cards.body: Two imperatives and no please, which is the register of an instruction rather than rudeness. Le code is what a till calls the PIN; le code secret is the formal term.
cards.head: The machine
cards.label: two instructions

cards.fr: le paiement sans contact
cards.body: Below fifty euros in France the card usually needs no code at all. You tap and she says nothing, which means the only spoken number in the whole transaction was the total.
cards.head: Under fifty
cards.label: no code needed

cards.fr: Vous voulez le ticket ?
cards.body: Le ticket at the counter, le ticket de caisse on the printed thing itself. If you missed the total, this is the last chance to find out what it was.
cards.head: And then
cards.label: your last chance at the figure

cards.fr: magasiner
cards.body: What faire les courses and faire du shopping are called in Quebec. This lesson drills the France forms and this word is here so you recognise it, not so you produce it.
cards.head: In Quebec
cards.label: recognition only

cards.fr: un dépanneur
cards.body: The corner shop, open late. Same job as une supérette in France. Again: recognition only, and it is not wrong anywhere, it is simply somewhere else.
cards.head: In Quebec
cards.label: recognition only

sections.title: Paying, And The Machine

sections.say: Four fixed things to say. Without them a learner either buys something they did not want or walks out mid-sentence, and both happen constantly.

cards.fr: Je peux vous aider ?
cards.body: In a French shop this is an approach rather than an offer, and it happens within about ten seconds of the door. Vous cherchez quelque chose ? is the same move.
cards.head: She approaches
cards.label: she starts, again

cards.fr: Je regarde seulement, merci.
cards.body: The whole answer, and it ends the exchange politely. It is the single most useful thing in this mission and it is four words.
cards.head: You answer
cards.label: the complete answer

cards.fr: C'est un peu cher pour moi.
cards.body: Un peu is what makes it sayable. C'est cher on its own sounds like a complaint about her shop; pour moi puts it on your wallet, which nobody can argue with.
cards.head: Too expensive
cards.label: un peu does the work

cards.fr: Je vais réfléchir, merci.
cards.body: Closes the conversation without refusing anything, which is why it is the one French shoppers actually use. A futur proche, and lesson 15 in A2 owns that; here it is one fixed phrase.
cards.head: Getting out
cards.label: refuses nothing, ends everything

cards.fr: Vous avez ça en trente-huit ?
cards.body: The size question with no word for size in it. French sizes are numbers, so the number does the work and ça points at the thing in your hand. She may ask it first: Vous faites quelle taille ?
cards.head: Asking for a size
cards.label: the number is the size

sections.title: Not Buying Is Also A Move

sections.say: Three cards, none of them tested. Everything scored in this lesson is France, in euros, and the number she says is the number you pay.

cards.fr: Au Québec, les taxes s'ajoutent à la caisse.
cards.sub: [oh kay-BEK lay taks sa-ZHOOT a lah KESS]
cards.body: In France the shelf says vingt euros and the till says vingt euros. In Quebec the shelf says vingt dollars and the till says more, because the taxes go on at the end. The label is not a promise.
cards.head: Same basket, two countries
cards.label: the label and the till, together

cards.fr: Vingt-deux dollars quatre-vingt-dix.
cards.body: You are not mis-hearing the accent. You expected the number you read, and the expectation is what broke. The move is the same as everywhere else here: wait for the till, and if you missed it, ask. Lesson 24 in A2 gave you six ways.
cards.head: What that does to your ear
cards.label: expectation, not accent

cards.fr: magasiner  /  un dépanneur
cards.body: Magasiner is faire les courses and un dépanneur is the corner shop. This lesson drills the France forms and neither of these appears in anything scored. They are here to be recognised, not produced. Neither is wrong: they are somewhere else.
cards.head: Two words, recognition only
cards.label: recognise, do not produce

sections.title: The Label Is Not The Price

sections.say: Four, one per screen. Three of them cost you money and the fourth costs you the conversation.
sections.title: What Goes Wrong

errors.why: The most expensive habit in this lesson, and it is not a French mistake at all. One word gets the figure repeated, and lesson 24 in A2 spent a whole mission on why it costs you nothing.
errors.right: Pardon ?
errors.wrong: Handing over a note and hoping.

errors.why: Understood perfectly and one rung too blunt across a counter. Nobody corrects a customer, so nobody learns it. Lesson 7 in A2 taught vouloir; this is where the form choice does something.
errors.right: Je voudrais une baguette.
errors.wrong: Je veux une baguette.

errors.why: The figure inside sur names the note you gave her, not the coins coming back. It is the one place where the number in the sentence is not yours to keep.
errors.right: Sur vingt euros is what you handed over.
errors.wrong: Hearing sur vingt euros as your change.

errors.why: Answering an approach with yes commits you to being helped. Four words end it politely, and without them people buy things or walk out mid-sentence.
errors.right: Je regarde seulement, merci.
errors.wrong: Oui, merci.

sections.say: Four questions that arrive after the total and before you have finished paying. None of them is a number, and none of them was in your script.

lines.en: Do you have the store card?
lines.fr: Vous avez la carte du magasin ?

lines.en: Is it a gift?
lines.fr: C'est pour offrir ?

lines.en: Do you need a bag?
lines.fr: Il vous faut un sac ?

lines.en: Do you have change?
lines.fr: Vous avez la monnaie ?

sections.title: The One You Did Not Plan For

questions.q: Line 1. When is this asked, and what does saying non cost you?
questions.why: It arrives as an interruption, with the figure already showing. It is a loyalty card and not having one changes nothing about the price you pay.
opts: Before you order, and it costs you your place in the queue
While the total is on the screen, and non costs you nothing
After you have paid, and non means no receipt
At the door, and non means you cannot come in

questions.q: Line 2. You say oui. What happens next?
questions.why: Offrir is to give as a present. Oui commits you to standing there while it is wrapped, so this is one to answer deliberately rather than reflexively.
opts: She gift-wraps it, which takes several minutes
She puts it in a bag
She asks for the exact money

questions.q: Line 3. What is she actually telling you?
questions.why: In France the bag usually costs, so il vous faut un sac ? is a sale rather than an offer. Falloir here means need, and she is asking whether you need one enough to pay for it.
opts: That you have bought too much
That there is probably a charge for it
That she has run out of bags

questions.q: Line 4. She asks this BEFORE you have paid. Why?
questions.why: It is a request, not curiosity about your wallet. Je n'ai que des billets is the straight answer, and it is better than searching your pockets while the queue waits.
opts: She wants to know if you can afford it
She is short of coins and is asking you to help
She is checking you have a card
She is telling you the price has changed

sections.say: Six of her lines, and the figure is inside each one. You have heard every one of them at least three times by now.
sections.title: Write What She Said

sections.say: The thing you did not read on the tram. Every answer is on one line of it, and none of them needs adding up.
sections.text:
BOULANGERIE MARTIN
14 rue des Halles, TOURS
Mardi 12/03  08h41  Caisse 2

Baguette tradition          x6      1,30      7,80
Croissant beurre           x12      1,15     13,80
Quiche lorraine 4 parts     x3      9,50     28,50
Plateau salé 24 pieces      x1     47,00     47,00
Jus d'orange 1L             x2      2,60      5,20

SOUS-TOTAL                                  102,30
Remise fidélité 5%                          - 5,00
TOTAL A PAYER                                97,30

Espèces                                     100,00
RENDU                                         2,70

Horaires : 7h00 - 19h30, fermé le lundi
Conservez ce ticket pour tout échange.
sections.title: The Receipt In Your Pocket

glossary.note: The figure before anything is taken off. It is not what you pay and it is the larger of the two.
What comes off. Une réduction and une promotion are the words on the shelf; remise is the word on the receipt.
The last line. What she handed back, printed, which is how you find out whether you caught it.
The line above shows what you handed over, not what you owed. The two are different numbers and the receipt prints both.
An imperative aimed at you. Without the ticket there is no exchange, which is the whole reason it says so.

questions.a: Ninety-seven euros thirty. TOTAL A PAYER is the line, at 97,30. SOUS-TOTAL at 102,30 is what it would have been before the discount, and it is the bigger number of the two, which is why reading the wrong line always errs upward.
questions.q: What did the customer actually pay, and which line says so?

questions.a: The Espèces line reads 100,00. It records what was handed over rather than what was owed, and RENDU on the next line is what came back.
questions.q: The customer handed over a hundred euros. How do you know from the receipt?

questions.a: The first is le prix unitaire, what one costs, and the second is what the whole quantity costs. Six baguettes at 1,30 makes the 7,80 in the right-hand column.
questions.q: Why are there two numbers next to each item?

questions.a: That you cannot. The Horaires line reads fermé le lundi. It also tells you to keep the ticket for any exchange, so the ticket is necessary and Monday is still impossible.
questions.q: You come back on a Monday to exchange something. What does the receipt tell you?

questions.a: A five percent loyalty discount. It is written with a minus sign, and it sits between the subtotal and the total, which is the position on a French receipt where deductions go.
questions.q: What is la remise fidélité, and how is it marked as coming off rather than going on?

questions.a: RENDU, at 2,70. It is the last figure printed and it is the one that was said fastest at the till, which is the argument for reading the receipt at all.
questions.q: Which single line would tell you whether you caught the change correctly at the counter?

sections.say: Your four moves, the two refusals, and lesson 24 in A2's first three rungs. Say them to the phone before you say them to a cashier.
sections.title: Say Your Four

sections.say: Eleven turns, start to finish. She starts, you answer, and two numbers arrive that nobody repeats unless you ask.
sections.title: The Whole Counter

turns.ai: Bonjour !
turns.en: Good morning!

alts.en: Hello.
alts.fr: Bonjour.

alts.en: Good morning. How are you?
alts.fr: Bonjour, madame. Ça va ?

turns.user: Bonjour, madame.
turns.userEn: Good morning.

turns.ai: Vous désirez ?
turns.en: What would you like?

alts.en: Two baguettes, please.
alts.fr: Deux baguettes, s'il vous plaît.

alts.en: I'll take two baguettes.
alts.fr: Je vais prendre deux baguettes.

turns.user: Je voudrais deux baguettes, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: I would like two baguettes, please.

turns.ai: Et avec ceci ?
turns.en: Anything else with that?

alts.en: That'll be all, thanks.
alts.fr: Ce sera tout, merci.

alts.en: And four croissants.
alts.fr: Et quatre croissants.

turns.user: Une quiche, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: A quiche, please.

turns.ai: Combien je vous mets de croissants ?
turns.en: How many croissants shall I give you?

alts.en: Half a dozen.
alts.fr: Une demi-douzaine.

alts.en: Four, thanks.
alts.fr: Quatre, merci.

turns.user: Quatre, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Four, please.

turns.ai: Ce sera tout ?
turns.en: Will that be all?

alts.en: Yes, that'll be all.
alts.fr: Oui, ce sera tout.

alts.en: No, an orange juice as well.
alts.fr: Non, un jus d'orange aussi.

turns.user: Ce sera tout, merci.
turns.userEn: That will be all, thanks.

turns.ai: C'est pour offrir ?
turns.en: Is it a gift?

alts.en: No, it's for me.
alts.fr: Non, c'est pour moi.

alts.en: Yes, please.
alts.fr: Oui, s'il vous plaît.

turns.ai: Alors, ça vous fait vingt-trois euros quarante.
turns.en: So, that comes to twenty-three euros forty.

alts.en: Twenty-three forty?
alts.fr: Vingt-trois quarante ?

alts.en: OK, twenty-three euros forty.
alts.fr: D'accord, vingt-trois euros quarante.

turns.user: Vingt-trois euros quarante, d'accord.
turns.userEn: Twenty-three forty, right.

turns.ai: Vous réglez comment ?
turns.en: How are you paying?

alts.en: Can you say that again, please?
alts.fr: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

alts.en: More slowly, please.
alts.fr: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.

turns.user: Pardon ?
turns.userEn: Sorry?

turns.ai: Vous réglez comment ? Carte ou espèces ?

alts.en: By card, please.
alts.fr: Par carte, s'il vous plaît.

alts.en: Cash.
alts.fr: En espèces.

turns.user: En espèces, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: In cash, please.

turns.ai: Vous n'avez pas plus petit ?

alts.en: No, sorry.
alts.fr: Non, désolé.

alts.en: Yes, hold on.
alts.fr: Si, attendez.

turns.user: Je n'ai que des billets, désolé.
turns.userEn: I only have notes, sorry.
