sections.setting: Boulangerie Martin, Tours, a Tuesday morning. Two people in the queue behind you.

sections.say: Her half and yours, together, one last time.

cards.say: Vous désirez ?
cards.back: Vous désirez ? She starts, and the initiative never comes back.
cards.front: You have just walked in and she speaks first

cards.say: Ça fait quinze euros soixante.
cards.back: Ça fait... The frame. Ça vous fait, ça fera and le total est de are the same move.
cards.front: Two syllables, and a number is directly behind them

cards.say: Ça fait combien ?
cards.back: Ça fait combien ? Not Quel est le prix, which is what a classroom teaches.
cards.front: The most frequent question in a French shop

cards.say: Combien je vous mets ?
cards.back: Combien je vous mets ? Answer with a container: un kilo de, une tranche de.
cards.front: She wants a quantity, not a thing

cards.say: Et avec ceci ?
cards.back: Et avec ceci ? She is upselling, and silence gets you asked again.
cards.front: No verb and no noun in the whole question

cards.say: Pardon ?
cards.back: Pardon ? One word, and it costs you nothing. Lesson 24 in A2, rung 1.
cards.front: You caught everything except the figure

cards.say: Je vous rends deux euros soixante.
cards.back: Je vous rends deux euros soixante. Said faster than the first, and to your back.
cards.front: The second number of the transaction

cards.say: Vous avez la monnaie ?
cards.back: Vous avez la monnaie ? She is short of coins. Je n'ai que des billets.
cards.front: She asks it BEFORE you pay, and it is a request

cards.say: Vous n'avez pas plus petit ?
cards.back: Vous n'avez pas plus petit ? A smaller note, never a smaller object.

cards.say: Je vous rends la monnaie sur vingt euros.
cards.back: sur vingt euros. It names the note you handed over.
cards.front: The figure in this phrase is not yours to keep

cards.say: Vous réglez comment ?
cards.back: Vous réglez comment ? Par carte, s'il vous plaît. Three words.

cards.say: Je regarde seulement, merci.
cards.back: Je peux vous aider ? Je regarde seulement, merci.
cards.front: She approached you within ten seconds of the door

sections.title: Everything She Said

sections.say: Twenty-two missions. Here is what changed.
sections.body: You came in able to ask for things and left able to be charged for them. The seven moves are the same seven in a bakery, at a market stall and at a supermarket till, so the next counter is not a new problem. Two numbers arrive in every transaction and neither is repeated, and you now know the two-syllable warning that one of them is coming. And when the figure goes past you anyway, there is one word that gets it back.

stats.v: 6, and they are lesson 24 in A2's

sections.title: Where You Are

sections.say: Four rounds of eight. The first round is the only place in this app where you cannot read the answer.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Eight you have to hear. Nothing is written down.
rounds.label: Catch the figure

questions.q: Listen. What is the total?
questions.say: Ça fait quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros trente.
questions.why: Quatre-vingt-dix-sept, then trente. The dix in the middle is the ten euros that separates it from quatre-vingt-sept.

questions.q: Listen. What is the total?
questions.say: Ça vous fait vingt-trois euros quarante.
questions.why: Vingt-trois euros quarante. The vous inside the frame adds a syllable and changes nothing about where the figure sits.

questions.q: Listen. What is the total?
questions.say: Ça fait six euros quatre-vingt-quinze.
questions.why: The cents run longer than the euros here. Quatre-vingt-quinze is five syllables after a two-syllable currency word.

questions.q: Listen. What is the total?
questions.say: Ça fait cinquante euros pile.
questions.why: Pile means on the nose, so there are no cents at all. It is the one word that tells you the number has finished early.

questions.q: Listen. What is the total?
questions.say: Ça fait deux euros dix.
questions.why: Deux euros dix and douze euros are almost the same mouthful. The currency word sits in the middle of one and at the end of the other.

questions.q: Listen. How much is coming back to you?
questions.say: Je vous rends deux euros soixante.
questions.why: Je vous rends is change, not a bill. The figure is the same shape as a total and it goes in the opposite direction.
opts: Nothing, that is what you owe

questions.q: Listen. What does the figure in this sentence refer to?
questions.say: Je vous rends la monnaie sur vingt euros.
questions.why: Sur names what you gave her. It is the one place in the lesson where the number in the sentence is not yours to keep.

questions.q: Listen. How many cents?
questions.say: Le total est de quarante-deux euros.
questions.why: The sentence stops on the currency word. When nothing follows euros there are no cents, and that silence is the whole signal.

rounds.say: Eight on the shape of the encounter rather than the words.
rounds.label: Which move is this

questions.q: She says « Combien je vous mets ? ». What does she want?
questions.why: Combien is how much. She wants a container: un kilo de, une tranche de. Answering with a noun leaves her holding the scoop.

questions.q: She says « Et avec ceci ? ». Where in the encounter are you?
questions.why: Move 4. There is no verb and no noun in the question, so nothing in the words tells you it is about your order.
opts: She is upselling, after your first request
She is asking how you pay

questions.q: Which of these does NOT introduce the amount you owe?
questions.why: Same frame, opposite direction. De rendu on the end is what makes it your change, and the frame alone never tells you which figure is coming.
opts: Ça fait deux euros soixante-dix de rendu.
Le total est de quarante-deux euros.

questions.q: Which of these comes FIRST in a French shop?
questions.why: It is the price of entry and it comes before the noun rather than after it. Skipping it is the one thing that reliably changes the room.

questions.q: She asks « Vous avez la monnaie ? » before you have paid. Why?
questions.why: It is a request rather than curiosity. Je n'ai que des billets is the straight answer and it keeps the transaction moving.
opts: She is short of coins and is asking for help
She is checking you can afford it
She wants to see your card
She is telling you the price

questions.q: « Vous réglez comment ? » is asking about
questions.why: Comment is how, not how much. Lesson 24 in A2 taught the same question at a restaurant table and the answer is still three words.
opts: Whether you have a loyalty card

questions.q: She says « Il vous faut un sac ? ». What is she actually doing?
questions.why: In France the bag usually costs. Falloir means need, and she is asking whether you need one enough to pay for it.
opts: Telling you she has no bags

questions.q: How many of the seven moves does the customer start?
questions.why: Bonjour is yours and everything after it is an answer. That asymmetry is the shape of a till rather than a gap in your French.

rounds.say: Eight on the half you produce, which is the short half.
rounds.label: Your four moves

questions.q: Ask what it costs, the way it is said at a counter. Three words: « Ça ... ? »
questions.why: Fait, not coûte, and combien on the end. Quel est le prix ? is published in this corpus and is what a classroom teaches; this is what is said in a shop. The cedilla is not being tested, the word choice is.
accept: Ça fait combien ?
ça fait combien
Ca fait combien ?
ca fait combien
questions.answer: Ça fait combien ?

questions.q: You are ordering across a counter. Fix this.
questions.why: Je veux is grammatical, understood, and one rung too blunt across a counter. Nobody corrects a customer, which is why nobody learns it. Veux and voudrais do not fold together, so the form is genuinely being tested.
accept: Je voudrais une baguette.
je voudrais une baguette
Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
questions.answer: Je voudrais une baguette.
questions.prompt: Je veux une baguette.

questions.q: She says « Vous réglez comment ? ». Best answer?
questions.why: Three words answer it completely. The long one is understood and marks you out as translating rather than talking.
opts: Je voudrais payer maintenant, avec ma carte bancaire.

questions.q: She asked « Combien je vous mets ? ». Fix the answer.
questions.why: She asked how much, not what. Naming the container is what answers it, and lesson 8 in A1 owns the rule that the container removes the des.
accept: Un kilo de tomates.
un kilo de tomates
Un kilo, s'il vous plaît.
un kilo
questions.answer: Un kilo de tomates.
questions.prompt: Des tomates.

questions.q: She says « Je peux vous aider ? » and you want to be left alone.
questions.why: Four words end it politely. Oui commits you to being helped and non on its own is the one answer that sounds rude.

questions.q: Say it is a bit expensive for you. Six words: « C'est ... cher pour moi. »
questions.why: Un peu is what makes it sayable, and it does not fold into the version without it. C'est cher pour moi sounds like a complaint about her shop.
accept: C'est un peu cher pour moi.
cest un peu cher pour moi
un peu
questions.answer: C'est un peu cher pour moi.

questions.q: Which of these is the classroom version rather than the counter version?
questions.why: It is published in this corpus and it is correct. It is also what nobody says at a till, which is exactly why it was worth naming.
opts: Quel est le prix, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: You are paying cash. Which is the answer form?
questions.why: The other three are all published and none of them answers a question. An infinitive is how a phrase is stored; it is not how it is said back.

rounds.say: Eight on asking again, and the repair ladder belongs to lesson 24 in A2.
rounds.label: When you miss it

questions.q: Say it out loud. She gave you the total and you caught none of it.
questions.why: One word, said flat and quickly. Said as a question with a rising end it is ordinary; drawn out it turns into an apology, which is the thing that makes a repair into an incident.

questions.q: Say lesson 24 in A2's rung 2 out loud, to a cashier who has already moved on.
questions.why: Six syllables in one run with no pause in the middle. At a till the whole thing is one short sentence, so asking for all of it costs almost nothing more than rung 1.
questions.target: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: She repeated the total once, at exactly the same speed. Which rung now?
questions.why: Rungs 1 and 2 both just ask for a repeat, and she cannot fix a problem you have not named. Rung 3 is the first that says it was the speed. Lesson 24 in A2 owns the repair ladder.
opts: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: Why is asking again cheaper at a till than almost anywhere else?
questions.why: You know she said a figure. Naming what you missed narrows it completely, which is the reasoning lesson 24 in A2 set out for reaching for the lowest rung that will actually fix the problem.
opts: There is only one thing in the sentence you could have missed
The price is always written down
French people speak slowly at tills

questions.q: The cheapest thing you can say when you caught nothing. One word.
questions.why: Lesson 24 in A2 put it at rung 1 because it gives away nothing about why you missed it and because it is what a French speaker says without thinking.
accept: Pardon
Pardon ?
pardon
questions.answer: Pardon ?

questions.q: You did not catch the total and you hand over a note that is obviously too big. What has it cost you?
questions.why: It works, which is the problem. The transaction completes, nobody corrects you, and the habit survives because it never visibly fails.
opts: You will not know what you paid until you read the receipt

questions.q: She says « Vous n'avez pas plus petit ? ». What is plus petit?
questions.why: Never a smaller object. Handing over a fifty for a baguette is what triggers it, and it is asked in every bakery in France before nine in the morning.

questions.q: A friend reads your receipt and says this. Fix it.
questions.why: Cent deux euros trente is the SOUS-TOTAL, before the discount. TOTAL A PAYER is the line that says what left your pocket, and reading the wrong one always errs upward.
accept: Tu as payé quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros trente.
tu as payé quatre vingt dix sept euros trente
quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros trente
questions.answer: Tu as payé quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros trente.
questions.prompt: Tu as payé cent deux euros trente.

sections.say: Three things, and the first one is the whole lesson.
sections.body: The number comes once. Asking again is part of the script, and lesson 24 in A2 gave you six ways to do it. Before the figure there is a two-syllable warning, and ça fait, ça vous fait, ça fera and le total est de are all the same warning wearing different clothes. After the figure there is a second one, said faster, which is your change. Everything else at a counter is seven moves in a fixed order, and you start exactly one of them.
sections.title: What You Take With You
points: The number comes once. Asking again is part of the script.
Ça fait, ça vous fait, ça fera, le total est de. One move, four costumes, and a figure is one syllable behind it.
Two numbers arrive in every transaction. The second one is your change and it is said faster than the first.
Seven moves in a fixed order, and Bonjour is the only one you start.
In Quebec the label is not the price, because the taxes go on at the till. Wait for the till.

errorTriggers.description: Does not catch the figure, and hands over a note rather than asking. The transaction completes, so the habit never visibly fails.
Catches the euros and loses the cents, because they arrive as a bare number after the currency word with nothing marking the join.
Cannot say which of the seven moves a line belongs to, so answers the wrong question or says nothing.
Fails on the questions with nothing to anchor on: Et avec ceci ?, Ce sera tout ?, Ça fait...
Orders with je veux, which is grammatical, understood, and one rung too blunt across a counter. Nobody corrects a customer.
Answers a three-word question with a full sentence, which is understood and marks the speaker as translating rather than talking.
Reads a change figure as a price, most often on sur vingt euros, where the number names the note handed over rather than the coins coming back.
Says nothing when the figure goes past, and pays with a note chosen by guesswork rather than asking for the number again.
Reaches too high or too low on lesson 24 in A2's repair ladder: asking for a repeat when the speed was the problem, or apologising before asking at all.

grammarIntroduced: The seven-move structure of a French counter transaction, received in the cashier's voice rather than produced in the learner's
Recognition of the four frames that introduce a total, ça fait, ça vous fait, ça fera and le total est de, as one move in four costumes
Price reception at native speed inside another speaker's turn, as APPLICATION of a1.28's price shape rather than a second teaching of it
Change reception as a second figure, said faster than the first, which is what the published canDo means by count change
That sur vingt euros names the note handed over rather than the change returned
The quantity containers of a1.29 produced under counter pressure, with no new claim made about the partitive
A four-item refusal script, so that a learner who does not want to buy can leave without going silent
That in Quebec the shelf price is not the price paid, because the taxes are added at the till, taught as an expectation and never as an arithmetic operation
The repair move applied to a number, cited from a2.07 by itemId and unit id, with zero repair rows authored here
That the amount, the change and the coins are this unit's, and l'addition and the restaurant script are a2.07's

acts.title: The word that was not a word
acts.milestone: You know why the rule you learned last lesson produces a word that does not exist, and you know that the answer is five things rather than thirty-three.

acts.title: What you already have
acts.milestone: You can see that lesson 16's shape has not moved at all, and you can see the six places where the part of it you build breaks.

acts.title: Five groups
acts.milestone: You can put any of the thirty-three in its group, you get every compound of them free, and you have met the second form of every irregular verb you already knew.

acts.title: The ones that look derivable
acts.milestone: You have seen what you would have produced, beside what the language has, for all six of the verbs that invite it. And you can say eu and spell dû.

acts.title: Out loud
acts.milestone: You answered for five verbs the lesson never showed you, you held the conversation the kettle lost, and you spelled eleven forms you could not have built.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: You wrote past forms for verbs that appear nowhere in this lesson, which is the half of it a list could never have taught you.

recorded.desc: THE KETTLE ON A MONDAY, AND THE SAME COLLEAGUE AS lesson 16 in A2. She has asked a friendly question and is waiting for an answer she expects to be short. THE LEARNER'S OWN LINE IS THE TAKE THAT HAS TO BE RIGHT. « Samedi, j'ai... j'ai prendu... » is somebody who is not hesitating out of shyness: the first word came out fine, the second one was produced by a rule, and it is wrong in a way he cannot hear. READ « prendu » PLAINLY AND WITH CONFIDENCE. He believes it. A hesitant or apologetic reading turns the scene into somebody guessing, and the whole point is that he was not guessing. HER LAST LINE IS THE EXPENSIVE ONE. « Pardon ? Tu as fait quoi ? » is a person who did not receive a word, not a person being patient with a foreigner. No warmth-about-a-mistake, no encouragement, no slowing down. She simply did not get it.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE GROUP TRAP, AND IT IS A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. Four lines, one take, in this order: « J'ai prendu le bus. » then « J'ai pris le bus. », then « J'ai ouvri la porte. » then « J'ai ouvert la porte. » READ THE WRONG ONES PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly. Both are perfectly pronounceable French shapes and both are exactly what a careful learner produces; a reading that signals the error teaches that the error is audible, and to a learner who has not met the real form it is not. DO NOT SEPARATE THE TWO HALVES OF EACH PAIR WITH A LONG PAUSE. The pair is the teaching and it works when the two lines sit against each other.

THE HARDEST TWO LETTERS IN THE LESSON, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, FIVE LINES, AND THE BRIEF NAMES THIS TAKE SPECIFICALLY. In this order: « J'ai eu peur. » « J'ai eu froid. » « Non, je n'ai pas eu le temps. » « J'ai bu un café. » « J'ai vu Marie. » APART, THE LEARNER COMPARES FIVE PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF ONE VOWEL WITH AND WITHOUT A CONSONANT IN FRONT OF IT. THE VOWEL IS THE SAME IN ALL FIVE AND MUST BE THE SAME. /y/ every time: eu, bu, vu. The whole teaching is that « eu » is that vowel with nothing at all in front of it, and a reader who colours the bare one differently from the two with consonants is teaching a distinction that does not exist. DO NOT LENGTHEN « eu ». It is short, unstressed and easy to miss, and the learner is being taught to catch it as it really arrives. In the third line it sits between « pas » and « le temps » and it should be barely there.
clipIds: Non, je n'ai pas eu le temps.

recorded.desc: THE CIRCUMFLEX PAIR, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, AND THE BRIEF NAMES THIS TAKE SPECIFICALLY. Four lines in this order: « J'ai dû partir. » « J'ai bu du thé. » « la somme due » « J'ai reçu ton message. » THE FIRST TWO ARE THE POINT AND THEY MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE WHERE THEY OVERLAP. « dû » in the first line and « du » in the second are the same sound, /dy/, and the whole mission rests on the learner hearing that there is nothing to hear. Read them identically. Any difference at all, of length or weight or vowel colour, teaches that the accent is audible, and it is not. NOT A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. All four lines are correct French and none of them is an error being demonstrated. THE FOURTH LINE IS THE CONTROL. The cedilla in « reçu » changes how the c is said and the learner should hear that it does, so that the contrast with the circumflex, which changes nothing audible at all, has something to sit against.

THE FIVE GROUPS, ONE TAKE, AS FIVE LINES IN THE ORDER THE MAP PRINTS THEM: « J'ai pris le bus. » « J'ai dit oui. » « J'ai vu Marie. » « J'ai ouvert la porte. » « J'ai fait le ménage. » THE FIRST TWO WORDS OF ALL FIVE ARE IDENTICAL AND MUST SOUND IDENTICAL. « J'ai » is the constant across the whole lesson and the second word is the only thing that changes; a reader who varies the opening is hiding the one variable the learner is being asked to attend to. GIVE THE SECOND WORD ITS ORDINARY WEIGHT AND NO MORE. These are not headline words being demonstrated, they are the middles of ordinary sentences, and the learner has to be able to catch them where they actually sit.

THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to rec-a2-20-eu and rec-a2-20-roof: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and a paired reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. THE SECOND WORD IS WHAT IS BEING SPELLED and it is usually one or two syllables in the middle of a short sentence. Do not lift it and do not pause in front of it. ONE LINE HOLDS « dû » AND ONE HOLDS « du », and they are the same sound. Nothing in the reading may separate them: the learner is being asked to work out which word is meant from what the sentence says, and the take must not help. SAY IT THE WAY SOMEBODY WOULD SAY IT, at the pace of somebody dictating a phone number to a friend.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS SIX SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same colleague, later in the week, and this time the exchange works. EVERY QUESTION IS ASKED WITHOUT INVERSION and should sound completely ordinary: « Tu as lu le journal ? » is a statement with a question mark on it, which is what people say. NEITHER « as » NOR « a » MAY BE STRESSED anywhere in the take. They are the words carrying the tense and the learner has to get used to catching them unstressed, because that is the only way they will ever hear them.
clipIds: Et toi, tu as fait quoi samedi ?
Oui, il a fait très chaud.

lessons.intro: Last lesson you were given a way of building the second word of a past sentence out of the group the verb is in, and it works for almost every verb in French. Thirty-three verbs do not play. Their second word cannot be worked out from anything, and they are the ones people say all day: took, did, said, saw, had, been. What makes this a lesson rather than a list is that thirty-three is not the number you have to hold. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, five are in none of them, and once you can sort a verb you can produce forms nobody has shown you.

oneSound.body: Dû and du are one sound. So are « il dit » and « j'ai dit », and « il fait » and « j'ai fait ». And so is every one of these forms against the version of itself that agrees, which is why the change lesson 18 in A2 is about to teach you will be invisible when you hear it. The ear is useful in this lesson for the shape of a short second word and for nothing else.
oneSound.title: What the ear cannot separate

examples.note: And the one without, in a sentence where nothing else is the same.

pastForm.body: Lesson 16 in A2 showed you how to build the second word out of the group the verb is in: -er to -é, -ir to -i, -re to -u. That is true of almost every verb in the language and false of the thirty-three in this lesson. For these, the second word is not built. It is a word in its own right, and the only thing you can do with it is know it.
pastForm.title: The second word, when you cannot build it

examples.note: Faire ends in -re, so the rule reaches for -u. The form is fait.
Courir ends in -ir, so the rule reaches for -i. The form is couru.

theFront.body: Lesson 9 in A2 said it about the present: « Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. » Cover the front of apprendre and prendre is underneath. The past form works the same way: appris is pris with ap in front, compris is pris with com in front, and remis and promis are mis with a front on them. Four of the seven in this group are free the moment you have the other three.
theFront.title: Cover it, and the rest is free

examples.note: appris. Cover the ap and pris is underneath.
remis. Cover the re and mis is underneath, on the naming form lesson 9 in A2 wrote itself.

theGroup.body: They are not thirty-three separate facts. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, and five are in no group at all. The four are -is, -it, -u and -ert, and the fifth is the five that belong to nothing. A group is worth having because it is smaller than the list and because it takes new members: once you know that ouvrir goes to ouvert you know offrir, couvrir and souffrir as well, and nobody had to tell you.
theGroup.title: Five groups, and four of them have an ending

examples.note: The head of the -is group, and the one the regular rule gets most wrong.
The head of the -ert group, on a verb that ends in -ir and refuses -i.

alsoAWord.body: Five of them are already words you may have met, and none was labelled a past form when you did. A form used often enough stops being a form and becomes a word. Ouvert is on shop doors, couvert is on the weather forecast, écrit is on a form, cru is on a menu and mort is an ordinary adjective. Every one of those is the past form of a verb in this lesson, and if you have met the word you already have half of the sentence.
alsoAWord.title: Five of them you may already know

examples.note: A shop that is open, and the past form of ouvrir.
A covered sky, and the past form of couvrir.

firstWord.body: Three of these put a different word in front instead of avoir, and the form is all this lesson teaches you about them. Which verbs do it, and what happens to the form afterwards, is lesson 18 in A2. There is nothing to decide here and nothing to learn about it: venu, né and mort have the forms they have, and this lesson shows them the way they actually appear so that you recognise them. Five of them belong to nothing. Two come from a verb you cannot see in them, one is shorter than its verb, and one is a different word. You will need all of this again at lesson 30 in A2, where the whole conversation is about what you studied and how it went.
firstWord.title: Three of them do not use avoir

examples.note: An ordinary -u form with a first word that is not avoir.
And the one that is shorter than the verb it comes from.

littleRoof.body: The little roof is the only thing keeping the past form of devoir apart from du, which means "some". It is the one accent in this set that changes what a word means. Nothing in this app can test it. A typed answer, a spot-the-error and the dictée all strip accents before comparing, so all three would accept du and say it was right. The two words are one sound, so no listening question can ask either.
littleRoof.title: Dû, and the only accent here that changes a word

examples.note: With the roof, and it is the past form of devoir.
Without it, and it is the word for "some". One sound, two words.

theMachine.body: One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between. That is lesson 16's line and it still holds: the shape has not changed. What has changed is that for these verbs the second word cannot be worked out from the first. Run the regular rule on prendre and it gives you « prendu », which is not a word; run it on ouvrir and it gives you « ouvri », which is not one either. The rule is not being applied carelessly. It is being applied correctly to verbs it does not cover.
theMachine.title: The rule that produces a word that does not exist

examples.note: What the rule would have given here is prendu, which is not a word.
And here, ouvri, which is not one either. Both are what a careful learner produces.

twoLetters.body: Two letters, one sound, and it is not the sound either letter suggests. The e is silent and the u is the French u, so what comes out is one pure vowel. You cannot read this one and get it right. Read it before you have heard it and you will put an o or an uh in it every time, which is the opposite of everything else in this lesson.
twoLetters.title: Eu, and the sound it is not

examples.note: Two letters, one sound, and the sound is a pure French u.
The same two letters again, so the ear has something to compare.

lessons.title: Participes passés irréguliers

drills.coach: The wrong one is on the left of each pair, and it is what you get by doing the thing lesson 16 in A2 taught you. It is not carelessness. It is a rule being applied correctly to a verb it does not cover. The naming form is on the front and the form the language has is on the back.
drills.title: What the rule would give

drills.q: mettre. Which is the past form?
drills.why: The -is group, with prendre. The first option is what the -RE rule gives and it is not a word.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: They are not thirty-three separate facts. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, and five are in no group at all. Read the second word of each sentence and put it in its group.
drills.title: One group each

drills.q: courir ends in -ir. Which group is couru in?
drills.why: The -u group, which takes members from every kind of verb there is. The ending of the naming form decides nothing.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. The compound is on the front and the form is on the back.
drills.title: Cover the front

drills.q: reprendre. Which is the past form?
drills.why: Cover the re and prendre is underneath, so it is pris with re in front.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Two letters, one sound, and it is not the sound either letter suggests. The e is silent and the u is the French u, so what comes out is one pure vowel.
drills.title: The one you cannot read

drills.q: avoir. Which is the past form?
drills.why: Two letters, said as one vowel, and there is no route to them from avoir.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The little roof is the only thing keeping the past form of devoir apart from du, which means "some". It is the one accent in this set that changes what a word means.
drills.title: With it and without

drills.q: devoir. Which is the past form?
drills.why: With the roof. Without it the word means "some" and has nothing to do with devoir.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The naming form is on the front and nothing else is. This is what the exam asks for.
drills.title: No group named

sections.body: Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in. Say the first word, and while it is out of your mouth ask which of the five groups the verb is in rather than what its ending should be. Four of the groups have an ending and the fifth is five words you have to have.
sections.title: The move

sections.body: Lesson 9 in A2 said it about the present: « Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. » Cover the front of apprendre and prendre is underneath. The past form works the same way: appris is pris with ap in front, compris is pris with com in front, and remis and promis are mis with a front on them. Four of the seven in this group are free the moment you have the other three.
sections.title: Cover the front

sections.body: refaire gives refait, which is fait with a front on it. apercevoir gives aperçu, which is reçu with a front on it. Neither verb exists in this app as a word of its own, which is why neither has a screen: the front-covering move gives you both without one.
sections.title: Two more, and where they belong

sections.body: Nothing in this app can test it. A typed answer, a spot-the-error and the dictée all strip accents before comparing, so all three would accept du and say it was right. The two words are one sound, so no listening question can ask either. The same is true of the cedilla on reçu and of every accent in these tables.
sections.title: What nothing here can test

sections.body: Three of these put a different word in front instead of avoir, and the form is all this lesson teaches you about them. Which verbs do it, and what happens to the form afterwards, is lesson 18 in A2. And the little word that goes in front of a verb like s'asseoir is lesson 19 in A2. The one case where a past form agrees after avoir needs the words that replace an object, which is lesson 21 in A2.

goals.t: Get four of them free every time you learn one

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.hint: Swipe. Six cards, and the second one is the whole lesson.

cards.body: Thirty-three verbs have a past form you could not have worked out. These are not rare. A hundred and seventy sentences in this app already put « pris » behind a first word, and two hundred and sixty-nine put « été ».
cards.head: thirty-three verbs
cards.label: the list

cards.body: Four groups by ending, which are -is, -it, -u and -ert, and five that are in none of them. Thirty-three things to say and five things to know.
cards.head: They are not thirty-three separate facts. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, and five are in no group at all.
cards.label: and the shape

cards.body: Lesson 16 in A2 gave you a machine for building the second word out of the group the verb is in. For these thirty-three it produces a word that does not exist, so the move is not to build but to reach.
cards.head: Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in.
cards.label: the instruction

cards.body: That lesson had you cover the front of a compound verb to find the verb underneath. The past form works the same way: appris is pris with ap in front, and remis is mis with re in front.
cards.head: Lesson 9 in A2 did the same thing
cards.label: where you have seen this

cards.body: It holds the past form of every irregular verb you have already learned: lesson 5's, lesson 6's, lesson 7's and lesson 8's. You start from nothing on none of them.
cards.head: -u, and it is 13 of them
cards.label: the biggest group

cards.body: They are fait, été, eu, né and mort. Two of the five come off the two commonest verbs in the language, so you will meet them constantly and stop having to think.
cards.head: Five of them belong to nothing. Two come from a verb you cannot see in them, one is shorter than its verb, and one is a different word.
cards.label: and the five

sections.title: Thirty-Three, Or Five

sections.say: Lesson 16 in A2 said it one lesson ago: « One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between. » Nothing about that changes here. The first word is the same, the gap is the same, and the negative goes in the same place. The only thing this lesson touches is the second word.
sections.title: The Shape Has Not Moved

examples.en: I took the bus.
examples.fr: J'ai pris le bus.
examples.note: [ZHAY PREE luh BÜSS] A form of avoir, then the second word, then what the sentence is about. Lesson 16's shape exactly.

examples.en: I did not understand.
examples.fr: Je n'ai pas compris.
examples.note: [zhuh nay pa kohⁿ-PREE] And the negative, with the ne shortened to n' and the pas in the gap. That is lesson 16's rule and this lesson does not add a word to it.

examples.en: I suffered a lot.
examples.fr: J'ai beaucoup souffert.
examples.note: [ZHAY boh-KOO soo-FEHR] A short adverb in the gap, which is the same lesson's again. The second word is the only thing that is new.

examples.en: I did the housework.
examples.fr: J'ai fait le ménage.
examples.note: [ZHAY FEH luh may-NAZH] And here is what is new. Faire ends in -re, the machine says -u, and the form is fait.

sections.say: The wrong one is on the left of each pair, and it is what you get by doing the thing lesson 16 in A2 taught you. It is not carelessness. It is a rule being applied correctly to a verb it does not cover. Read each line left to right: the verb, what the machine gives, and what the language has.
sections.title: Where The Rule Stops

examples.en: prendre gives prendu, and the form is pris
examples.fr: prendre · prendu · pris
examples.note: An -RE verb, so the machine says -u and out comes a word that does not exist. It is the commonest wrong past form an English speaker produces, and it comes from following a rule correctly.

examples.en: mettre gives mettu, and the form is mis
examples.fr: mettre · mettu · mis
examples.note: The same machine on the same kind of verb, and the same non-word out of the other end. Mettre and prendre are in one group and the group is -is.

examples.en: faire gives faisu, and the form is fait
examples.fr: faire · faisu · fait
examples.note: Faire ends in -re, so the machine reaches for -u again. Nothing about fait can be got from faire and it is the commonest verb in the whole set.

examples.en: ouvrir gives ouvri, and the form is ouvert
examples.fr: ouvrir · ouvri · ouvert
examples.note: An -IR verb, so the machine says -i, and this time the real form ends in a t. Four verbs do this and they are the whole -ert group.

examples.en: courir gives couri, and the form is couru
examples.fr: courir · couri · couru
examples.note: Another -IR verb, and the machine says -i again. This one lands in the -u group instead, which is the group that takes members from everywhere.

examples.en: voir gives voiri, and the form is vu
examples.fr: voir · voiri · vu
examples.note: There is no rule at all for an -OIR verb in lesson 16 in A2, so the machine has nothing to run and the learner guesses. Every -OIR verb in this lesson is in the -u group.

sections.say: They are not thirty-three separate facts. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, and five are in no group at all. Five rows, and the number beside each one is how many verbs are in it. Tap a row to hear its first member.

rows.say: J'ai pris le bus.

detail.say: J'ai pris le bus.
detail.body: Seven verbs, and three of them are the other four with something on the front. prendre and mettre are the heads and both of them end in -re, which is what makes the machine reach for -u. J'ai pris le bus. [ZHAY PREE luh BÜSS]
detail.title: The -is group

rows.say: J'ai dit oui.

detail.say: J'ai dit oui.
detail.body: Four verbs, and two of them end in -uire, where the -re comes off and a t goes on. It is the smallest group and the most predictable one once you have seen it. J'ai dit oui. [ZHAY DEE WEE]
detail.title: The -it group

rows.say: J'ai vu Marie.

detail.say: J'ai vu Marie.
detail.body: Thirteen verbs, more than a third of the list, and it takes members from everywhere: verbs in -oir, in -re and in -ir. Every irregular verb from lesson 5, lesson 6, lesson 7 and lesson 8 is in here. J'ai vu Marie. [ZHAY VÜ ma-REE]
detail.title: The -u group

rows.say: J'ai ouvert la porte.

detail.say: J'ai ouvert la porte.
detail.body: Four verbs and that is all of it. Every one ends in -rir and would take -i if the machine were allowed to run. Learn one and you have the other three. J'ai ouvert la porte. [ZHAY oo-VEHR la PORT]
detail.title: The -ert group

rows.say: J'ai fait le ménage.

detail.say: J'ai fait le ménage.
detail.body: Five of them belong to nothing. Two come from a verb you cannot see in them, one is shorter than its verb, and one is a different word. J'ai fait le ménage. [ZHAY FEH luh may-NAZH]
detail.title: And the five

cards.body: I did the housework. faire is the commonest irregular verb in the language and its past form is in no group. It is also the same sound as « il fait », which is the present, so nothing you hear will separate them.
cards.head: J'ai fait le ménage.
cards.label: the commonest of all

cards.body: I was ill. There is no route from être to été. The same three letters are also the word for summer, which is a coincidence and a useful one: you have seen the shape before.
cards.head: J'ai été malade.
cards.label: from nowhere

cards.body: I was frightened. Two letters, one sound, and it is not the sound either letter suggests. The e is silent and the u is the French u, so what comes out is one pure vowel.
cards.head: J'ai eu peur.
cards.label: and from nowhere again

cards.body: He was born here. naître has six letters and né has two, and nothing else in the set gets shorter. Its first word is not avoir either, which is lesson 18 in A2.
cards.head: Il est né ici.
cards.label: shorter than its verb

cards.body: mourir goes to mort, which is not mourir with anything done to it. It is published in this app as an ordinary adjective meaning "dead", and that is the form.
cards.head: mort
cards.label: a different word entirely

cards.body: dying of laughter The same word, in the phrase you are most likely to meet it in.

sections.say: Three of these put a different word in front instead of avoir, and the form is all this lesson teaches you about them. Which verbs do it, and what happens to the form afterwards, is lesson 18 in A2. These three are shown the way they actually appear so that you recognise them, and there is nothing here to decide.

cards.body: An -RE verb, so the machine says -u and out comes a word that does not exist. It is the commonest wrong past form an English speaker produces, and it comes from following a rule correctly.
cards.head: prendu

cards.body: The same machine on the same kind of verb, and the same non-word out of the other end. Mettre and prendre are in one group and the group is -is.

cards.body: Faire ends in -re, so the machine reaches for -u again. Nothing about fait can be got from faire and it is the commonest verb in the whole set.

cards.body: An -IR verb, so the machine says -i, and this time the real form ends in a t. Four verbs do this and they are the whole -ert group.
cards.head: ouvri

cards.body: Another -IR verb, and the machine says -i again. This one lands in the -u group instead, which is the group that takes members from everywhere.

rule.body: Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in. An -RE verb can land in -is, an -IR verb in -u or in -ert. The end of the naming form tells you what the machine would do, not what the language has.

sections.title: Two Letters, One Sound

questions.q: J'ai eu peur. What comes out for those two letters?
questions.why: The e is not said and the u is the French u. Two letters, one sound, and it is not the sound either letter suggests.

questions.q: J'ai bu un café against J'ai eu peur. What is the difference?
questions.why: The vowel is identical. Bu is that vowel with a b in front of it and eu is the same vowel with nothing in front, which is what makes eu the hardest of the three to catch.

questions.q: Non, je n'ai pas eu le temps. Where is it in this one?
questions.why: In the gap, where lesson 16 in A2 put it, and it is very short. This is where it will actually arrive when somebody says it to you.

rule.body: The little roof is the only thing keeping the past form of devoir apart from du, which means "some". It is the one accent in this set that changes what a word means.

sections.body: Say the first word, and while it is out of your mouth ask which of the five groups the verb is in rather than what its ending should be. Four of the groups have an ending and the fifth is five words you have to have. Lesson 16 in A2 gave you the whole shape one lesson ago: a form of avoir, then the second word, and the small ones in the gap. Nothing about that changes here and none of it is taught again. What changes is the second word, for thirty-three verbs, and twenty-eight of the thirty-three fall into four groups by their ending.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in. They are not thirty-three separate facts. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, and five are in no group at all.
-is, -it, -u and -ert, and the -u group is 13 of the thirty-three on its own.
Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. That is lesson 9's line and it is exactly as true of the past form as it was of the present.
Five of them belong to nothing. Two come from a verb you cannot see in them, one is shorter than its verb, and one is a different word.
You cannot read this one and get it right. Read it before you have heard it and you will put an o or an uh in it every time, which is the opposite of everything else in this lesson.

Nothing in this app can test it. A typed answer, a spot-the-error and the dictée all strip accents before comparing, so all three would accept du and say it was right. The two words are one sound, so no listening question can ask either.
Five of them are already words you may have met, and none was labelled a past form when you did. A form used often enough stops being a form and becomes a word.

Three of these put a different word in front instead of avoir, and the form is all this lesson teaches you about them. Which verbs do it, and what happens to the form afterwards, is lesson 18 in A2. You will need all of this again at lesson 30 in A2, where the whole conversation is about what you studied and how it went.

errorTriggers.description: Runs lesson 16 in A2's regular rule on an irregular verb and produces a word that does not exist: « j'ai prendu », « j'ai ouvri ». THE ERROR THIS LESSON EXISTS TO PREVENT, and it is produced by applying a rule correctly rather than by carelessness, which is why it survives correction.

Puts a form in the group its naming form points at: courir into -i because it ends in -ir, prendre into -u because it ends in -re. It comes from treating the ending of the naming form as evidence, which is exactly what lesson 16 in A2 taught and exactly what does not hold here.

Learns a compound verb as a separate item instead of covering its front: treats « repris » as a thirty-fourth thing to memorise. It costs nothing today and it is the reason the list feels infinite, because every compound of every member looks like a new fact.

Reads « eu » and says something with an o or an uh in it. THE ONE ERROR IN THIS LESSON THAT IS ABOUT A SOUND: the two letters spell a single French u and nothing about them suggests it, so a learner who meets the form on paper before hearing it says it wrongly every time.

Writes « du » for the past form of devoir. The only accent in the set that changes what a word means, and the one error in the lesson that no typed surface, no spot-the-error and no listening question in this app can catch, because all three strip it or cannot hear it.

Leaves the naming form behind avoir: « j'ai prendre le bus ». It is lesson 16 in A2's error arriving by a new route, in which the learner looks for the past form, does not find one, and ships the verb as it stands rather than producing a non-word.

grammarAssumed: The passé composé with avoir, in six persons, introduced in a2.05
The regular past participle: -er to -é, -ir to -i, -re to -u, introduced in a2.05
That ne … pas encloses the auxiliary and not the participle, introduced in a2.05
That the participle is invariable after avoir, introduced in a2.05
The placement of a short adverb between auxiliary and participle, introduced in a2.05
The present of prendre, mettre and their compounds, and the compound-verb principle, introduced in a2.15
The present of aller, venir and tenir, introduced in a2.02
The present of faire, dire and lire, introduced in a2.12
The present of vouloir, pouvoir and devoir, introduced in a2.13
The present of savoir and connaître, introduced in a2.14
grammarIntroduced: The irregular past participles, thirty-three forms, presented as four morphological classes by termination (-is, -it, -u, -ert) plus a residue of five suppletive or unclassifiable forms
That the conjugation class of the infinitive does not predict the participle class, so an -RE verb may give -is, an -IR verb -u or -ert, and an -OIR verb -u
That a prefixed verb takes the participle of its base verb, extending a2.15's compound principle from the present to the past participle
The participle of avoir as eu, /y/, an orthography with no phonetic correspondence to its letters
The circumflex on dû as the sole orthographic distinction from the partitive du, and its loss in the feminine due
That five participles in the set are lexicalised as independent adjectives or nouns in the published corpus
être as auxiliary is named for venu, né and mort and reserved for a2.21; participle agreement is neither taught nor exemplified here

recorded.desc: Four cards, the same person said twice on each. ONE TAKE PER CARD. The stressed form carries the phrase stress because it ends the phrase; do not add more than that.
Four sentences, read as ordinary speech. In Moi, je suis prêt the moi is set off by a short pause and je is quick and unstressed.
ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, the four lines adjacent and in order. elle and elles MUST be read identically: no audible s, no lengthening. The first question depends on it.
Je lui parle has lui unstressed; Je parle avec lui has lui carrying the stress. sans elle is sahⁿ ZEHL, the z moved across, never a pause before elle.

c'est elle and c'est eux carry the liaison t onto the pronoun: seh TEHL, seh TUH. Ce sont eux is suh sohⁿ TUH. Read the written and said pair at the same pace; the difference is which one people choose, not how it sounds.
The wrong version is in promptSound and must be read at the same pace and intonation as the right one. Only the correct fr is played in the audio step.
Four chunks the learner has already met, read as ordinary speech. Excusez-moi as one word with the stress on moi.

lessons.intro: English says I before a verb and me everywhere else, and you pick between them without thinking. French does the same with je and moi, and with three more pairs. You already say Et toi ? and chez moi. This lesson is the rule behind them.

known.body: Et toi ? since lesson 1 in A1. Chez moi since lesson 13 in A2. Moi non plus since lesson 21 in A1. Every one of them is this set, and every one follows the same rule: no verb right after it.
known.title: You have been saying these for months

cestEux.body: Ce sont eux is what you write. C'est eux is what you will hear, and it is correct French too. With moi, toi, lui, elle, nous and vous there is only c'est.
cestEux.title: What you write, what you say

himOnly.body: In front of a verb, lui is him or her, and lesson 22 in A2 made a point of it. After a little word it is him and nothing else. For her, say elle: avec elle, sans elle, pour elle.
himOnly.title: The lui that keeps its gender

examples.note: in front of the verb, him or her

euxElles.body: eux is them for men, and for any group with a man in it. elles is them only when every person is a woman. It works the way ils and elles already do.
euxElles.title: One man in the group is enough

onItsOwn.body: je, tu, il and ils need a verb straight after them (only ne or a small word like le or lui can squeeze in between). When the person is on its own, after a little word, after c'est, as a one-word answer or out in front, French uses the other set. Lesson 9 in A1 gave you the first set and saved this one for later.
onItsOwn.title: No verb right after it

examples.note: a verb right after it, so je

sameFour.body: elle, nous, vous and elles are the same word in both jobs. Only je, tu, il and ils change: moi, toi, lui, eux. So the choice only ever matters for four people, and those four are the ones people say most.
sameFour.title: Half of them you already have

sections.body: The left column is the set lesson 9 in A1 gave you, and it only ever goes right in front of a verb. The middle column is everything else: after a little word like avec, sans, pour or chez; after c'est; alone as an answer; out in front for weight, with the left-hand word coming back for the verb; after que in a comparison; and joined with et. Four rows change and four do not. After a little word, lui is him only and her is elle, and eux covers any group with a man in it.

sections.text: Ce soir, Marc et Julie font une fête chez eux. Moi, je viens avec ma sœur Léa. Elle ne connaît pas les autres invités, alors elle reste à côté de moi. Eux, ils ont oublié les verres. Julie rit : « Sans eux, pas de fête. »

grammarIntroduced: The stressed (disjunctive) pronouns moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles as a set, completing the deferral on a1.05 sheet-stressed

Distribution: after a preposition, after c'est, as a verbless answer, left-dislocated for emphasis with the clitic subject resumed, after que in a comparison, and in coordinated subjects resumed by nous or vous
That four forms differ from the subject clitics (moi, toi, lui, eux) and four are homographic with them (elle, nous, vous, elles)
That stressed lui is masculine only, against the gender-neutral indirect-object lui of a2.24
eux for masculine or mixed plural reference, elles for all-feminine
The register pair ce sont eux (written) and c'est eux (spoken)
Recognition only of the stressed pronoun after an affirmative imperative (Excusez-moi, Montrez-moi); the imperative itself is not taught

recorded.desc: IL PARLE, IL FINIT AND IL VEND, ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, ONE VOICE, IN THAT ORDER, AND THE THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE IN LENGTH AND IN WEIGHT. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. The three endings are one letter, two letters and none, and not one of them is a sound: eel parl ee-SEE, eel fee-nee ee-SEE, eel vahⁿ ee-SEE. The third one must not be clipped, hurried or allowed to trail off because it is shorter on the page, and the first two must not have their endings leaned on because they have one. If a listener can tell from the audio alone which of the three has the shortest spelling, the recording has taught the opposite of what the screen teaches. Read them at conversational pace, one after another, with no teaching pause between them. RECORDED APART, IN THREE SESSIONS, the learner compares three performances instead of three cells and the whole screen is lost.

THE D PAIRS, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE BACK TO BACK, SINGULAR THEN PLURAL: Il vend ici / Ils vendent ici, Elle rend le livre / Elles rendent le livre, Il descend ici / Ils descendent ici. Here the difference MUST be audible, which is the opposite instruction from the cells clip and is why the two are separate recordings. The plural ends on a d and the singular does not: vahⁿ, then vahⁿd. It is a released consonant at the very end of the word, not a syllable, so do not put a vowel after it and do not lengthen it. In every pair the PRONOUN must sound identical on both sides, because it is: il and ils are one sound and so are elle and elles. Any difference in the pronoun, in pace or in emphasis destroys the pair, because the learner will use it instead of the d. The scene break card and the trap drill both play from this clip and both need the wrong-then-right ordering preserved.

THE SINGULAR TRIPLE, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. je vends, tu vends, il vend, then je réponds, tu réponds, il répond. Do not help. Do not differentiate them, do not touch the final letter, do not let the s of vends or the d of vend surface in any of the three. Two of the three carry letters the third does not and none of those letters is a sound, which is the entire claim of the mission this plays under. If a listener can tell any of these three apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Read them at conversational pace, one after another, with no pause for teaching.

All six forms as one continuous take, in the usual pronoun order (je, tu, il, nous, vous, ils), by one voice at one speed, then the eleven dictée sentences in the same take. The first three must be INDISTINGUISHABLE from each other, because they are: three spellings and one sound. The fourth and fifth add a whole syllable each and the d in front of it is said. The sixth adds only the d. Do not stress the verb anywhere; the weight belongs at the end of the phrase. The dictée sentences are the ones a learner will replay four times while typing, so they need to be even in pace and completely flat in emphasis: any lean on an ending is a hint the screen is not supposed to give.

The seven naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice. Every one of them ends in the same DR sound and that sameness is the teaching: the learner should come away hearing -dre as one ending rather than seven word-endings. The nasal vowel before the d is a vowel and not an N: vahⁿdr, not van-dr. Do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. One woman in her fifties at an ordinary market pace, in a hurry in the way somebody with a list is in a hurry, and entirely unbothered. The last line (« D'accord, merci. Je vais voir l'autre rangée. ») must be brisk and pleasant rather than pointed: the whole scene turns on nobody minding and nobody checking, so any hint of doubt or of correction in her voice would destroy it. She has already decided and she is being polite about it.
clipIds: Bonjour. Je cherche les fromages de la ferme.

lessons.intro: The last of the three regular patterns, and the one where the il form is finished before you expect it to be. Six endings, five of which you already have, and one of which is not there at all.

stem.body: vendre gives vend-. attendre gives attend-. perdre gives perd-. Take the last two letters off the naming form and what is left does not move, whoever is speaking. That is the same two letters you took off parler and off finir, and the same machine lesson 1 in A2 gave you. Nothing new has happened to the method. What is new is one of the six things you put on the end of it.
stem.title: What is left when -re comes off

examples.note: vend- with the je ending on it.
The same vend-, with the nous ending, which you can hear.

theD.body: Every one of these verbs has a d at the end of its stem, and a French consonant at the end of a word is not said while the same consonant in the middle of one is. il vend is vahⁿ and ils vendent is vahⁿd, because the -ent puts letters after the d even though the -ent itself is silent. So the three singular forms lose the d and the three plural forms keep it. That is the one thing your ear can do for you here, and it does nothing at all for the three that matter most.
theD.title: Silent at the end, said in the middle

examples.note: The same verb with letters after the d, so the d arrives.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on a -re verb means on vend and never on vendons: the spoken we takes the bare form, so the commonest way of saying we in French lands on the one cell of the six where nothing is written after the stem at all.
nousOn.title: The we that writes nothing

examples.note: The written one, with an ending you can hear.
The spoken one, taking the il form and writing nothing.

nothing.body: The il form of a regular -re verb is the stem and then the page stops. Not a silent letter you cannot hear, the way -e and -es and -ent are silent: there is no letter. il vend, elle attend, on répond. It looks short because it is short, and the reason it feels wrong is that the two lessons before this one both put something there. Nothing is missing and nothing has been taken away.
nothing.title: il vend, and there is no more of it

examples.note: The stem, and then the full stop.
The same thing on a second verb, so it is a rule and not a fact about vendre.

threeGroups.body: One frame, three verbs, three groups. il parle takes an -e, il finit takes an -it, il vend takes nothing at all. All three endings are inaudible, so this is a page distinction from beginning to end and no recording will ever help you with it. Those three cells are the whole of what the three regular patterns disagree about on the il form, and once you have them there is no fourth group waiting.
threeGroups.title: il parle, il finit, il vend

examples.note: One letter, from the group you met first.

notThisFamily.body: prendre, mettre and battre end in -re and are built another way, and so are apprendre, comprendre, permettre, promettre and combattre. prendre is one of the most common verbs in the language, so you will meet it long before anybody teaches it to you. Run this pattern on it and you produce a form no French speaker says. Knowing that a verb is not in this family is worth as much as building the ones that are, and lesson 9 in A2 is where the other family is taught.
notThisFamily.term: the ones that only look like it
notThisFamily.title: Ending in -re is not enough

examples.note: This one is in the family, and the il form is the bare stem.
And so is this one, whatever the length of the naming form suggests.

theSingularThree.body: Three spellings and one sound. -s, -s and nothing all arrive as nothing, exactly the way -e, -es and -ent did on an -er verb in lesson 1 in A2 and -is, -is and -it did on an -ir verb in lesson 3 in A2. So in the singular the pronoun is still carrying the person on its own, and the only place these three differ is the page. This is why the dictée in this lesson is longer than the listening.
theSingularThree.title: je vends, tu vends, il vend

examples.note: Ends in nothing, and is said exactly the same way.

sections.body: Three groups, three endings on the il form, and one of them is nothing. The two earlier units each shipped a sheet of their own: lesson 1 in A2 holds the -er endings in full and lesson 3 in A2 holds the -ir endings in full, and both are still the place to go for one pattern on its own. Neither of them could hold the table above, because neither of them knew the other two patterns existed yet. This one does, and it is the last one that will be needed, because there is no fourth regular group. Read the third row of it and nothing else if you are in a hurry: parle, finit, vend. One letter, two letters, none, and not one of the three reaches the ear. That is the whole of what the three regular patterns disagree about on the il form, and it is why this lesson spends its weight on writing rather than on listening. The rest of the table is the part you could have worked out: the plural endings are the same three you have had since lesson 1 in A2, and the -s on je and tu is the same silent -s you have been writing since lesson 10 in A1.
sections.title: Why this sheet holds three patterns and not one

sections.body: The method has not changed across three units and it will not change again: find the stem, add the person. What each unit gave you was a different short set of endings to add, and with this one the set is complete. Everything after it in this level is a verb that has to be memorised outright, starting with the three that end in -re and are built another way. prendre, mettre, battre and their compounds apprendre, comprendre, permettre, promettre, combattre are all at lesson 9 in A2, and one of them is among the most common verbs in the language, so you will meet it long before you are taught it. The habit worth carrying out of this lesson is a writing habit rather than a listening one. You have now met a form that is complete while looking unfinished, and the thing to do about it is to stop. The one thing your ear will give you here is the d: silent at the end of a word, said whenever letters follow it, which means the three plural forms have it and the three singular forms do not.

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have taken a third naming form apart and found the same two letters coming off it. You have put six endings on the stem, one of which is not there, and you have written the form for a verb this lesson never showed you. You know which three cells are one sound and which three wake the d up, and you know the three verbs that end the same way and are built another. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

questions.answer: attend

questions.q: Fix this. You, about yourself: « Je vend ici. »
questions.why: The bare stem belongs to il and to nowhere else. This is the mistake that comes from learning the il form too well, and no recording will ever catch it.
accept: Je vends ici
vends
questions.answer: Je vends ici.

questions.q: On ___ des billets ici. (vendre)
questions.why: on means we and takes the il form, so the spoken we lands on the cell that writes nothing.
accept: vend
on vend
questions.answer: vend

rounds.say: One frame, three verbs. Only one of them writes nothing.
rounds.label: Three groups, three endings

questions.q: il parle, il finit, il vend. How many letters do the three endings have between them?
questions.why: One for -e, two for -it, and none at all for the third. All three are silent, which is why the page is the only place they exist.

questions.q: Il ___ ici. (parler)
questions.why: An -er verb takes -e on il. It is silent, and it is still a letter you have to write.
accept: parle
il parle
questions.answer: parle

questions.q: Il ___ ici. (finir)
questions.why: An -ir verb takes -it on il. Also silent, also two letters you have to write.
accept: finit
il finit
questions.answer: finit

questions.q: Fix this. One man, at the market: « Il vende le pain. »
questions.why: The -e belongs to the -er verbs. Carrying it across to a -re verb is the commonest way this goes wrong, because the -er pattern was learned first.
accept: Il vend le pain
vend
questions.answer: Il vend le pain.

questions.q: Which group writes nothing on the il form?
questions.why: Only this one. -er takes -e and -ir takes -it, and both of those are letters even though neither is a sound.

questions.q: Elles ___ le livre. (rendre)
questions.why: A plural subject takes -ent, and the d in front of it is said. elle and elles are one sound, so the d is the only audible sign of the number.
accept: rendent
elles rendent
questions.answer: rendent

rounds.say: The one thing your ear can do here, and the three things it cannot.
rounds.label: What the d tells you

questions.q: Listen. One person, or several?
questions.say: Ils vendent ici.
questions.why: A d arrived at the end of the verb. The pronoun ils is said exactly like il, so that d is the whole of the evidence.
opts: It is not a real form
Either, the sound does not say

questions.q: Listen. elle and elles are said the same. What told you it was one?
questions.say: Elle rend le livre.
questions.why: The verb stopped at the vowel. Nothing follows the d in the singular, so the d is at the end of the word and a French word does not say it there.
opts: No d at the end of the verb

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: Just the d, and only because it is at the end. Put anything after it, as -ons and -ez and -ent all do, and it comes back.

questions.q: Which of these could your ear NOT separate?
questions.why: Both are singular, both lose the d, and one of them writes an s the other does not. Three spellings and one sound is still true here.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.say: Nous vendons ici.
questions.why: Only one of these four ends on a nasal vowel after the d. The others are the bare form, a d on its own, and an -ay.

questions.q: Listen. How many people?
questions.say: Il descend ici.
questions.why: Nothing after the vowel, so the d is silent and the subject is singular. The plural of this verb would have put the d back.
opts: Several, and the verb says so
One, and the verb says so
Several, and the verb does not say so

rounds.say: Ending in -re is not enough. Two of these are about the ones that are not yours.
rounds.label: Where the family stops

questions.q: Which of these four verbs is in this lesson family?
questions.why: Only descendre. The other three end in -re and are built another way, and nothing in the naming form tells you that.

questions.q: prendre, mettre and battre all end in -re. Where are they taught?
questions.why: Lesson 9 in A2 takes all three and their compounds together. Until then, recognising that a verb is not in this family is the whole of what you need.
opts: Nowhere, they are learned one at a time

questions.q: Ils ___ le train. (entendre)
questions.why: Stem entend-, plural ending -ent. The -ent is silent and it still puts letters after the d, so the d is said.
accept: entendent
ils entendent
questions.answer: entendent

questions.q: Say it: he sells here.
questions.why: Stop at the vowel. If a d arrives at the end of the verb you have said several people, and this is the one place that mistake is audible.

questions.q: Fix this. The neighbours, at the next table: « Ils vend des fruits. »
questions.why: The written s of ils is silent, so the verb has to carry the number on its own. The bare stem is the singular cell and gives it away.
accept: Ils vendent des fruits
vendent
questions.answer: Ils vendent des fruits.

questions.q: Il ___ ici. (descendre)
questions.why: The longest naming form in the set and the shortest il form. descendre gives descend-, and the il cell writes nothing after it.
accept: descend
il descend
questions.answer: descend

sections.say: Four things, and then the pattern stops being regular.
sections.body: You can build the present tense of any regular -re verb, including ones nobody has shown you, and you can write the one cell in the three regular patterns where the page stops at the stem. Three groups, three endings on the il form, and one of them is nothing. That set is now finished: lesson 1 in A2 and lesson 3 in A2 gave you the other two and there is no fourth. What is left in this level are the verbs that had to be memorised outright, and the next unit begins them.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: The il form takes nothing, and that is the ending.
Cut the last two letters off the naming form, then put the person on what is left.
je and tu take an s, nous vous and ils take the endings you already had, and il takes nothing.
The d at the end of the stem is said whenever something follows it, and prendre, mettre, battre are not in this family at all.

errorTriggers.description: Writes the bare stem where je or tu is the subject, because the il form was the one that had to be learned.
Puts something after the stem on the il form: il vende, il vends, il vendt. The form looks unfinished and the reflex is to finish it.
Carries another group's third-person ending across: il vende with lesson 1's -e, or il vendit with lesson 3's -it.
Says the d where it is silent or drops it where it is said, so a singular arrives sounding plural or the other way round.
Runs the vendre model on prendre, mettre or battre, because the naming form looks identical.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
The present tense of regular -er verbs as a stem plus six endings, introduced in a2.01
That -e, -es and -ent are silent and -ons and -ez are not, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -ir verbs, introduced in a2.10
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, introduced in a2.01
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of regular -re verbs, as a stem plus six endings
That the third-person singular of a regular -re verb carries no written ending at all
That the three regular groups differ in the third person by one letter, two letters and none
That the singular of a regular -re verb is three spellings and one sound
That a stem-final d is silent at the end of a word and said when letters follow it
That a verb ending in -re is not necessarily in this family

lessons.intro: Comparing two things in French is one sentence shape with one word in the middle of it, and that word is the whole choice. Get the shape once and it takes any describing word you will ever learn. Then the article arrives, and it brings an ending nobody can hear.

most.body: Put le, la or les in front of the same frame and you have gone from more than that one to more than all of them. Nothing else changes. The article is also what carries the agreement, so it is the word to pick first and the word that decides the ending.
most.title: The article does the work

examples.note: and it works for the worst as well

than.body: que is what the second thing hangs off, and nothing else does that job: you can never put it straight after the describing word. Il est plus grand. on its own is grammatical and unfinished, exactly the way taller is in English. Say it to somebody who does not already know what you are comparing to, and the first thing they ask is plus grand que qui.
than.title: que, and it is not optional

agree.body: Lesson 10 in A2 taught that a describing word matches what it describes. Nothing about the frame suspends that. le plus grand jardin, la plus grande maison, les plus grands jardins, les plus grandes maisons: four spellings, and two of them sound identical, so this is a thing you can only get right in writing.
agree.title: The ending still follows the noun

examples.note: and meilleure agrees the same way

frame.body: Something, then a middle word, then a describing word, then que, then the thing you are comparing it to. Those five slots stay where they are for every comparison you will ever make in French. You are never building a new sentence shape, only dropping different words into the same one.
frame.title: The part that never moves

better.body: English has one better and French splits it. meilleur goes with a noun and behaves like any describing word, with four endings. mieux goes with a verb and never changes. The corpus says mieux about six and a half times as often as meilleur, so if you can only keep one, keep that one.
better.title: Two words for one English one

examples.note: with chante, and the article in front: le mieux

middle.body: plus, moins or aussi. Three words, and picking one of them is the entire decision. Everything before it and everything after it stays exactly as it was, which is why you can do this at speed with a describing word you have only just learned.
middle.title: The one word that changes

examples.note: plus, in the corpus long before this lesson
aussi, and the describing word agrees

lessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives

drills.coach: The frame is already right. Read the English and pick which of the three goes in the middle.
drills.title: Three words, one slot

drills.q: He meant he is taller than his brother. Which one says that?
drills.why: The first is correct French and means he is tall. The third makes him the tallest of a group. Only the second compares two people.
opts: Il est plus grand que son frère.
drills.coach: A comparison names both things. If you can only find one of them, the sentence is half said.
drills.title: And the second thing

drills.coach: Two piles. One thing, or several. The ending is the only thing that tells you, and only in writing.
drills.title: The last letter

drills.q: Ce gâteau est ... que l'autre. Which word?
drills.why: est, so it is describing the cake and it is meilleur. mieux would be describing an action, and there is no action here.
drills.coach: Look at the word in front of the gap. est, or something being done.
drills.title: Which better word

sheets.title: The whole frame, on one page

sections.body: The left column is the only thing that changes. Everything to the right of it is the frame, and the frame is the same for every describing word in the language. The bottom three rows are the two words that refuse the frame and the one that does not, which is the part worth screenshotting.
sections.title: How to read this

rowDetails.body: The s is silent in front of a describing word and comes back when nothing follows it. plü grand, and PLÜSS on its own.
rowDetails.title: plus, and what it means

rowDetails.body: English usually flips it and says shorter. French says less tall and is happy with it.
rowDetails.title: moins, and what it means

rowDetails.body: There is no superlative of aussi. Nothing can be the most equal, so the third column is empty on purpose.
rowDetails.title: aussi, and what it means

rowDetails.body: The plain form. Nothing is added, and this is the one every other cell is built from.
rowDetails.title: One masculine thing

rowDetails.body: grande and grandes are the only forms of the four where the d is pronounced. The e wakes it up; the s changes nothing.
rowDetails.title: One feminine thing, and you can hear it

rowDetails.body: An s on the article and an s on the describing word, and neither of them is said. It sounds exactly like the singular.
rowDetails.title: Several masculine things

rowDetails.body: les plus grandes sounds exactly like la plus grande. Nothing in speech separates them, which is why every scored question on this rule is typed.
rowDetails.title: Several feminine things, and it exists only on paper

rowDetails.body: Refuses plus. meilleur has all four endings: meilleur, meilleure, meilleurs, meilleures.
rowDetails.title: bon: good, better, best

rowDetails.body: Refuses plus. mieux never changes, for anybody. It is the one the corpus uses six and a half times as often as meilleur.
rowDetails.title: bien: well, better, best

rowDetails.body: Takes BOTH, and both are ordinary. So the rule is not that plus is forbidden; it is that exactly two words have their own form.
rowDetails.title: mauvais: bad, worse, worst

sections.say: Pick the middle word and keep the frame.
sections.hint: Swipe. Three of these are the choice. The fourth is not optional.

cards.fr: plus
cards.body: The s hides in front of a consonant, comes back as a z in front of a vowel, and is said in full when nothing follows it.
cards.head: the one you will use most
cards.label: MORE

cards.fr: moins
cards.body: You would say shorter; French says less tall. Both are ordinary. This one takes a fortnight to stop feeling translated.
cards.head: English goes the other way
cards.label: LESS

cards.fr: aussi
cards.body: The same word that means also. Sitting between est and a describing word, it can only mean as much as.
cards.head: also, doing another job
cards.label: THE SAME

cards.fr: que
cards.body: The second thing hangs off que and off nothing else, so you can never put it straight after the describing word. Leave que out and the sentence is grammatical and unfinished, which is a worse place to be than wrong.
cards.head: and it is not optional
cards.label: THAN

questions.q: The first one. Who is taller?
questions.why: plus puts him above you. The two words on either side of it are identical in all three of the first lines, so the middle one is the whole message.

questions.q: The second one. Who is taller?
questions.why: moins puts him below you, so you are the taller one. English would have said he is shorter and French does not have to.

questions.q: The third one. Who is taller?

questions.q: The fourth one. Which is longer?
questions.why: moins again, and this time the describing word has an ending on it because rue is feminine. The ending changes nothing about which one is longer.

cards.sub: [SEH luh plü GRAHⁿ zhar-DEHⁿ dü kar-TYAY]
cards.body: Bigger than that one, against the biggest of all of them. The frame did not move. le arrived in front of it.
