recorded.desc: The two orders. Each card is ONE TAKE: the English gloss read at conversational pace, then the French, with no pause long enough to sound like two examples. The learner must hear one sentence becoming another rather than two sentences being compared.

The article against the pronoun. ONE TAKE PER CARD, both sentences in it, and NO extra stress on le, la or les. Stressing the shared word would teach that the difference is audible, and the entire point is that it is not: what follows it is the only signal.
Four rows, four short sentences, read separately. Luh, lah and lay must be clearly distinct from one another; the fourth row is the elided form and must NOT be read in a way that hints at a gender.

wrongThenRight. The wrong sentence « Je vois le. » must be read at NORMAL pace and NOT trailed off, because a French ear hears it as an unfinished sentence rather than a mistake and the learner needs to hear it sounding almost right.
The shortened form. « Je l'aime. » is read ONCE and neutrally. Any reading that leans towards a man or a woman would contradict the card, which says the sentence carries neither.

audioFirst. Four lines, ONE TAKE, one voice, no gaps that let the learner rehearse between them. Lines 1 and 2 differ by one vowel and that difference is the whole question; line 4 must sound exactly as neutral as it does on the elision card.

The wrap. ONE TAKE per card holding both sentences. Ne must NOT be given extra length: it is unstressed in speech and often barely there, and a recording that pronounces it carefully teaches a register nobody uses.

The two-word verb. Read so that « je l'ai » is one breath group and the participle follows, because the pronoun leaning on the auxiliary is exactly what the card claims and the rhythm is the only evidence for it.

Twelve lines, ONE VOICE, read at dictation pace with the same interval before each. « Je l'ai vue. » must be read IDENTICALLY to « Je l'ai vu. » would be: the whole point of the line is that the ending is not there to hear, and a reader who distinguishes them makes the exercise measure something that is not there.

lessons.intro: You have known le, la and les since your fourth lesson, and you have been using them in front of nouns ever since. This is the other job they do. The words are the same, the choice between them is the same, and the only new thing is where they sit: French puts this one in front of the verb, where English puts it behind. That is the whole lesson, and it is worth a whole lesson because word order is the last thing anybody gives up.

inFront.body: English has one place for this word and it is behind the verb. French has one place for it and it is in front. Nothing else about the sentence moves: the subject stays first, the verb keeps its ending, and the word you would have said last is said second instead. The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. The reason this is worth a whole lesson rather than a footnote is that word order is the last thing a second language gives up. You will know this rule and still say it the English way under pressure, and the only cure is having said it the French way often enough that it arrives first.
inFront.title: The one thing that changes, and it changes every time

examples.note: Three words, and the middle one is the one English would have put last.
Two words that look alike in a row, and only the second is the verb.

theWrap.body: « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » is the line you have carried since the near future, and it still holds. There is only one verb in these sentences, so the question of which verb never arises. The question that does arise is what counts as the verb, and the answer is that the pronoun has joined it. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. Ne goes outside both, pas goes after both, and the pronoun never leaves the verb's side. Lesson 19 in A2 taught you the same thing about its own small word one lesson before this, so this is one habit rather than two.
theWrap.title: What ne and pas go round, now that there is an extra word

examples.note: Ne outside, then the pronoun and the verb together, then pas.
And the shortened form behaves no differently inside the wrap.

whichOne.body: The choice between le, la and les is not a new decision. It is the noun's gender and number, which is exactly what lesson 5 in A1 taught you to store and what lesson 6 in A1 taught you to say. Plural takes les and the gender is not consulted at all. Singular takes le or la, and if you cannot gender the noun you cannot pick, which is why this lesson keeps the noun visible on every card that asks you to choose. Nothing here re-teaches gender. It simply becomes the thing you are spending, rather than the thing you are learning.
whichOne.title: A question lesson 5 in A1 already answered

examples.note: La photo is feminine, and the card shows you the noun so you are not guessing.
Plural, so the question never arrives.

sameWords.body: « what comes next decides » is the line lesson 5 in A2 gave this pattern, and you have met it four times: venir de, il y a, aller, and prendre. This is the fifth and it works slightly differently, so it is worth saying rather than leaving you to notice. Here the word after it decides, and so does where it sits: an article leans on a noun, a pronoun leans on a verb. In « Je vois le film » the le is holding up a noun and you met it in lesson 6 in A1. In « Je le vois » there is no noun for it to hold up, and the word straight after it is a verb. Same three letters, and the thing beside them tells you which job is being done.
sameWords.title: The shape you have met four times, and lesson 5 in A2 named it

examples.note: The lesson 6 in A1 job. A noun follows, so it is the article.
This lesson's job. A verb follows, so it is the pronoun.

shortened.body: Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was. You have met this before: lesson 8 in Sounds teaches it properly and at length, and nothing about it is new here. What IS new is what it costs you in this lesson. You spend the first half learning that le is masculine and la is feminine, and then meet a form where that distinction is gone from the sound and gone from the page. « Je l'aime » is him or it is her, and the sentence does not say. Nobody can be tested on it and nobody can hear it. It is not a gap in your French; it is a gap in the language, and the surrounding conversation is what fills it.
shortened.title: The form that loses the gender, and lesson 8 in Sounds owns why

examples.note: Him or her. The English gloss carries both because the French carries both.
And the plural does not shorten. Les keeps its shape and adds a z sound, so the plural survives where the two singulars do not.

theEnding.body: When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending. Nothing in the sound changes. The ending is written and it is never heard. « J'ai vu la photo » names the thing afterwards and nothing happens. « Je l'ai vue » says it first, and an e goes on the end of the second word. Both sentences sound exactly the same, which is not a quirk of these two verbs: vu, vue, vus and vues are one sound, the way you were told endings would be back in the very first A2 lesson. So this is a writing rule, and the only place in this lesson that can prove you have it is the dictée and the one typed question in the exam.
theEnding.title: What happens in the past, and why only writing shows it

examples.note: Named after the verb, so nothing goes on the end.
Said before the verb, so the e goes on. The respelling is identical to the row above it on purpose.

whatOrWho.body: Say the verb, then ask what, or who. See what? The film. Know who? Marie. Whatever answers that question is the word this lesson replaces, and in English it sits directly after the verb every time. That position is the only thing you have to give up. The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Not every verb has one. « I sleep » answers nothing, and a verb with no answer to what or who has nothing for a pronoun to stand in place of.
whatOrWho.title: How to find the word this lesson is about

examples.note: See what? The film. It is sitting where English always puts it.
Know who? Marie. A person answers the question exactly as a thing does.

frontOfBoth.body: In the past the verb arrives as two words, and there is an obvious place to put a small word: between them. That is the wrong place. The pronoun goes in front of BOTH of them, which is the rule you already have applied to a verb that happens to start earlier than you expected. The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. « Je l'ai vu », never « J'ai le vu ». Say the person, say the pronoun, and only then start the verb.
frontOfBoth.term: in front of the first word
frontOfBoth.title: Where the pronoun goes when the verb is two words long

examples.note: The pronoun, then ai, then vu. Everything verb-shaped is behind it.
And with the wrap as well: ne, pronoun, first word, pas, second word.

sections.body: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Say the verb and ask what, or who; whatever answers is the word you replace, and in English it sits behind the verb. In French it sits in front, between the subject and the verb, and nothing else in the sentence moves.

beats.text: A friend of a friend's kitchen, somewhere off the Cours Julien, and six people around a table that seats four. You have been doing well. Two hours of French and nobody has switched to English for you once.
The woman beside you is refilling glasses. She has just been talking about somebody who is running late, and she turns and asks you something with an easy answer.

cards.fr: Je regarde la photo.  ·  Je la regarde.
cards.sub: [zhuh ruh-GARD lah foh-TOH] then [zhuh lah ruh-GARD]
cards.body: The same test on the feminine. « When English says nothing, French says le. » is what lesson 6 in A1 's, and it is about the first sentence only. The second one is not English saying nothing; it is English saying "it", in the other place.
cards.head: la, twice
cards.label: a noun follows · a verb follows

cards.fr: J'achète les livres.  ·  Je les achète.
cards.body: And the plural. By the fifth time you should be looking for it: one form, two jobs, and the thing beside it settles which. Lesson 5 in A2, lesson 15 in A2 and two others have all been a version of this.
cards.head: les, twice
cards.label: a noun follows · a verb follows

sections.title: The Same Three Words

sections.say: Four words and one position. Tap any row to hear it. The choice between them is lesson 5 in A1's and lesson 6 in A1's, and it is the only part of this lesson that is not new.

rows.say: Je le vois.

detail.say: Je le vois.
detail.body: [zhuh luh VWAH] I see it. One masculine noun, or one man. Lesson 5 in A1 taught you to store the gender and this is where you spend it.
detail.title: « le »

rows.say: Je la vois.

detail.say: Je la vois.
detail.body: [zhuh lah VWAH] I see her. One feminine noun, or one woman. Same place in the sentence, and the only thing that changed is the vowel.
detail.title: « la »

rows.say: Je les vois.

detail.say: Je les vois.
detail.body: [zhuh lay VWAH] I see them. More than one, of either gender or both. The gender is not consulted, exactly as lesson 6 in A1 said of the article.
detail.title: « les »

rows.say: Je l'aime.

detail.say: Je l'aime.
detail.body: [zhuh LEM] I love him. Or her. Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was. Lesson 8 in Sounds owns it.
detail.title: « l' »

sections.title: Four Forms, One Place

sections.say: Six sentences, six different subjects, and the word in front of the verb does not respond to any of them. Lesson 19 in A2 was the opposite and it was one lesson ago, so this is worth a screen.
sections.title: The Subject Has No Say

examples.en: He looks at him.
examples.fr: Il le regarde.
examples.note: [eel luh ruh-GARD] Two le-shaped words in a row, and only the second one belongs to the verb.

examples.en: She knows her.
examples.fr: Elle la connaît.
examples.note: [ehl lah koh-NEH] A feminine subject and a feminine pronoun with nothing to do with each other. La is the gender of the person known, not of the person knowing.

examples.en: We invite them.
examples.fr: Nous les invitons.
examples.note: [noo lay zaⁿ-vee-TOHⁿ] And the s of les is audible here, because a vowel follows it.

examples.en: You see it.
examples.fr: Vous le voyez.
examples.note: [voo luh vwah-YAY] Vous, and le is unchanged.

examples.en: They buy them.
examples.fr: Ils les achètent.
examples.note: [eel lay zah-SHEHT] Ils, and les is unchanged. The verb ending is silent, which is lesson 1's business and not this lesson's.

examples.en: You know him.
examples.fr: Tu le connais.
examples.note: [tü luh koh-NEH] « The pronoun changes with the subject, because it is the subject. » is lesson 19's line about ITS small word. This one is the other kind: it takes the gender of the thing it stands for and ignores the subject entirely.

sections.say: Four sentences that name the thing, and the same four with it replaced. Read across rather than down: the word gets shorter and it moves.
sections.title: Name It, Then Replace It

examples.en: I see the film. / I see it.
examples.fr: Je vois le film.  ·  Je le vois.
examples.note: [zhuh luh VWAH] See what? Le film. That is the what or the who, and it goes from four words after the verb to one word before it.

examples.en: I look at the photo. / I look at it.
examples.fr: Je regarde la photo.  ·  Je la regarde.
examples.note: [zhuh lah ruh-GARD] Look at what? La photo. Feminine, so la, and lesson 5 in A1 is the only reason you know that.

examples.en: I buy the books. / I buy them.
examples.fr: J'achète les livres.  ·  Je les achète.
examples.note: [zhuh lay zah-SHEHT] Buy what? Les livres. Plural, so les, and the gender never comes up.

examples.en: I know Marie. / I know her.
examples.fr: Je connais Marie.  ·  Je la connais.
examples.note: [zhuh lah koh-NEH] Know who? Marie. A person, and nothing about the rule changes for one.

examples.en: I see him every week.
examples.fr: Je le vois chaque semaine.
examples.note: Published, in this lesson's own theme, and written by somebody who was not teaching this. The word is in front of the verb because that is where it goes, not because a lesson said so.

examples.en: I see her every day.
examples.fr: Je la vois tous les jours.
examples.note: The feminine, same shape, same theme. Two sentences the rule did not produce and which obey it anyway.

sections.say: Three rounds. Say the subject, then reach for the word, and it goes in before the verb every time. The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it.
sections.title: Say It Before You Think

check.q: « Je vois le film. » See what? Now say it without the noun.
check.why: Le film is the what or the who, so it becomes le, and le goes in front of vois. The second option is the English order with French words in it.

items.en: I see the film.
items.fr: Je vois le film.

items.en: I see it.
items.fr: Je le vois.

check.q: « Je regarde la photo. » Replace the noun.
check.why: La photo is feminine, so la, not le. Lesson 5 in A1 is doing the work here and this lesson only decides where the word lands.

items.en: I look at the photo.
items.fr: Je regarde la photo.

items.en: I look at it.
items.fr: Je la regarde.

check.q: « Je connais Marie. » Replace the name.
check.why: A person replaces exactly like a thing. Both wrong answers put the word where English puts it, and the first of them is the sentence the scene opened on.

items.en: I know Marie.
items.fr: Je connais Marie.

items.en: I know her.
items.fr: Je la connais.

groups.label: and it never goes on the end

sections.say: Four cards and then six to prove it. The first card is the sentence your own language will hand you every time you stop concentrating.

rule.body: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Not sometimes, and not the way English does it. The word goes between the subject and the verb, and there is nothing else to decide once you know which word it is.
rule.title: In front of the verb, every time

cards.fr: Je vois le.
cards.ipa: /ʒə vwa lə/
cards.tip: Every word correct and the sentence stops dead. Le at the end is a word waiting for a noun that never comes, which is why a French ear hears it as unfinished rather than as wrong.
cards.promptLabel: the order English hands you gives
cards.promptSound: Je vois le.

cards.fr: Je le vois.
cards.ipa: /ʒə lə vwa/
cards.tip: Subject, word, verb. Nothing was added and nothing was removed.
cards.promptLabel: and the same three words in the French order
cards.promptSound: Je le vois.

cards.fr: Je la connais.
cards.ipa: /ʒə la kɔ.nɛ/
cards.tip: The scene ended on the other version of this one. Knowing the gender was never the problem.
cards.promptLabel: a person, and it behaves the same
cards.promptSound: Je la connais.

cards.fr: Je les vois.
cards.ipa: /ʒə le vwa/
cards.tip: Three forms and one position. The position is what this lesson is for.
cards.promptLabel: and the plural, in the same place
cards.promptSound: Je les vois.

drill.promptSay: Je le vois.
Je la connais.
Je les vois.

Nous les invitons.

sections.title: Which Side Of The Verb

sections.say: Four verbs this lesson has not conjugated once. Nothing about them is new and nothing about the rule changes, which is the point of asking.
sections.title: Verbs Not Taught Here

check.q: « Tu cherches les clés. » Replace the noun.
check.why: Chercher was never on a screen here and did not need to be. The third option moved the word correctly and dropped the verb ending, which is lesson 1's rule.

items.en: I listen to it.
items.fr: Je l'écoute.

items.en: You are looking for them.
items.fr: Tu les cherches.

check.q: « Elle prend le train. » Replace the noun.
check.why: Prendre is irregular and belongs to another lesson, and carrying a pronoun is no different for it than for any other verb. The word goes in front, and the verb keeps whatever ending it always had.

items.en: She takes it.
items.fr: Elle le prend.

items.en: We finish it.
items.fr: Nous la finissons.

sections.say: Four, one per screen, and the first one is the sentence the lesson opened on.
sections.title: What Goes Wrong

errors.why: The word in the English place. This is the error the scene ends on, and it is not carelessness: it is what happens when the sentence is already moving and the place has gone past.
errors.right: Je la connais.
errors.wrong: Je connais la.

errors.why: Reaching for the word that means "her" on its own. French has one of those and it is not used here. The word that goes in front of the verb is la, and it looks exactly like the article.
errors.right: Je la connais.
errors.wrong: Je connais elle.

errors.why: Both the pronoun and the noun in one sentence. You replace the noun or you keep it; you never say both. If the noun is still there, you did not need the word at all.
errors.right: Je la regarde.
errors.wrong: Je le regarde la photo.

errors.why: The wrap closed round the verb alone and left the word outside it. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together.
errors.right: Je ne le vois pas.
errors.wrong: Je ne vois pas le.

sections.say: Three cards, and the first one takes something away from you. Lesson 8 in Sounds owns this rule and teaches it properly; this is only what it costs here.
sections.hint: Two of the three words become the same word.

cards.fr: Je l'aime.
cards.sub: [zhuh LEM] I love him. Or her.
cards.body: Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was. Half a lesson on le being masculine and la feminine, and now it is gone. Not hidden: absent. The conversation tells you.
cards.head: him, or her
cards.label: and the sentence does not say

cards.fr: Je l'invite.  ·  Je l'achète.
cards.body: Two more verbs and the same thing happens. It is a property of the vowel that follows, not of any particular word, which is exactly what lesson 8 in Sounds says about every other place this happens.
cards.head: and it is not just aimer
cards.label: any verb starting on a vowel

cards.fr: Je les invite.
cards.body: Les keeps its shape in front of a vowel and gains a z sound instead. So the plural is still audible when both singulars have stopped being, and that asymmetry is worth noticing: the form that never carried gender is the one that survives intact.
cards.head: the plural survives
cards.label: les does not shorten

sections.title: When The Gender Goes

sections.say: Four lines. Two of them differ by one sound and listening will separate them. The third pair does not differ at all, and no question in this lesson will ever ask you about it.

lines.en: I see it.
lines.fr: Je le vois.

lines.en: I see her.
lines.fr: Je la vois.

lines.en: I see them.
lines.fr: Je les vois.

lines.en: I love him. Or her.
lines.fr: Je l'aime.

sections.title: What Listening Settles

questions.q: Je le vois against Je la vois. What separates them?
questions.why: Luh against lah. One sound, and it is the whole gender. This is the one place in the lesson where the ear does the work for you.
opts: One vowel, and it carries the gender

questions.q: And Je l'aime. Which gender is it?
questions.why: Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was. A question offering only masculine and feminine would have no correct option, so this lesson asks none.

sections.say: One negation rule, five lessons old, and this adds a sentence to it rather than a rule. « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. »
sections.hint: The word and the verb travel together.

cards.fr: Je le vois.  ·  Je ne le vois pas.
cards.sub: [zhuh luh VWAH] then [zhuh nuh luh vwah PAH]
cards.body: « Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. » from lesson 21 in A1, and « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » is lesson 15's. One verb, so neither arises. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together.
cards.head: both inside
cards.label: ne · le vois · pas

cards.fr: Je ne vois pas le.  ·  Je ne le vois pas.
cards.sub: the first one leaves the word stranded behind pas
cards.body: If the word were an ordinary object it would sit after the verb and outside the wrap, which is what the first sentence does. It is not an ordinary object; it belongs to the verb. So it goes where the verb goes, inside.
cards.head: not this
cards.label: the word pushed out of the wrap

cards.fr: Je ne la connais pas.  ·  Je ne l'aime pas.
cards.sub: [zhuh nuh lah koh-neh PAH] then [zhuh nuh lem PAH]
cards.body: « Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. » is how lesson 19 in A2 put it, and that reason does not apply here: this word does not change with the subject. Same behaviour, different cause.
cards.head: you have done this before
cards.label: Lesson 19 in A2, one lesson ago

sections.title: Saying No

sections.say: The verb arrives as two words in the past, and there is an obvious place to put a small word between them. It is the wrong place. The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it.
sections.hint: The whole verb, not half of it.

cards.fr: J'ai vu le film.  ·  Je l'ai vu.
cards.sub: [zhay vü luh FEELM] then [zhuh lay VÜ]
cards.body: Lesson 16 in A2 gave you the two-word past and lesson 17 in A2 gave you the second words. Neither is new. What is new: the small word goes in front of the FIRST, so everything verb-shaped ends up behind it.
cards.head: name it, or replace it
cards.label: the noun after · the word in front

cards.fr: J'ai le vu.  ·  Je l'ai vu.
cards.sub: the first one splits the verb in half
cards.body: Ai and vu are one verb wearing two words, and nothing goes between them. Say the subject, say the small word, and only then start the verb. That is the same instruction as the present tense; the verb has just started earlier than you expected.
cards.head: not between them
cards.label: the place that looks right

cards.fr: Je ne les ai pas vues.
cards.sub: [zhuh nuh lay zay pah VÜ] I did not see them.
cards.body: The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. The second word stays outside, which is exactly what lesson 20 in A2 settled one lesson ago about a three-part verb. Nothing here is a new negation rule.
cards.head: and saying no
cards.label: ne · word · first word · pas · second word

sections.title: In Front Of Both

sections.say: When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending. Nothing in the sound changes. The ending is written and it is never heard. Four pairs. In each one the left sentence names the thing afterwards and the right one says it first.
sections.title: The Ending Nobody Hears

examples.en: I saw the film. / I saw it.
examples.fr: J'ai vu le film.  ·  Je l'ai vu.
examples.note: [zhuh lay VÜ] Masculine and singular, so nothing goes on. This is the form the other three are built from and the one that hides the rule.

examples.en: I saw the photo. / I saw it.
examples.fr: J'ai vu la photo.  ·  Je l'ai vue.
examples.note: [zhuh lay VÜ] Feminine, so an e. Look at the respelling: it is the same as the line above, character for character, and that is not an oversight.

examples.en: I bought the books. / I bought them.
examples.fr: J'ai acheté les livres.  ·  Je les ai achetés.
examples.note: [zhuh lay zay ahsh-TAY] Plural and masculine, so an s. Still nothing to hear.

examples.en: I looked at the photos. / I looked at them.
examples.fr: J'ai regardé les photos.  ·  Je les ai regardées.
examples.note: [zhuh lay zay ruh-gar-DAY] Feminine and plural, so both letters. Four spellings, one sound, which is the rule lesson 1 in A2 stated and lesson 18 in A2 paid off.

Who Do You Know

sections.setting: The same kitchen, later, and this time the sentences finish. Every question is about a person or a thing, which is the only situation this whole lesson is for.

cards.say: Je le vois.
cards.back: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it.

cards.say: Je le vois.
cards.back: Je le vois. Le film is the what or the who, so it becomes le, and le goes in front.
cards.front: Je vois le film. Say it without the noun.

cards.say: Je la regarde.
cards.back: La. Lesson 5 in A1 decides which, and this lesson decides where.
cards.front: La photo is feminine. Which word replaces it?

cards.say: Je l'aime.
cards.back: Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was.

cards.say: Je ne le vois pas.
cards.back: Je ne le vois pas. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together.

cards.say: Je l'ai vu.
cards.back: In front of both of them. Je l'ai vu, never J'ai le vu.
cards.front: Where does the word go when the verb is two words long?

cards.say: Je l'ai vue.
cards.back: Je l'ai vue. When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending.
cards.front: J'ai vu la photo. Now replace the noun.

cards.say: Elle la connaît.
cards.back: No. It takes the gender of the thing it stands for and ignores the subject. Lesson 19's small word was the opposite.
cards.front: Does the word change when the subject changes?

sections.body: The exam has six rounds and most of it is typed or corrected rather than picked, because a word-order mistake is a whole-sentence mistake and four options cannot show one.

stats.v: 1. The word goes in front of the verb.
0. le, la and les are lesson 6 in A1's and you have had them since A1.
0. All seven were already in your corpus, and four more were never shown at all.
1 of 2. Le against la, yes. The shortened form, never.

sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds of five. Most of it asks you to produce or repair a whole sentence, because that is the only shape a word-order error has.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Five on the one decision in the sentence.
rounds.label: Where it goes

questions.q: Fix the order: « Je vois le. »
questions.why: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Every word was already right and only the order was not, which is what makes this the hardest kind of mistake to hear yourself make.
accept: Je le vois.

questions.q: « Je vois le film. » Type it again with the noun replaced.
questions.why: See what? Le film. So le, and it goes in front of vois rather than after it.
accept: Je le vois.

questions.q: Which one is French?
questions.why: The first is the English order, the second reaches for a word French does not use here, and the fourth keeps the noun as well as the word. You replace the noun or you keep it.

questions.q: Fix the order: « Tu connais le. »
questions.why: The same mistake in another person. The place does not depend on who is speaking.
accept: Tu le connais.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Luh against lay. Singular against plural, and that difference is genuinely audible, unlike almost everything else this lesson turns on.

rounds.say: Five on a choice lesson 5 in A1 already taught you to make.
rounds.label: Which of the three

questions.q: « Je regarde la photo. » Which word replaces la photo?
questions.why: Photo is feminine and singular, so la. The noun is on the screen so the gender is there to be read rather than remembered.

questions.q: « J'achète les livres. » Type it again with the noun replaced.
questions.why: Plural, so les, and the gender is not consulted at all.
accept: Je les achète.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT tell you which word to use?
questions.why: The subject has no say. It takes the gender of the thing it stands for, which is the opposite of lesson 19's small word and worth keeping separate.
opts: Whether the verb starts on a vowel

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Luh against lah. One vowel, and it carries the whole gender. This is the one thing in the lesson listening will settle.

questions.q: The thing looked at is la photo. Fix the word: « Je le regarde. »
questions.why: The position was right and the gender was not. Both have to be, and only one of them is this lesson's.
accept: Je la regarde.

rounds.say: Five on a rule you have had for five lessons.
rounds.label: Saying no

questions.q: Make « Je le vois. » negative. Type the whole sentence.
questions.why: The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. Ne outside, pas after, and the word stays where it was.
accept: Je ne le vois pas.

questions.q: Fix it: « Je ne vois pas le. »
questions.why: The word was left outside the wrap, behind pas. It belongs to the verb, so it goes where the verb goes.
accept: Je ne le vois pas.

questions.q: Which one is right?
questions.why: « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » There is one verb here, so the only question is what counts as the verb, and the word in front has joined it.

questions.q: Make « Je les achète. » negative. Type the whole sentence.
questions.why: The plural behaves no differently. Ne, then both words, then pas.
accept: Je ne les achète pas.

questions.q: Lesson 19 in A2 said « Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. » Why does that sentence not explain this lesson?
questions.why: The behaviour is identical and the reason is not. Lesson 19's word is the subject said twice; this one is the thing acted on. Both belong to the verb, so both go inside.
opts: Because the wrap is different here
Because this word does not change with the subject at all

rounds.say: Five on the form that takes something away.
rounds.label: The shortened form

questions.q: « Je l'aime. » Is the person a man or a woman?
questions.why: Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was. No question anywhere in this lesson asks it the other way, because there would be no correct answer to mark.

questions.q: « J'invite Marie. » Type it again with the name replaced.
questions.why: Inviter starts on a vowel, so la shortens, and the gender disappears with it. Nothing you can do about that and nothing you need to.
accept: Je l'invite.
Je l'invite.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The singular shortens and the plural does not. Lan-VEET against lay zan-VEET, and the plural is the longer of the two because les kept its shape.

questions.q: Which of these never shortens in front of a vowel?
questions.why: Les keeps its shape and adds a z sound instead. The form that never carried a gender is the one that survives intact.

questions.q: The person is Camille. Fix the order: « J'aime la. »
questions.why: Two things wrong and only one of them is a choice. The word goes in front, and once it is in front of a vowel it shortens whether you meant it to or not.
accept: Je l'aime.

rounds.say: Five on a tense you already have, with one word added.
rounds.label: In the past

questions.q: Fix the order: « J'ai le vu. »
questions.why: The word went between the two halves of the verb. It goes in front of both, which is the same instruction as the present tense on a verb that starts earlier.
accept: Je l'ai vu.

questions.q: « J'ai vu la photo. » Type it again with the noun replaced. Watch the ending.
questions.why: When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending. La photo is feminine and it is now in front of the verb, so vu takes an e. Nothing in the sound changes. The ending is written and it is never heard.
accept: Je l'ai vue.

questions.q: Why does « J'ai vu la photo. » have no ending on vu?
questions.why: When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending. The first option is nearly a rule and it is not this one; the ending appears precisely when the word has moved in front.
opts: Because the thing seen is named after the verb, not before it

questions.q: « J'ai acheté les livres. » Type it again with the noun replaced.

sections.body: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Everything else in this lesson was something you already owned, spent in a new place.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it.
le, la and les are lesson 6 in A1's three words and the choice between them is lesson 5 in A1's. Neither was re-taught here, and both were needed on every screen.
« what comes next decides » is lesson 5's line, and this was the fifth time. Here the word after it decides, and so does where it sits: an article leans on a noun, a pronoun leans on a verb.
Before a vowel both le and la become l', and at that point nothing in the sentence tells you which one it was. Lesson 8 in Sounds owns the rule itself.
The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. One negation rule, five lessons old, and this added a sentence rather than a rule.
When the pronoun comes before the verb, the second word takes its ending. Nothing in the sound changes. The ending is written and it is never heard.
Lesson 19 in A2 gave you me, te and se in this same slot, so the small words you already carry and these are one system rather than two.
Next: lesson 22 in A2 takes the other kind of word into the same slot, and lesson 23 in A2 takes two more. The position you learned today is the position all of them use.

errorTriggers.description: Puts the word where English puts it, behind the verb. « Je vois le. » THE error of this lesson: the brief predicts it will be produced consistently rather than occasionally, because word order is the last thing a second language gives up, and it is the sentence the opening scene dies on.

Places the word correctly and picks the wrong one of the three, usually le for a feminine noun. « Je le regarde » for la photo. The position is this lesson's and the gender is lesson 5 in A1's, so this is a prerequisite failing rather than a new one, and the drill sends the learner back to the noun.

Closes the wrap round the verb alone and strands the word outside it. « Je ne vois pas le. » lesson 19 in A2's extension is about a word that changes with the subject and does not by itself cover a word that does not.

Leaves the second word bare when the pronoun has come before it. « Je l'ai vu. » for a feminine thing. Nothing in the sound ever asked for the ending, so there is no reason inside the learner's ear to add one.

recorded.desc: THE FOUR SILENT FORMS, IN ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED, AND THEY MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM EACH OTHER. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson and it is the opposite of the usual note. Do not help. Do not differentiate them. Do not lean on the ending of ils parlent to make it clearer than il parle, and do not add the faintest vowel after a silent -e. If a listener can tell any of these four apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Read them at conversational pace with no pause for teaching between them. Four recordings made in four sessions are four performances and the drift between them will be heard as French; one take is the only way this works.

All six forms as one continuous take, in paradigm order, by one voice at one speed, then the six full sentences in the same take. The two audible endings must sound ORDINARY rather than emphasised: -ons is a nasal vowel with no N on the end of it, and -ez is AY, identical to the naming form parler. Do not stress the verb anywhere. These are the most frequent words in the language and they are never leaned on in speech, and the whole trap this lesson drills is an English speaker putting weight where French puts none.

The homophone pairs, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE BACK TO BACK, so the identity is real rather than an artefact of two sessions: « Il parle français. » then « Ils parlent français. », then « Elle travaille ici. » then « Elles travaillent ici. » The point of every pair is that the two halves are the same, so any difference in pace, pitch or emphasis between them is a defect. The third pair is different and must be recorded differently: « Tu cherches la gare. » against « Il cherche la gare. » are NOT identical, because tü and eel are audibly different, and that pair is what proves the pronoun is doing the work. Keep the verbs identical and let the pronouns differ naturally.

The stress trap, WRONG THEN RIGHT in one take. The wrong version is an English speaker leaning on the ending: ils par-LENT with a real second syllable, tu cher-CHES with an audible s, elle travaille with a small uh after it. The right version is flat, one syllable for the verb, weight at the end of the phrase and nothing on the word. Both halves must be spoken by the same voice at the same pace, because the difference being taught is where the weight sits and not how careful the speaker is. Do not caricature the wrong one; it should sound like a competent learner, which is what makes it worth correcting.

The thirty naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice. Every one of them ends in the same AY sound and that sameness is the teaching: the learner should come away hearing -er as one ending rather than thirty word-endings. Do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, one woman in her thirties at an ordinary reception-desk pace. The beat where she moves on (« Bon. Je vous mets au mardi, alors. ») must be brisk and unbothered rather than pointed: the whole scene turns on nobody minding, so any hint of impatience or of correction would destroy it. There is a four-second wait written into the stage direction before that line and it should be audible as a pause, not filled.
clipIds: Bon. Je vous mets au mardi, alors.

lessons.intro: Nine in ten French verbs work exactly like this one, so learning the pattern once gives you thousands of them. Six endings, four of which make no sound at all, which is why the little word in front of the verb is doing more work than you think.

stem.body: parler gives parl-. regarder gives regard-. chercher gives cherch-. It does not move, whoever is speaking, so once you have it you have all six forms of that verb and you never have to learn them separately. This is why a regular verb is worked out rather than memorised, and why etre and avoir were the exception rather than the rule.
stem.title: What is left when -er comes off

examples.note: cherch- with the tu ending, which makes no sound.
The same cherch-, with the nous ending, which does.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, so it costs you no new ending at all: on parle, on regarde, on cherche. Every table in this level prints nous, and almost every conversation you hear will use on. Writing nous is never wrong; it just sits a register above where the conversation is.
nousOn.title: One meaning, two registers

examples.note: The written one, with the ending you can hear.
The spoken one, taking the il form.

audibleTwo.body: These two are syllables of their own, so they arrive at the ear as clearly as anything else in the sentence. -ons is a nasal vowel, OHⁿ, with no N sound at the end of it. -ez is AY, which means vous parlez and the naming form parler are said exactly the same way. Those two are the whole of what your ear gets from an -er verb.
audibleTwo.title: -ons and -ez

examples.note: The vous ending, audible, and identical to parler.

flatEnding.body: English puts weight on the end of a verb: he WALKS, they WALKED. French has nothing there to weigh, because in four of the six forms there is no sound at the end at all. Leaning on the ending is the single most recognisable thing an English speaker does to a French verb, and it is a habit rather than a gap in knowledge. The weight goes at the end of the phrase, not the end of the word.
flatEnding.title: Nothing to lean on

examples.note: Said flat, and the last thing you hear is parl.
The weight lands on fort, which is where the phrase ends.

infinitive.body: parler, regarder, chanter. This is the form a verb is listed under and it is not a form anybody uses in a sentence. Its last two letters are the instruction: cut them off and what is left is the part that never changes. Thirty of the verbs in this lesson end this way, and so do roughly nine in ten French verbs.
infinitive.title: The form in the dictionary

examples.note: parler, cut back to parl-, with the je ending on it.
And the vous ending, which sounds exactly like the naming form itself.

silentEnding.body: -e, -es and -ent are all silent. il parle and ils parlent are six letters apart on the page and identical in the air. French writes distinctions it does not say, and this is the first place you meet that: the spelling is doing work for the reader that the sound is not doing for the listener. Nothing is dropped or slurred. The letters were never pronounced.
silentEnding.title: Letters that are written and not said

sections.title: parler, all nine pronouns

sections.body: Four of the six endings are silent, and they are silent completely: nothing is slurred or dropped, and the letters were never pronounced in the first place. The -e of je parle and il parle makes no sound. The -es of tu parles makes no sound, and the s there is the same silent s you already write on tu es. The -ent of ils parlent makes no sound either, and it is the longest ending in the set and the emptiest one, which is why it is the ending learners most want to pronounce and the one that marks a sentence as read rather than spoken. So je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent are four spellings and one sound, and out loud only the pronoun in front separates them. That is the reason French keeps its subject pronouns everywhere English could drop them: the verb is not carrying the person, so something has to. Only two endings survive the trip to somebody else's ear. The -ons of nous parlons is a nasal vowel with no N sound at the end of it, and the -ez of vous parlez is AY, which is exactly how the naming form parler is said, so vous parlez and parler are one sound and two jobs.
sections.title: The letters you do not say

sections.body: These six endings do not change again. The next unit keeps every one of them and moves a single letter in the stem in front of them, for a reason you can predict from the spelling, so nothing you have learned here is spent. The -IR and -RE units after it swap the endings for two other short sets and leave the method exactly as it is: find the stem, add the person. The unit on the past tense will take the naming form you started from, change its last two letters, and produce something that sounds identical to what you started with, which is a problem it will hand you fully formed rather than one you have to see coming. And the two later units on agreement rest on one thing you already have: French writes distinctions it does not say. You met that here, on four endings that exist entirely for the reader.
sections.title: What carries forward

sheets.title: The thirty verbs
contains: Why none of them changes its stem

sections.body: Every verb here has a stem that does not move. Take the last two letters off and what is left is the same for all six persons and stays the same however the verb is used, so one pattern gives you thirty verbs and about a hundred and eighty forms. That is not true of every verb ending in -er. A small group changes one letter in the stem, and they are deliberately not on this list even though several of them are more common than some that are: manger, commencer, acheter, appeler, préférer, payer, essayer and jeter all keep these endings exactly and move something in front of them. They are the next unit and they will make more sense once this one is automatic. One verb ending in -er belongs to neither group. aller looks exactly like the thirty and behaves like nothing in this lesson, and it has a unit of its own. If you try the machine on it you will produce something that no French speaker says, so it is worth knowing by name from the start rather than discovering it at speed.

Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

questions.why: Writing takes nous, and nous takes -ons. The first option is not wrong French; it is just the spoken register in a written place.

questions.q: You are saying the same thing out loud to a friend. Which would you actually say?
questions.why: Speech takes on, and on takes the il form. Both of the first two are correct French and only one of them is what a room sounds like.

sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that picks this up.
sections.body: You can build the present tense of any regular -er verb, including ones nobody has shown you, and that is most of the verbs in the language. You know which two of the six endings survive the trip to somebody else's ear and which four do not, which is why French keeps its subject pronouns when English could drop them. The next unit takes the same six endings and moves one letter in the stem in front of them, for a reason you will be able to predict. Nothing about the endings changes again.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person.
Cut the last two letters off the naming form, then put the person on what is left.
-ons and -ez are the two you hear. -e, -es, -e, -ent give the ear nothing.
Write the nous form and say the on one. on takes the il ending, so it costs you nothing new.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the naming form under pressure, or cuts the wrong amount off it: je travailler, je travail.
Writes the wrong silent ending, because no sound distinguishes them: je parles, ils parle, elle travaillent.
Tries to name the person from the verb, which for four of the six forms is not information the sound carries.
Puts the nous ending on on, or writes on where a written register wants nous.
Leans on the ending out loud, sounding -ent or adding a vowel after a silent -e. A habit, not a knowledge gap.

That -e, -es and -ent are silent and -ons and -ez are not

nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one

acts.milestone: Aucune de tes phrases ne se termine plus par une préposition qui ne se rattache à rien. EN: None of your sentences ends on a preposition attached to nothing any more.

acts.title: Quatre formes, trois sons

opener.line: Quatre mots écrits, et ton oreille n'en entend que trois : ici tu apprends à choisir avec les yeux. EN: Four written words and your ear hears only three: here you learn to choose with your eyes.

acts.milestone: Tu accordes lequel avec le nom écrit devant, même quand rien ne s'entend. EN: You can agree lequel with the noun in front, even when nothing is audible.

acts.title: à devient auquel

opener.line: Deux mots qui se touchent et n'en font plus qu'un : ici tu apprends la première des deux soudures, et la seule forme qui y résiste. EN: Two words that touch and become one: here you learn the first of the two fusions, and the one form that resists it.

acts.milestone: Tu écris auquel, auxquels et auxquelles en un mot, et à laquelle en deux. EN: You write auquel, auxquels and auxquelles as one word, and à laquelle as two.

acts.title: de devient duquel

opener.line: Il existe une seule place où dont ne peut pas aller : ici tu apprends à la reconnaître en comptant les mots. EN: There is exactly one place dont cannot go: here you learn to spot it by counting words.

acts.milestone: Tu sais quand de prend dont et quand il prend duquel, sans hésiter. EN: You know when de takes dont and when it takes duquel, without hesitating.

acts.title: La raison pour laquelle

opener.line: Quatre mots qui ne se séparent jamais, et que tu écriras dans presque toutes tes lettres : ici tu apprends les blocs. EN: Four words that never come apart, and that you will write in almost every letter: here you learn the blocks.

acts.milestone: Tu poses la raison pour laquelle et grâce auquel sans les découper ni les traduire mot à mot. EN: You can use la raison pour laquelle and grâce auquel without cutting them up or translating them word for word.

acts.title: Rien devant : ce qui, ce que

opener.line: Parfois la chose dont tu parles n'a aucun nom dans ta phrase : ici tu apprends le petit mot qui prend sa place. EN: Sometimes the thing you are talking about has no name in your sentence: here you learn the small word that stands in for it.

acts.milestone: Tu écris ce qui et ce que sans y penser, et le test que tu connais fait le reste. EN: You write ce qui and ce que without thinking, and the test you already know does the rest.

acts.title: Ce dont

opener.line: Certains verbes traînent un de derrière eux, et l'anglais ne le montre jamais : ici tu apprends à l'entendre. EN: Some verbs drag a de behind them and English never shows it: here you learn to hear it.

acts.milestone: Tu entends le de du verbe avant d'écrire, et tu poses ce dont au lieu de ce que. EN: You hear the verb's de before writing, and you put ce dont where you used to put ce que.

acts.title: Tout ce qui, tout ce que

opener.line: L'anglais dit all I need en trois mots, et le français en demande cinq : ici tu apprends les deux qui manquent. EN: English says all I need in three words and French wants five: here you learn the two that are missing.

acts.milestone: Tu n'écris plus jamais tout qui ni tout que : le ce reste, et seule la fin bouge. EN: You never write tout qui or tout que again: the ce stays and only the ending moves.

acts.title: Ce qui reprend toute une phrase

opener.line: Parfois ce que tu reprends n'est pas un mot mais tout ce que tu viens de dire : ici tu apprends la virgule qui le permet. EN: Sometimes what you pick up is not a word but everything you have just said: here you learn the comma that allows it.

acts.milestone: Tu reprends une phrase entière avec ce qui, ce que ou ce dont, et tu gardes qui pour les noms. EN: You can pick up a whole sentence with ce qui, ce que or ce dont, and keep qui for nouns.

acts.title: Écrire la fiche

opener.line: Un réparateur va lire ta fiche avant de voir ton objet : ici tu écris pour quelqu'un qui n'a que tes phrases. EN: A repairer will read your card before seeing your thing: here you write for somebody who has nothing but your sentences.

acts.milestone: Tu écris dix lignes où chaque détail est accroché au bon nom, et où rien ne pend dans le vide. EN: You can write ten lines in which every detail is attached to the right noun and nothing is left dangling.

recorded.desc: The workshop intake text (act 1), one female Québécoise voice, one take, read at dictation pace. The two short sentences in the middle are read flat and evenly, as somebody reading their own notes; from « Alors j'ai recommencé » the delivery opens out. NO PAUSE BETWEEN THE PREPOSITION AND lequel anywhere in this lesson's recordings: « avec lequel » is one group, or the learner hears a seam that is not there.

The four devant cards (act 1). One coach voice. Card three quotes lesson 11's line and must be read as a quotation, slightly quicker, so it is heard as something already known rather than as new teaching. Card four reads its two short sentences with a real pause between them.

Samuel and the coach (act 2), two voices, one take. Samuel's first line is the WRONG form, with the preposition stranded at the end, and it must be read naturally, as somebody reading their own draft aloud. The coach does not correct it in tone, only in words.

The four place cards (act 2). One voice. Cards one and two hold the same words in two orders and must be read back to back at the same pace, because the card claims the difference is the ORDER and nothing else.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, at conversational speed. Every preposition plus lequel is one breath group. Nothing is repeated and no line is slowed for help.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, one voice, same pace. The stranded-preposition versions in promptSound are NEVER spoken.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. LESQUELS AND LESQUELLES ARE READ IDENTICALLY, because they are identical; any helpful difference there destroys the mission, whose whole claim is that only the noun in front separates them.
The four form cards (act 3). One voice. Card four reads the two plurals one after the other with no difference at all, then the noun in front of each, which is where the distinction actually lives.

Nadia and Samuel (act 4), two voices, one take. Nadia says « vous » to the visitor and « tu » to Samuel; the register change is audible and deliberate. The soudure « auquel » is read as one word, never as two.
The four à cards (act 4). One voice. Card two reads « à laquelle » as two clearly separate words, immediately after card one's single word « auquel », and that contrast IS the teaching.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, one voice. The two-word versions in promptSound are never spoken.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. auquel, auxquels and auxquelles are all read as one word each; only « à laquelle » carries an audible join.
Samuel and the coach (act 5), two voices, one take. The two opening lines share every word except the group carrying the de, so they must be read at the same speed and the same pitch.
The four de cards (act 5). One voice. Card one reads « dont » and card two reads « à côté duquel » about the SAME drawer, so the pair is recorded back to back in one take.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. The compound prepositions (à côté de, au bout de, près de) are read as single groups, with no pause before duquel.

The letter from the borough (act 6), one voice, one take, read as a formal document at an even pace. Each fixed block (la raison pour laquelle, les conditions dans lesquelles, le point sur lequel, grâce auquel) is one breath group, and no preposition is stressed.
The four block cards (act 6). One voice. Every block is read whole, at speaking speed, never spelled out word by word: the card claims these are single units and the delivery has to agree.

Nadia and the coach (act 7), two voices, one take. Nadia's first line names a noun and her third names none, and the two are read with exactly the same rhythm so the difference is grammatical rather than dramatic.
The four ce cards (act 7). One voice. Card three quotes lesson 11 and is read as a quotation. There is no pause between ce and the word that follows it, on any card.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. Each line opens on the ce group, and ce qui and ce que are never separated by a pause.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, one voice. The versions missing the ce are never spoken.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. The mission asks the learner to hear which verb carries a de, so the verbs are not stressed and nothing marks them out.
The four ce dont cards (act 8). One voice. Card one and card two both open on « ce dont » and must sound identical up to the verb.
Samuel and the coach (act 9), two voices, one take. Samuel drops the ce in his first line and it is read naturally, without hesitation: he believes it is correct.
The four tout cards (act 9). One voice. « tout ce qui » is read as three quick syllables in one group, never as tout, pause, ce qui.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, one voice. The versions without the ce are never spoken.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. Every tout ce group is one breath, and the learner answers on what follows the gap.

Samuel's message to the group (act 10), one voice, one take, read as somebody reading a message aloud. THE COMMAS ARE AUDIBLE: each « , ce qui » opens with a real pause on the comma, which is the only thing that separates it from a clause attached to a noun.
The four comma cards (act 10). One voice. Cards one and two hold nearly the same words and differ only in whether a noun sits in front of the gap, so they are recorded back to back in the same take.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. Every comma before a ce group is a real pause. Nothing else in the line is stressed.

The model repair card (act 11), one voice, read as somebody reading a public notice aloud rather than performing it. The heading is read once, then a clear break. Every preposition plus lequel group stays joined, and the two ce openings keep their comma pause.

lessons.intro: You can already join two sentences about the same thing with qui and que. What stops you now is everything those two words cannot reach: the tool you worked with, the room you walked through, the reason you came, and the thing that worries you which no noun in your sentence names at all. This lesson gives you the rest of the family, and one look that tells you which of them you need.

tout.body: tout n'est pas un nom, donc il ne reprend rien. Le ce reste : tout ce qui, tout ce que, tout ce dont. L'anglais dit all I need et laisse tomber les deux mots. EN: tout is not a noun, so ce stays.
tout.title: tout ne remplace pas le ce

forme.body: lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles. Tu prends le genre et le nombre du nom de devant, jamais ceux de la chose. Les deux pluriels se disent pareil. EN: Take the gender and number of the noun in front; the two plurals sound the same.
forme.title: Quatre formes, trois sons

place.body: En anglais, avec, sur et dans restent à la fin de la phrase. En français, la préposition monte devant le petit mot et n'en bouge plus. EN: English leaves with, on and in at the end; French moves the preposition in front and leaves it there.
place.title: La préposition passe devant

besoin.body: avoir besoin de, parler de, avoir envie de, s'occuper de. Quand le verbe porte un de, la forme est ce dont et rien d'autre. EN: when the verb carries a de, the form is ce dont.
besoin.title: Le verbe qui réclame de

devant.body: Avant de choisir ton mot, tu regardes ce qui est écrit devant. Un nom : tu le reprends. Rien : tu écris ce. C'est le seul geste de toute la leçon. EN: Look at what is written in front of the gap. A noun means you pick it up; nothing means you write ce.
devant.title: Ce qui est écrit juste avant le trou

neutre.body: Aucun nom devant le trou : ce prend sa place, et tu gardes le test que tu connais pour choisir qui ou que derrière. EN: with no noun in front, ce stands in, and the test you already know picks qui or que.
neutre.title: Quand rien n'est écrit devant

phrase.body: Après une virgule, ce qui ne reprend pas un nom : il reprend tout ce que tu viens de dire. Une phrase n'est pas un nom, donc le ce est obligatoire. EN: after a comma, ce qui picks up the whole sentence, and a sentence is not a noun.
phrase.title: Devant la virgule, une phrase entière

examples.note: ce qui reprend la phrase entière

raison.body: la raison pour laquelle, les conditions dans lesquelles, le point sur lequel, grâce auquel. Tu apprends le bloc complet, pas mot à mot. EN: learn these as whole blocks rather than word by word.
raison.title: Des blocs à apprendre entiers

examples.note: le bloc le plus utile de tous

compose.body: à côté de, au bout de, près de, en face de, le long de : ce sont des groupes. Après un groupe, dont ne passe plus et tu écris duquel. EN: after a compound preposition ending in de, dont is impossible and duquel takes over.
compose.title: Un groupe qui finit par de

soudure.body: Deux prépositions seulement se soudent : à donne auquel, auxquels, auxquelles, et de donne duquel, desquels, desquelles. Le féminin singulier résiste aux deux. EN: Only à and de fuse; the feminine singular resists both.
soudure.title: à et de se collent au mot

examples.note: à laquelle reste en deux mots

lessons.title: Lequel, ce qui et ce que

drills.coach: Regarde devant le petit mot : y a-t-il un nom ? Deux piles : un nom est écrit devant, ou il n'y a rien. EN: two piles, by whether a noun is written in front.
drills.title: Un nom, ou rien

drills.why: La préposition passe devant. EN: the preposition moves in front.
drills.coach: Cherche avec, sur ou dans à la fin de ta phrase. S'il y en a un, il doit monter. EN: look for a stranded preposition and move it to the front.
drills.title: La préposition monte

drills.coach: Deux piles, et ne regarde que le nom écrit devant. EN: two piles, and look only at the noun written in front.
drills.title: Le genre du nom de devant

drills.q: Le cours ... je me suis inscrit commence en mars.
drills.why: à plus lequel donne auquel. EN: à plus lequel gives auquel.
drills.coach: Demande-toi si le verbe porte un à. S'il le porte, il faut souder, sauf au féminin singulier. EN: if the verb carries an à, fuse it, except in the feminine singular.
drills.title: à se colle

drills.q: Le parc ... Nadia habite ferme à vingt heures.
drills.why: près de est un groupe, donc duquel. EN: près de is a group, so duquel.
drills.coach: Compte les mots qui portent le de. Un seul mot, dont. Un groupe, duquel. EN: count the words carrying the de.
drills.title: dont ou duquel

drills.coach: Lis chaque bloc à voix haute, en entier, sans le découper. EN: read each block aloud whole, without cutting it up.
drills.title: Les blocs entiers

drills.q: ... m'énerve, c'est le bruit.
drills.why: Aucun nom devant, donc ce qui. EN: no noun in front, so ce qui.
drills.coach: Cherche un nom juste devant le trou. Il n’y en a pas, donc il faut ce. EN: look for a noun in front; there is none, so ce is required.
drills.title: Le ce qui manque

drills.q: C'est exactement ... j'ai besoin.
drills.why: avoir besoin de, donc ce dont. EN: avoir besoin de, so ce dont.
drills.coach: Dis le verbe tout seul : avoir besoin DE. Le de est là, donc ce dont. EN: say the verb on its own; if it carries de, write ce dont.
drills.title: Le verbe qui réclame de

drills.q: ... est sur l'établi part demain.
drills.why: tout ne remplace pas le ce. EN: tout does not replace the ce.
drills.coach: tout n'est pas un nom, donc il ne reprend rien et le ce reste. EN: tout is not a noun, so the ce stays.
drills.title: tout garde son ce

drills.coach: Deux piles. Regarde ce qui est devant la virgule : un nom seul, ou une phrase entière. EN: sort by what sits in front of the comma.
drills.title: Un nom, ou toute la phrase

drills.coach: Lis chaque phrase à voix haute et nomme le mot écrit devant le trou. Si tu ne peux pas le nommer, la phrase est cassée. EN: read each one aloud and name the word written in front of the gap.
drills.title: Une fiche qui tient

sections.body: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce. Tu regardes d'abord ce qui est écrit juste devant le trou. Si c'est un nom, il reste à choisir le mot qui le reprend. Si ce n'est pas un nom, ou s'il n'y a rien, tu écris ce, et seulement ensuite tu regardes derrière. EN: A noun in front: you pick it up. Nothing in front: you write ce. Look in front first; look behind second.

sections.body: lequel est fait de le et de quel, et les deux morceaux s'accordent ensemble avec le nom de devant. C'est pour ça qu'il y a quatre formes écrites et que le pluriel prend un s des deux côtés. À l'oreille, lesquels et lesquelles ne se distinguent pas. EN: lequel is le plus quel, and both halves agree with the noun in front; the two plurals sound identical.

sections.body: Quand le de vient du verbe et qu'il est seul, dont fait tout le travail : le tiroir DONT je parle. Quand le de termine un groupe (à côté de, au bout de, près de), dont ne passe plus, et c'est duquel qui prend le relais. C'est la seule frontière entre les deux, et la leçon 12 du B1 traite dont pour lui-même. EN: a lone de takes dont; a de that ends a compound preposition takes duquel.

sections.body: Quand aucun nom n'est écrit devant, ce prend sa place, et le mot qui suit se choisit exactement comme avant : « Derrière qui, pas de sujet. Derrière que, toujours un sujet. » Si le verbe de la relative réclame un de, la forme est ce dont. EN: Behind qui, no subject. Behind que, always a subject. And if the clause's verb wants de, the form is ce dont.

overview.subFr: Lequel, ce qui et ce que
overview.introFr: Tu sais déjà coller deux phrases avec qui et que. Ce qui te bloque maintenant, c'est tout ce que ces deux mots n'atteignent pas : l'outil avec lequel tu as travaillé, la raison pour laquelle tu es venu, et la chose qui t'inquiète sans qu'aucun nom la désigne. Cette leçon te donne le reste de la famille, et un seul regard qui te dit lequel il te faut.
overview.titleEn: Lequel, Ce Qui and Ce Que

sections.say: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce.

sections.title: Ce que tu sauras faire

sections.say: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce.
sections.text:
Le samedi matin, rue Ontario, un local ouvre ses portes et douze personnes entrent avec des objets cassés. Nadia pose une fiche sur le comptoir et demande toujours la même chose : « Racontez-moi la panne. »

Ce matin-là, je suis arrivé avec une lampe de bureau qui ne s'allumait plus. J'ai dit : « J'ai ouvert le boîtier avec un tournevis. Le tournevis est trop petit. » Nadia a levé les yeux. Sur l'établi, derrière elle, il y avait six tournevis.

Alors j'ai recommencé autrement. « Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier est trop petit. La boîte dans laquelle vous rangez les vis est bleue, et il m'en manque une. Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil. »

Elle a écrit trois lignes, elle est allée chercher une vis, et la lampe s'est allumée. Rien n'avait changé dans les faits. Deux petits mots avaient rattaché chaque détail à la bonne chose.

rule.body: Si ta phrase se termine par avec, sur, dans ou pour, il manque un déplacement. La préposition monte devant le petit mot, et que devient lequel. EN: a clause that ends on a preposition needs that preposition moved to the front, and que becomes lequel.

sections.text:
L'arrondissement a répondu au local de réparation en huit lignes.

« Madame, nous avons bien reçu le dossier pour lequel vous avez écrit le douze mars. La raison pour laquelle votre demande n'a pas été traitée plus tôt est simple : il manquait le plan du local. Les conditions dans lesquelles vous travaillez ont été vérifiées par un inspecteur. Le point sur lequel il revient est la sortie de secours, à côté de laquelle vous stockez des cartons. Le délai au bout duquel votre autorisation sera renouvelée est de deux ans. L'outil grâce auquel nous suivons les dossiers vous enverra un rappel. »

Nadia a lu la lettre deux fois. Elle a remarqué que chaque phrase accrochait une information à un nom précis, et qu'aucune préposition ne traînait à la fin. Elle a souligné quatre groupes et les a recopiés sur une fiche, au-dessus de l'établi, pour les réutiliser.

sections.text:
Message de Samuel au groupe du samedi, jeudi, vingt et une heures.

« Bonjour à tous. Nadia part en août, ce dont nous devons parler avant la rentrée. Le local a été repeint la semaine dernière, ce qui change vraiment l'ambiance. Par contre, il manque deux pièces pour la machine à coudre, ce que je trouve embêtant, parce que c'est la machine pour laquelle nous avons le plus de demandes.

Autre chose : le prix des ampoules a baissé, ce dont les habitués seront contents. J'ai rangé tout ce qui traînait sur l'établi et j'ai jeté tout ce qui était cassé. Ce qui reste est dans la caisse grise.

Dernier point. Samedi dernier, personne n'est venu, ce qui ne s'était jamais vu. Ce dont j'ai peur, c'est qu'on perde l'habitude. Dites-moi ce que vous en pensez. »
sections.title: Le message du jeudi soir

sections.text:
FICHE DE RÉPARATION : lampe de bureau

L'objet que j'apporte est une lampe de bureau qui ne s'allume plus depuis mardi. Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier était trop petit, et j'ai abîmé une vis. La boîte à côté de laquelle j'ai posé la lampe est grise ; la vis est peut-être tombée dedans.

Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil noir, qui chauffe au bout de deux minutes. Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'une pièce de rechange et d'un tournevis plus fin. Tout ce qui reste à faire tient en dix minutes.

La raison pour laquelle je reviens samedi, c'est la pièce. Voici le numéro auquel vous pouvez me joindre entre neuf heures et midi. Ce que je voudrais vraiment, c'est apprendre à la réparer moi-même.
sections.title: Le modèle que tu vas imiter

glossary.note: Une pièce de rechange remplace celle qui est cassée.
Un objet abîmé n'est pas cassé, mais il a souffert.
Un fil qui chauffe est un fil dont la température monte.

glossary.en: reach me, get hold of me
glossary.note: Me téléphoner ou me contacter.

questions.a: « Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier était trop petit. » La préposition avec est montée devant lequel.
questions.q: Quelle phrase dit avec quel outil la personne a travaillé ?

questions.a: « La boîte à côté de laquelle j'ai posé la lampe » : boîte est féminin singulier, donc de laquelle en trois mots.
questions.q: Quelle phrase contient un groupe qui finit par de, et quelle forme suit ?

questions.a: « Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil noir » et « Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'une pièce de rechange ».
questions.q: Deux phrases commencent sans aucun nom devant. Lesquelles ?

questions.a: avoir besoin DE : le de vient du verbe, donc ce dont.
questions.q: Pourquoi ce dont et non ce que dans la seconde ?

sections.say: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce.
steps: Écris tes faits en phrases courtes, sans te relire. EN: write your facts as short sentences, without rereading.
Pour chaque fait, cherche le nom auquel il appartient. EN: for each fact, find the noun it belongs to.
Colle les deux, et regarde ce qui est écrit devant le trou. EN: join the two, and look at what is written in front of the gap.
Un nom : accorde lequel, et fais monter la préposition. EN: a noun means agreeing lequel and moving the preposition to the front.
Aucun nom : écris ce, puis regarde derrière pour choisir. EN: no noun means writing ce, then looking behind to choose.
sections.title: Cinq étapes avant d'écrire
