turns.ai: Bonjour. Racontez-moi la panne.
turns.en: Good morning. Tell me about the fault.

alts.en: The appliance I am telling you about has stopped heating. (parler de, so dont.)
alts.fr: L'appareil dont je vous parle ne chauffe plus.

alts.en: What has stopped working is the right-hand side. (No noun in front, so ce qui.)
alts.fr: Ce qui ne marche plus, c'est le côté droit.

turns.user: Le grille-pain que j'apporte ne chauffe plus d'un côté.
turns.userEn: The toaster I am bringing in has stopped heating on one side. (que, because je follows it.)

turns.ai: Avez-vous déjà ouvert le boîtier.
turns.en: Have you already opened the case.

alts.en: Yes, with the pliers I hold the wires with. (Feminine noun, so laquelle.)
alts.fr: Oui, avec la pince avec laquelle je tiens les fils.

alts.en: No, I do not have the tools you cannot do anything without. (Masculine plural, so lesquels.)
alts.fr: Non, je n'ai pas les outils sans lesquels on ne peut rien faire.

turns.user: Oui, avec un couteau, parce que le tournevis avec lequel je travaille est trop gros.
turns.userEn: Yes, with a knife, because the screwdriver I work with is too big. (avec moves in front of lequel.)

turns.ai: Où avez-vous posé les vis.
turns.en: Where did you put the screws.

alts.en: On the bench at the end of which you keep the cloths. (au bout de, masculine, so duquel.)
alts.fr: Sur l'établi au bout duquel vous rangez les chiffons.

alts.en: In the drawer I told you about last time. (parler de on its own, so dont.)
alts.fr: Dans le tiroir dont je vous ai parlé la dernière fois.

turns.user: Dans la boîte à côté de laquelle il y avait la lampe.
turns.userEn: In the box that had the lamp next to it. (à côté de is a group, so de laquelle.)

turns.ai: Et de quoi avez-vous besoin exactement.
turns.en: And what exactly do you need.

alts.en: What I would like is to learn to change it myself. (je follows, so ce que.)
alts.fr: Ce que je voudrais, c'est apprendre à la changer moi-même.

alts.en: Everything I need fits in one hand. (tout keeps its ce.)
alts.fr: Tout ce dont j'ai besoin tient dans une main.

turns.user: Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'une résistance neuve.
turns.userEn: What I need is a new heating element. (avoir besoin de, so ce dont.)

turns.ai: Pourquoi revenez-vous ici plutôt que dans un magasin.
turns.en: Why come back here rather than to a shop.

alts.en: For the method thanks to which you find the faults. (grâce à plus laquelle.)
alts.fr: Pour la méthode grâce à laquelle vous trouvez les pannes.

alts.en: The point on which you are the best is patience.
alts.fr: Le point sur lequel vous êtes les meilleurs, c'est la patience.

turns.user: La raison pour laquelle je reviens, c'est que vous expliquez.
turns.userEn: The reason why I come back is that you explain things. (The block never comes apart.)

turns.ai: Très bien. Je vous appelle quand la pièce arrive.
turns.en: Very good. I will call you when the part comes in.

alts.en: Thank you. You repaired the lamp in ten minutes, which had amazed me. (A whole sentence, so ce qui.)
alts.fr: Merci. Vous avez réparé la lampe en dix minutes, ce qui m'avait étonné.

alts.en: Everything you taught me last time has been useful. (tout ce que, with vous as the subject.)
alts.fr: Tout ce que vous m'avez appris la dernière fois m'a servi.

turns.user: Voici le numéro auquel vous pouvez me joindre le matin.
turns.userEn: Here is the number you can reach me on in the morning. (joindre à, so auquel.)

sections.setting: Tu reviens le samedi suivant, cette fois pour un grille-pain. Nadia reprend une fiche vierge et te pose ses questions habituelles.

sections.brief: Un objet à toi ne marche plus : une lampe, un grille-pain, un vélo, un ordinateur, une machine à coudre. Tu l'apportes à un atelier de quartier et tu remplis la fiche que le réparateur lira avant de t'appeler. Il ne verra pas l'objet avant de te lire.
sections.title: Écris ta fiche de réparation

criteria.label: Le bon mot à chaque fois
descriptors: 4 : Chaque relative porte le bon mot, et le choix suit ce qui est écrit devant le trou, jamais la traduction anglaise.
3 : Une seule relative se trompe, et le reste est juste.
2 : Plusieurs fois, un nom est écrit devant et tu écris quand même ce, ou l'inverse.
1 : Le choix semble fait au hasard, ou la même forme revient partout.

criteria.label: L'accord et la soudure
descriptors: 3 : lequel s'accorde chaque fois avec le nom de devant, et à et de se soudent partout sauf au féminin singulier.
2 : Un accord manque, ou une soudure est écrite en deux mots.
1 : lequel ne bouge jamais, ou les soudures sont faites au hasard.

criteria.label: La place de la préposition
descriptors: 3 : Aucune phrase ne se termine par une préposition, et chaque préposition est écrite devant le petit mot.
2 : Une phrase laisse avec, sur ou dans au bout.
1 : Plusieurs phrases gardent l'ordre anglais, et le lecteur doit deviner à quoi la fin se rattache.

criteria.label: La mission complète
descriptors: 2 : La fiche fait 110 à 150 mots, elle porte les six relatives demandées, et un réparateur peut reconnaître ton objet et ton problème sans le voir.
1 : Il manque une des six relatives, ou la longueur est hors des bornes, ou la fiche conviendrait à n'importe quel objet du même genre.

sections.briefEn: Something of yours has stopped working. Write the card the repairer will read before calling you back; they will not see the object first.
sections.produce: Écris une fiche de 110 à 150 mots avec au moins six relatives : au moins deux avec lequel après une préposition, une avec à ou de soudés, une avec un groupe qui finit par de, une avec ce qui ou ce que, et une avec ce dont.
scaffold: La boîte à côté de laquelle
Tout ce qui reste à faire

watchFor.pattern: The preposition stranded at the end on the English pattern: « le tournevis que j'ai ouvert le boîtier avec », « la table que je l'ai posé sur ».
watchFor.feedback: La préposition ne reste pas au bout. Fais-la monter : « le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier ».

watchFor.pattern: que kept after a preposition: « avec que », « sur que », « dans que ».
watchFor.feedback: que ne supporte aucune préposition devant lui. Après avec, sur ou dans, écris lequel.

watchFor.pattern: lequel left in the masculine singular for a feminine or plural antecedent: « la pince avec lequel », « les outils sans lequel ».
watchFor.feedback: Regarde le nom écrit devant : la pince donne laquelle, les outils donnent lesquels.

watchFor.pattern: The two plurals confused, since they sound identical: « les caisses dans lesquels », « les cartons dans lesquelles ».
watchFor.feedback: L'oreille ne t'aidera pas ici. caisses est féminin, cartons est masculin.

watchFor.pattern: The contraction of à written in two words, or applied to the feminine singular: « à lequel », « auquelle », « aulaquelle ».
watchFor.feedback: auquel, auxquels et auxquelles se soudent. Seul à laquelle reste en deux mots.

watchFor.pattern: dont used after a compound preposition: « près dont », « à côté dont », « au bout dont ».
watchFor.feedback: Après un groupe qui finit par de, dont n'existe pas. Écris duquel, de laquelle, desquels ou desquelles.

watchFor.pattern: duquel used where a lone de from the verb would have taken dont: « le tiroir duquel je parle ».
watchFor.feedback: parler de porte un de tout seul, donc dont. Compte les mots qui portent le de.

watchFor.pattern: The block broken apart or translated word for word: « la raison pourquoi », « la raison que », « grâce à lequel ».
watchFor.feedback: Le bloc ne se découpe pas : la raison pour laquelle, grâce auquel.

watchFor.pattern: The ce dropped where no noun precedes: « Qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil », « Que je voudrais, c'est... ».
watchFor.feedback: Aucun nom n'est écrit devant, donc ce prend sa place : « Ce qui m'inquiète ».

watchFor.pattern: ce que written after a verb that carries de: « ce que j'ai besoin », « ce que tu parles ».
watchFor.feedback: Dis le verbe tout seul : avoir besoin DE. Le de te donne ce dont.

watchFor.pattern: The ce dropped after tout: « tout qui reste à faire », « tout que tu as dit ».
watchFor.feedback: tout n'est pas un nom et ne reprend rien. Écris tout ce qui, tout ce que, tout ce dont.

watchFor.pattern: qui or que after a comma to pick up the whole preceding sentence: « il a réparé la lampe en dix minutes, qui m’a étonné ».
watchFor.feedback: Devant la virgule il y a une phrase, pas un nom. Écris ce qui, ce que ou ce dont.

graderNotes: Word count EXCLUDES the heading line (FICHE DE RÉPARATION : ...) and any signature. Count the body only, with 10% tolerance (99-165) before criterion « tache » loses its point.

DO NOT SCORE the prepositional relatives for PEOPLE (avec qui, à qui, chez qui) or où. They belong to the parallel lesson on dont and où and have not been taught here. A learner who uses one correctly is not rewarded and one who uses it wrongly is not penalised.
dont ON ITS OWN is treated as known, not as new: score it only in the one contrast this lesson owns, which is dont against duquel after a compound preposition. Do not mark dont for anything else.
The subjunctive belongs to the next lesson. Do not mark a mood error in any subordinate clause.
lequel for a person (la personne à laquelle je pense) is correct French and is accepted, but the lesson taught the thing case, so it is never required.
Judge the relative by what is WRITTEN in front of the gap in the learner text, not by what the learner probably meant. A sentence can be right for a different reason than intended and still scores.
An agreement that is correct but inaudible (lesquels against lesquelles) counts exactly as much as an audible one. The criterion is written accuracy.
Writer gender is unknown: judge adjective agreement for internal consistency only.
Accept any broken object and any francophone city. Accept regional vocabulary (grille-pain, toaster, char, magasin de quartier, ressort, résistance).
Feedback language: simple French (B1), addressed as « tu », with one short English gloss allowed per comment.
sections.modelAnswer:
FICHE DE RÉPARATION : grille-pain

L'objet que j'apporte est un grille-pain qui ne chauffe plus d'un seul côté. Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier était trop gros, et j'ai abîmé deux vis. La boîte à côté de laquelle j'ai posé l'appareil est grise ; une vis est peut-être tombée dedans.

Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil rouge, qui noircit près de la résistance. Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'une résistance neuve et d'un tournevis plus fin. Tout ce qui reste à faire tient en un quart d'heure.

La raison pour laquelle je reviens samedi, c'est la pièce. Voici le numéro auquel vous pouvez me joindre entre neuf heures et midi. Merci à la personne grâce à laquelle il remarchera.
sections.modelAnswerEn: REPAIR CARD: toaster. The thing I am bringing in is a toaster that has stopped heating on one side. The screwdriver I opened the case with was too big and I damaged two screws. The box I put the appliance next to is grey; a screw may have fallen into it. What worries me is the red wire, which is going black near the element. What I need is a new element and a thinner screwdriver. Everything left to do takes a quarter of an hour. The reason why I am coming back on Saturday is the part. Here is the number you can reach me on between nine and noon. Thank you to whoever gets it working again.

sections.say: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce.
sections.body: Tu accroches maintenant une phrase à un nom par-dessus une préposition, tu accordes lequel sans l'entendre, tu soudes à et de au bon endroit, et tu écris ce quand aucun nom ne précède. Le piège qui reste est la frontière entre dont et duquel : elle ne s'entend pas, elle se compte. Avant l'examen, reprends ta fiche et souligne chaque petit mot. Pour chacun, écris à côté le mot qui le précède. Si ce mot est un nom, le petit mot doit le reprendre ; sinon il te faut ce. La phrase où tu ne peux rien écrire à côté est celle qu'il faut réécrire. EN: Underline every relative pronoun in your card and name the word in front of it; the one where you cannot name anything is the one to rewrite.

questions.q: Six tournevis sur l'établi. Pourquoi « Le tournevis est trop petit » ne suffit-il pas ?
questions.why: Elle ne désigne aucun des six en particulier. EN: it points at none of the six in particular.

questions.q: Colle ces deux phrases en une seule.
questions.why: Un nom est écrit devant, donc tu le reprends. EN: a noun is written in front, so you pick it up.
accept: Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier est trop petit.
questions.answer: Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier est trop petit.
questions.prompt: J'ai ouvert le boîtier avec un tournevis. Le tournevis est trop petit.

questions.q: Devant un trou, que regardes-tu en premier ?
questions.why: Le devant décide s'il faut ce. EN: what is in front decides whether ce is needed.

questions.q: Une forme ne va pas. Écris la phrase correcte. EN: One form is wrong; write the sentence correctly.
questions.why: Aucun nom ne précède, donc ce prend sa place. EN: no noun precedes, so ce stands in.
accept: Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil.
questions.answer: Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil.
questions.prompt: Qui m'inquiète, c'est le fil.

questions.q: Complète avec deux mots.
questions.why: avoir besoin DE : le verbe porte un de. EN: the verb carries a de.
accept: Dis-moi ce dont tu as besoin.
questions.answer: Dis-moi ce dont tu as besoin.
questions.prompt: Dis-moi ___ tu as besoin.

questions.q: « La raison pour laquelle je viens ici » : quel mot est écrit devant pour laquelle ?
questions.why: Le nom la raison, et il commande la forme. EN: the noun la raison, and it sets the form.

questions.q: Écoute. Un nom est-il écrit devant le petit mot ?
questions.say: Le tournevis avec lequel j'ai ouvert le boîtier est trop petit.
questions.why: le tournevis est là, donc lequel le reprend. EN: le tournevis is there, so lequel picks it up.

questions.q: Complète avec deux mots.
questions.why: Rien ne suit le trou, donc ce qui. EN: nothing follows the gap, so ce qui.
accept: Je ne sais pas ce qui a lâché.
questions.answer: Je ne sais pas ce qui a lâché.
questions.prompt: Je ne sais pas ___ a lâché.

questions.q: Une relative française peut-elle finir par avec ?
questions.why: La préposition monte devant le petit mot. EN: the preposition moves in front.

questions.q: Une forme ne va pas. Écris la phrase correcte. EN: One form is wrong; write the sentence correctly.
questions.why: sur monte devant, et que devient laquelle. EN: sur moves in front and que becomes laquelle.
accept: La table sur laquelle tu poses la lampe est solide.
questions.answer: La table sur laquelle tu poses la lampe est solide.
questions.prompt: La table que tu poses la lampe sur est solide.

questions.q: Fais monter la préposition.
questions.why: dans ouvre la relative au lieu de la fermer. EN: dans opens the clause instead of closing it.
accept: Le carton dans lequel j'ai mis les vis a disparu.
questions.answer: Le carton dans lequel j'ai mis les vis a disparu.
questions.prompt: Le carton que j'ai mis les vis dans a disparu.

questions.q: Complète : « L'escabeau ... je monte est trop court. »
questions.why: La préposition ne reste pas au bout. EN: the preposition does not stay at the end.

questions.q: Écoute. Quelle préposition monte devant le petit mot ?
questions.say: Les outils sans lesquels on ne peut rien faire sont dans la boîte rouge.
questions.why: « sans lesquels ». EN: sans lesquels.

questions.q: Fais monter la préposition par.
questions.why: fenêtre est féminin singulier, donc laquelle. EN: fenêtre is feminine singular.
accept: La fenêtre par laquelle entre le bruit donne sur la rue.
questions.answer: La fenêtre par laquelle entre le bruit donne sur la rue.

questions.q: Que devient que quand une préposition arrive devant lui ?
questions.why: que ne supporte aucune préposition devant lui. EN: que takes no preposition in front of it.

questions.q: Combien de prépositions se soudent à lequel ?

questions.q: Avec quoi lequel s'accorde-t-il ?

questions.q: Une forme ne va pas. Écris la phrase correcte. EN: One form is wrong; write the sentence correctly.

sections.title: Une dernière fois

sections.say: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce.
sections.body: Un nom devant : tu le reprends. Rien devant : tu écris ce. Tu es entré dans cette leçon en sachant coller deux phrases avec qui et que, et tu en sors avec tout le reste de la famille : l'outil avec lequel tu travailles, le cours auquel tu t'inscris, le parc près duquel tu habites, la raison pour laquelle tu écris, et la chose qui compte sans qu'aucun nom la désigne. Un seul regard les sépare tous, et il se pose devant le trou. La prochaine leçon change de terrain : elle ouvre le subjonctif, le mode de ce qu'on veut, de ce qu'on craint et de ce dont on doute. EN: The next lesson opens the subjunctive, the mood of wanting, fearing and doubting.
sections.title: Un regard, en résumé
points: Le mot écrit devant le trou décide tout le reste.
Aucune relative française ne finit par une préposition.
Seules à et de se soudent, et jamais au féminin singulier.
tout ne remplace pas le ce, et une phrase entière n'est pas un nom.

errorTriggers.description: Writes a run of short separate sentences where one clause was needed, so nothing in the description says which of several identical things is meant.
Leaves the preposition at the end of the clause on the English pattern of the pen I write with, so the sentence ends on avec or sur and the clause never attaches.
Uses lequel for every noun, so a feminine or plural antecedent keeps a masculine singular form and the clause points at the wrong thing.
Writes à lequel or de lequel in two words, or fuses the feminine singular into aulaquelle, so the contraction is applied by guesswork rather than by rule.
Uses dont after a compound preposition (près dont, à côté dont), which does not exist, or uses duquel where a lone de would have taken dont.
Translates the reason why word for word as la raison pourquoi, or breaks one of the fixed blocks apart and reassembles it wrongly.
Writes qui or que with nothing in front of it, where French needs ce to stand in for the missing noun, so the clause opens with no antecedent at all.
Writes ce que after a verb that carries de (avoir besoin de, parler de), because English says what in both cases and the de is invisible in translation.
Drops the ce after tout, writing tout qui or tout que, because English says all I need with no equivalent of the two small words.
Uses qui or que after a comma to pick up the whole preceding sentence, on the English which pattern, where French needs ce qui, ce que or ce dont.
Builds a long card with several clauses and loses one piece on the way: the preposition, the agreement of lequel, the contraction, or the ce.

grammarIntroduced: lequel, laquelle, lesquels and lesquelles as the relative pronoun used after a preposition, agreeing with the antecedent
The fronted preposition: French moves avec, sur, dans and pour in front of the relative pronoun where English strands them at the end of the clause
The contraction of à with lequel: auquel, auxquels, auxquelles, and the feminine singular à laquelle that does not contract
The contraction of de with lequel: duquel, desquels, desquelles, and the feminine singular de laquelle that does not contract
The division of labour between dont and duquel: a lone de takes dont, and a de closing a compound preposition takes duquel
The fixed blocks la raison pour laquelle, les conditions dans lesquelles, le point sur lequel and grâce auquel
ce qui and ce que as the relative with no nominal antecedent, where the thing referred to is an idea rather than a noun
ce dont, for a clause whose verb or adjective governs de
tout ce qui, tout ce que and tout ce dont, and the obligatory ce that English has no word for
The sentence-level relative after a comma: ce qui, ce que and ce dont picking up a whole preceding clause

recorded.desc: THE SIXTEEN CELLS, FOUR TAKES, ONE PER GROUP, EACH GROUP'S FOUR IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within each take the FIRST AND THIRD lines must be acoustically identical and so must the SECOND AND FOURTH: « Il est grand. » and « Ils sont grands. » differ on the page and not in the mouth, and a reader who knows the third is spelled with an s will lengthen something or put a fraction of a z on it, and either instinct destroys the screen. If a listener with their eyes shut can tell the first from the third, the take is unusable. What MUST be audible is the second line against the first: the d of grande, the buzz of sérieuse, the v of sportive. The fourth take, marron, is the control and all four of its lines are one sound; read them evenly and do not vary the emphasis to keep it interesting.

THE FOUR LINES FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT, IN THIS ORDER: masculine singular, masculine plural, feminine singular, feminine plural, all of grand. The first pair and the second pair are each ONE take and must be indistinguishable within the pair; the learner is being asked to fail to hear a difference and to notice that they failed. Between the pairs the difference must be as clear as the language allows, because that is the half the ear does get. Land on the d of grande. Do not put one on grand.

THE -EUX GROUP, AND ONE PAIR MATTERS MORE THAN THE REST. « Il est sérieux. » then « Elle est sérieuse. » must be one take, same speed, same pitch, same length, so that the buzz on the end of the second is the only thing in the line that moved. Then « Ils sont sérieux. », which has to sound EXACTLY like the first line and not like a plural; then « Elles sont sérieuses. », which has to sound exactly like the second. Four lines, two sounds, and the learner is meant to hear that arithmetic rather than be told it.

THE -IF GROUP, SAME INSTRUCTION AS THE -EUX TAKE, and the thing to land is the f against the v. « Il est sportif. » ends in an f you can hear; « Elle est sportive. » ends in a v you can hear. English speakers hear those two as nearly the same and French speakers do not, so the take should not help by exaggerating either one. Read them at conversational weight and let the difference be what it actually is.

THE FOUR MARRON LINES, WHICH ARE THE SAME WORD FOUR TIMES. This is the only take in the lesson whose value is that nothing happens in it. All four must be identical on the last word: same length, same vowel, same nasal, no final consonant creeping in on the plural ones. A reader who varies them to keep the take alive has taught the opposite of the screen. Then the pair the class turns on: « Ses vestes sont vertes. » then « Ses vestes sont marron. », one take, back to back, identical up to the last word.

THE FOUR COLOURS THE LEARNER HAS NEVER MET, READ AS ORDINARY VOCABULARY. kaki, crème, bleu marine, bleu clair, each inside its sentence, at conversational pace with no teaching emphasis anywhere and in particular none on the colour. The whole value of the screen is that these are unremarkable words that happen to belong to a class, and a reading that announces them undoes that.

THE FOURTEEN DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to every other take in the lesson: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and any pair-reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. The plural s and the feminine e must be neither helped nor hidden; say the sentence the way somebody would say it, which is the whole difficulty the exercise exists to create.

THE TWELVE NAMING FORMS OF THE GROUP CHECK, READ AS A FLAT LIST AT CONVERSATIONAL PACE. Six cards then six drill words: grand, sérieux, sportif, marron, heureux, kaki, then curieux, impulsif, orange, généreux, vert, bleu marine. NOTHING IN THE READING MAY SIGNAL WHICH GROUP A WORD IS IN. That is the whole instruction and it is the opposite of the grid takes: the learner is being asked to decide from the last two letters they can SEE, and a reader who leans on the x of sérieux or the f of sportif has answered the question before it was put. Even weight, even pace, no rising list intonation that would make the last word sound like a conclusion, and roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

THE BREAK CARD. « sérieux » then « sérieuse », as one take, back to back, with the smallest gap the recording allows. They must sound like the same word twice with a different ending, because that is what they are. Any pause, any change of pitch, any extra weight on the second and the learner hears two words instead of one word finished two ways.

THE FLAT VIEWING. She is friendly, a little rushed, and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French. « Et vous, vous travaillez beaucoup ? » is casual and quick, the way you ask somebody something while showing them a kitchen. The English line afterwards is the important one and it must not sound like a defeat or a rebuke: she switches language cheerfully and without thinking about it, because it is the shortest route to a conversation, and she apologises for her own English rather than for the learner's French. That is exactly what makes it expensive, and nothing in the delivery should point at it.

lessons.intro: Every describing word in French has four shapes, and you do not learn them one word at a time. There are four groups, the last two letters of the plain form tell you which one you are in, and the last screen before the exam hands you three words this lesson never shows you and asks for all four shapes of each.

fourShapes.body: 4 patterns. Three of them have 4 written forms and 2 sounds. The fourth has one of each. A describing word takes a different shape depending on what it is describing: one thing or several, and a man or a woman, a bag or a jacket. You have seen this twice before, on colours and on six common words. What is new is that the shapes are not learned one word at a time. They come in 4 groups, and the last two letters of the word tell you which group you are in.
fourShapes.title: One word, four ways to write it

examples.note: And the same word, describing a woman.
Both changes at once, and they stack in that order.

theIfGroup.body: sportif becomes sportive. The f turns into a v and nothing else in the word moves, which makes it the easiest of the 4 to spot and the easiest to get wrong in writing, because the two letters sound so alike in English. This group is small in this course and large in French; sportif itself did not exist here until this lesson, which is why the exam hands you another one you have never seen and asks for it anyway.
theIfGroup.title: The group where f becomes v

examples.note: Ends in f, and the f is said out loud.

This is the whole lesson and it is worth more than the grid, because a grid only holds the words that are on it. whatYouCanHear.body: Lesson 1 in A2 said it about verbs: The spelling changes so the sound does not. The feminine is something you can hear in all three. The plural is something you can hear in none of them. That is worth knowing before you sit any listening test in French. Somebody says a sentence and you can tell from the sound whether they meant a man or a woman; you cannot tell whether they meant one or several. The number is carried by the words in front of the noun, and it is carried in writing by an s that has never been pronounced in the history of the language.

theOnesThatNeverChange.body: Lesson 16 in A1 put it this way: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. A colour borrowed from a thing keeps the thing’s shape. A colour borrowed from a thing keeps the thing’s shape. A chestnut is a chestnut whatever it is painted on, so marron never grows an e or an s, and neither does any colour made of two words. You met marron and orange as two words that behave oddly. They are not two words. kaki, crème, bleu marine, bleu clair and every other colour borrowed from a thing do exactly the same, and you have never been shown any of them. Put one beside an ordinary colour on the same noun and the difference is the whole thing: green grows an e and an s, and brown does not grow anything, ever, in any sentence you will ever write.

sections.body: The plain form tells you the other three. Read the last two letters of the masculine. -eux, -if, a colour that used to be a thing, or none of those. That is the whole decision, and the other three forms follow from it without another thought.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: 4 patterns. Three of them have 4 written forms and 2 sounds. The fourth has one of each.
sérieux ends in x, sportif ends in f, marron is a chestnut, and grand is none of those. Four endings, four patterns, and you can see all four without hearing a word.

Lesson 1 in A2 said the spelling changes so the sound does not. Here it is the other way round in one place and the same in the rest: The feminine is something you can hear in all three. The plural is something you can hear in none of them.
Lesson 16 in A1 gave you marron and orange as two words that behave oddly. They are a class, and kaki, crème, bleu marine, bleu clair are in it too.
You built four shapes each of 3 words, off two letters each, and this lesson showed you none of them.

Three adjectives break every rule on this screen and they are the three you use most. Lesson 11 in A2 is next and it is about nothing else. The lesson after that, lesson 12 in A2, is built on the feminine forms you have just learned to make.
Lesson 18 in A1 owns where the word goes and lesson 32 in A2 owns saying one thing is more than another. Neither of them is this.

errorTriggers.description: Uses the plain form for a woman, which is the error the scene opens on. It is not a slip; it is what a learner does when they have met the word once and only in one shape.
Puts an s on the plain form of a word ending in -eux. Lesson 17 in A1 taught the fact about two specific words and it reads as an oddity about those two rather than as a property of the letter.
Leaves the f in place and adds an e after it. The letter is replaced rather than added to, and in English the two sounds are close enough that the ear does not object.
Agrees a colour that was a thing first. The learner has just spent twenty screens learning that describing words change shape, and this class reads as the rule failing rather than as a class.
Puts the number ending on before the woman ending, or puts one on and forgets the other. Both come from treating the two as a single decision rather than as one after the other.

grammarAssumed: That a describing word changes shape to match what it describes, introduced in a1.13 through colour
The feminine -e and the plural -s on a describing word, and that the -s is never pronounced, introduced in a1.13
That marron and orange do not change, introduced in a1.13 as a fact about those two words
Six common describing words and their irregular feminines, introduced in a1.14
That a word already ending in -s or -x does not change in the masculine plural, introduced in a1.14 for vieux and mauvais
Where the describing word goes relative to the noun, introduced in a1.16
Noun gender and the determiners that carry it, introduced in a1.03 and a1.04
être in the present, introduced in a1.06, which is the frame every example in this lesson uses
That French spelling carries distinctions the ear does not, introduced in a2.01
grammarIntroduced: Adjective agreement as a system of four inflectional classes rather than as a property of individual lexemes
The -eux class: feminine in -euse, masculine plural identical to the masculine singular, feminine plural in -euses
The -if class: feminine in -ive by consonant substitution rather than by suffixation, with the regular plural -s
That the masculine plural of any adjective already ending in -s or -x is null-marked, generalised from a1.14 two lexemes to the whole class

The invariable class as a productive class rather than a closed list: denominal colour adjectives and compound colour adjectives, extended beyond a1.13 marron and orange to kaki, crème, bleu marine and bleu clair
That the feminine is phonologically realised in every regular class while number is not realised at all, which is the converse of the silent-agreement generalisation a2.01 introduced for verbs
The productivity of the classes, so an unseen adjective is inflectable from its masculine singular without further instruction

recorded.desc: The two rows and the frame pairs. Read the two rows as WORDS rather than as sentences, at an even pace. The sentence pairs are ONE TAKE each, both halves in it, so the learner hears one sentence becoming another rather than two being compared. The pronoun must carry NO extra weight: it is unstressed in speech and a reader who leans on it teaches that the learner will hear it coming.

The lesson 22 in A2 handshake. ONE TAKE PER CARD holding both lines. « Je parle à Marie. » and « Tu vas à Paris ? » must be read with IDENTICAL treatment of the à, because the whole card says the little word is the same and only what sits behind it differs.

Five pairs, ONE TAKE each. The English glosses are not recorded. In « J'y joue le samedi. » the y must not be lengthened: it is one sound inside the first syllable and a reader who separates it teaches a pronunciation nobody uses.

audioFirst. Four lines, ONE TAKE, one voice, no gaps that let the learner rehearse between them. Lines 3 and 4 both carry en and THE TWO MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE: they are the same word doing two jobs and the second question exists to make the learner hear that the ear cannot settle it.

Eight lines, read separately at a steady pace. The de and the du must sound exactly as unstressed as they do in ordinary speech; this screen is about a word disappearing and a reader who emphasises it before it goes makes the disappearance sound like a loss.

THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE LESSON. « Oui, j'ai. » must be read as a COMPLETE utterance with a falling intonation and no trailing hesitation, exactly as an English speaker would say it, and « Oui, j'en ai. » must be read the same way. The learner has to hear that the wrong one sounds finished, because that is why nobody corrects it. Do NOT read the wrong one as though it were being cut off.

Three lines and three frames, read separately. THE en IN ALL THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. They are the same word and the same sound and the entire teaching point is that only the next word separates them; a reader who marks the pronoun differently makes the exercise measure something that is not in the language.

The four trap cards, in order: « J'y vais à Paris. », « J'y vais. », « J'en veux du café. », « J'en bois. » The two wrong ones must be read FLUENTLY and without hesitation, because a learner who says them says them fluently and nothing in the sound is wrong. Do not signal the error.

il y a and il y en a. « Il y a » is three syllables run together at speed, as it is in speech, and « Il y en a » adds one without slowing down. The learner must hear that the phrase is one lump and that the extra word goes inside it rather than beside it.

The wrap. ONE TAKE per card holding both lines. Ne must NOT be given extra length: it is unstressed and often barely there, and a recording that pronounces it carefully teaches a register nobody uses.

Fourteen lines, ONE VOICE, read at dictation pace with the same interval before each. Several of them are three or four syllables long and the interval matters more than usual for that reason. « J'y vais. » and « J'en ai. » must be read at ordinary conversational speed rather than slowly: the whole exercise is whether the learner can hear a word that takes a tenth of a second to say.

lessons.intro: Two lessons ago you learned where a small word goes, and last lesson you learned that à plus a person turns into one. This lesson finishes the set, and the two words in it work in a way nothing you have met so far does: they do not stand in for a noun, they stand in for a little word AND the noun behind it, both at once. That is why nothing is left over afterwards, and it is why the mistake everybody makes is saying the little word one more time. The second half is harder and English gives you no help with it at all: French will not let you leave these words out, so the two-word answer your own language closes on does not close anything here.

frozen.body: Il y a is three words that arrived together, and they do not come apart. The middle word is the y on these screens, which is a good thing to know and a bad thing to act on. Lesson 14 in A2 taught the phrase in both its jobs and neither of them is re-taught here. What matters for this lesson is only that you can see your own word inside it, and that taking the phrase to pieces produces real French that means something else.
frozen.title: The y you have been reading since the beginning

examples.note: Three words that arrived together, with your y in the middle of them.
And the one place they take a passenger: y first, en second, and that order does not move.

inside.body: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it. Every pronoun you have met so far stood in for a noun and left everything else alone. These two swallow the little word in front of the noun as well, which is why nothing about them looks like the pronouns you already have. It is also why the mistake everybody makes is saying the little word again: you can hear that something is missing, and the thing that is missing is already there.
inside.title: What these two words are made of

examples.note: The place is named and the little word is in front of it, where you can see it.
And now there is no Paris and no à either. Both went into one letter.

theWrap.body: « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » is the line you have carried since the near future, and there is one verb in these sentences so the question of which verb never arises. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. That sentence is lesson 21's, word for word, and lesson 22 in A2 quoted it unchanged one lesson ago. It holds here for the same reason it held there: the small word belongs to the verb, so it goes where the verb goes. Ne outside both, pas after both.
theWrap.title: What ne and pas go round, and it has not changed

examples.note: Ne outside, then the pronoun and the verb together, then pas.
And with a two-word verb: ne, pronoun, first word, pas, second word.

sameSlot.body: « The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. » is lesson 21's line and it is true of these two words without a word changed. Je le vois. Je lui parle. J'y vais. J'en ai. Four sentences, three lessons, one position. That is worth saying out loud rather than leaving you to notice, because a learner who thinks each new pair of small words has its own placement rule ends up with three rules where there is one. There is one, it was learned two lessons ago, and this lesson spends it.
sameSlot.title: The one thing you do not have to learn, and lesson 21 in A2 taught it

examples.note: Subject, word, verb, exactly as it was for le and for lui.
And in front of BOTH words when the verb arrives as two, which is also not new.

theOrder.body: When both turn up, y comes first. Il y en a. These are the only two small words this lesson gives you, so this is the only order it can produce, and it is worth having because il y en a is one of the commonest answers in the language. Two of these small words in one sentence is a further question, and it is not answered here. You have three sets of these small words now and there are more ways of stacking them than this; that question is somebody else's and it is not answered on any screen here.
theOrder.title: When both of them turn up

examples.note: Both of them, in the one order they take.
And a number after them, which is where the answer usually goes.

threeEns.body: Before a thing it is a little word. Before a verb it is the pronoun. Nothing else separates them. Lesson 13 in A2 taught the one in front of a country and lesson 14 in A2 taught the one in front of a length of time, and this lesson teaches neither of them again. « À folds the article in. En throws it out. Chez leaves it alone. » is lesson 13's line and « Dans says when it starts. En says how long it took. One of them is a point and the other is a length, and English uses "in" for both. » is lesson 14's. What is new here is only the third one, and the only thing that separates it from the other two is where it sits. « what comes next decides » is lesson 5's name for this shape and you have met it six times before.
threeEns.title: One word, three jobs, three lessons

examples.note: A verb straight after it, so it is the pronoun.
A country straight after it, so it is the little word, and it is not this lesson.

twoWords.body: À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it. That is the whole of the choice, and it is made by the little word rather than by the meaning: if the sentence had à in it you want y, and if it had de, du, de la or des in it you want en. Neither word changes for anything. Not for the subject, not for the verb, not for the tense, and not for how many things you are talking about.
twoWords.title: Two words, and which one is decided before you speak

examples.note: à went in, so y came out.
de went in, so en came out. Same verb as the lesson before this one, and a different little word in front of it.

mustSayIt.body: French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence. English answers do you have any with two words and neither of them stands for the sugar. French cannot do that: the verb needs something after it and en is the something. English drops the word here and French keeps it. J'y vais is I am going. The same is true on the other side, and it catches people less often only because y sounds a little like there. Neither word is decoration and neither is ever optional.
mustSayIt.title: Why the sentence stops without it

examples.note: Three words in English and none of them is en, and French will not accept the two-word version.
And the same thing on the other word. « Oui, je vais. » is not a sentence either.

theQuantity.body: « Un is one of them. Du is some of it. » is lesson 8 in A1's line and you have had du, de la and des since then. En takes all three of them away, and it takes the noun with them. What stays is the number or the amount: j'en ai trois, j'en ai beaucoup, j'en veux un peu. English has nothing like this. I have three says nothing at all about what three of, and a French speaker hearing it would still be waiting.
theQuantity.title: How much, without saying what of

examples.note: The number stayed and des enfants went. Nothing in the sentence says children any more.
beaucoup de, and the de went inside en along with the noun.

personOrThing.body: « À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. » is lesson 22's line, from last lesson, and it is only half of what à does. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. Same little word, same disappearance, and the only thing that decides which pronoun comes out is whether what sat behind à was a person or not. Je parle à Marie becomes je lui parle. Je vais à Paris becomes j'y vais. Nothing else in either sentence changed.
personOrThing.title: What lesson 22 in A2 left for this lesson

examples.note: A place behind à, so it will be y.
And the same verb last lesson used, with a letter behind à instead of a person.

lessons.title: Y et EN

sections.body: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it. And the place it goes is not new: « The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. » is lesson 21's line and it has been true of three sets of small words in three lessons. French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence.
sections.title: The rule, in one line

rows: à plus a thing or a place
à plus something that is not a place at all
du, de la or des plus a thing
de plus a quantity, and the quantity stays
sections.title: What each one swallows

sections.body: When both turn up, y comes first. Il y en a. Il y a is three words that arrived together, and they do not come apart. That is the only pair these two words can make, and it is worth having because « Il y en a » is one of the commonest answers in the language. Two of these small words in one sentence is a further question, and it is not answered here. You now have three sets of these small words and there are more ways of stacking them than this one; that question belongs to a later lesson and nothing here answers it.
sections.title: Both at once

sections.body: Lesson 22 in A2 taught « À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. » and this lesson took the other half of it: « à plus a thing » becomes y. Between the three lessons you now have every small word that goes in front of a verb in this language except the ones you use for yourself, which lesson 19 in A2 already gave you. French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence.

overview.introFr: Le petit mot entre dans le pronom.

beats.text: A Saturday morning, a friend's kitchen in Lyon, and she is making something that needs three things she has run out of. You are the one nearest the cupboard.
You have been doing this for months now and you have stopped rehearsing. She asks over her shoulder, the way people ask when the answer is obviously yes or obviously no.

beats.en: Do you have any sugar?
beats.fr: Tu as du sucre ?
beats.speaker: Ton amie

beats.en: Yes, I do.
beats.fr: Oui, j'ai.
beats.stage: Two words, and then nothing. You know the answer, you know both words, and the sentence will not close. In English it closes on its own: yes, I do. Here it hangs, and you can hear that it is hanging.

beats.en: You have some?
beats.fr: Tu en as ?
beats.stage: She has not corrected you. She thinks she misheard, so she asks again, and she uses the word you were missing. It has been in front of you all morning and you have never had to say it.
beats.speaker: Ton amie

beats.prompt: Which of these closes the sentence?

options.en: Yes, I do.
options.fr: Oui, j'ai.

followUp.works: One extra letter, and the sentence has somewhere to end. Nothing else about it changed.
followUp.breaks: That is what came out, and it is not a sentence in French. The verb has nothing after it and the listener is still waiting.

beats.body: You had every word you needed and one of them does not exist in your language. Yes I do is a whole answer in English. In French the sentence stops in the middle, and there is nothing to hear.
beats.coach: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice.

beats.heading: The word that has to be there

beats.text: There are two small words that go in the place you already know, and each of them has a little word folded inside it. The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice.

sections.say: Two rows, and each one has a little word hidden inside it. The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice.

cards.fr: y  =  à + a thing
cards.body: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice. Every small word before these stood in for the noun and left the rest alone. These two take the little word as well, so nothing is left of it.
cards.head: What each one is made of

cards.fr: Je le vois.
cards.body: [zhee VEH] « The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. » is lesson 21's line and it is true of these two without a word changed. The first line is that lesson's own sentence, borrowed rather than copied.
cards.head: and the place is the one you know
cards.label: Lesson 21's sentence · this lesson's

cards.fr: Je vais à Paris.
cards.body: [zhuh veh a pa-REE] then [zhee VEH] À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. Paris is gone and so is the à, and the second sentence is two words long. The first line is lesson 13's own published row.

cards.label: named · and gone

cards.fr: Je parle de mon travail.

sections.title: Two Words, One Job

goals.s: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice. That is the one new idea in this lesson and everything else is something you already have.
goals.t: Swap a whole phrase for one small word

goals.s: À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it. A number can stay behind it and the noun still goes.
goals.t: Say how many without saying what of

goals.s: French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence. English answers with two words and French will not.
goals.t: Stop leaving it out

goals.s: Before a thing it is a little word. Before a verb it is the pronoun. Nothing else separates them. Lesson 13 in A2 and lesson 14 in A2 taught the other two and this lesson teaches neither of them again.
goals.t: Tell the three ens apart

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.say: « À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. » is lesson 22's line, from last lesson, and it is half of what à does. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it.
sections.hint: Look at what was sitting behind à.

cards.fr: Je parle à Marie.
cards.body: [zhuh PARL ah mah-REE] then [tü VAH ah pah-REE] Both sentences have à in them and there is nothing else to go on. What decides is whether the thing behind it breathes. The first line is lesson 22's own row.
cards.head: the same little word, twice
cards.label: a person behind it · a place behind it

cards.fr: Je lui parle.
cards.body: [zhuh lwee PARL] then [zhee VEH] « À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. » À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. One little word, two lessons, and only what sat behind it differs.
cards.head: and two different answers
cards.label: a person becomes lui · a place becomes y

cards.fr: Elle y répond.
cards.body: Répondre à is one of the verbs lesson 22 in A2 gave you, and its answer there was lui because a person was behind à. A letter is not a person, so it is y. Nothing about the verb or the rule changed.
cards.head: and the same verb settles it
cards.label: Lesson 22 in A2 answered lui · here it is y

cards.fr: Je pense à mon examen.
cards.body: [zhuh PAHⁿSS ah mohⁿ nehg-zah-MEHⁿ] then [zhee PAHⁿSS soo-VAHⁿ] An exam is not somewhere you can stand, and y is still the answer. That is worth meeting early, because the English word this looks like is « there » and it is about to stop helping.
cards.head: and it is not always a place
cards.label: an exam behind à · so still y

sections.title: A Person Or A Place

sections.say: English drops the word here and French keeps it. J'y vais is I am going. Five pairs, and only two of them are about a place at all.
sections.hint: Try translating the second line without the word "there".

cards.fr: Tu vas au marché ?
cards.body: [tü VAH oh mar-SHAY] then [wee, zhee VEH duh-MEHⁿ] au is à plus le, which lesson 13 in A2 owns, and y swallows the whole of it. Read the English answer again: there is no market in it, and no « there » either.
cards.head: a place, and English drops the word
cards.label: au marché · and then nothing

cards.fr: Je joue au tennis.
cards.body: [zhuh ZHOO oh tay-NEESS] then [zhee ZHOO luh sam-DEE] Jouer à, and the thing behind à is a game. Nobody stands in tennis, and y is still what comes out.
cards.head: a game, which is not a place
cards.label: au tennis · and it is still y

cards.fr: Tu penses à ton examen ? Oui, j'y pense souvent.
cards.sub: Je vais à Paris ; j'y vais en train.
cards.body: Two published sentences, both in this lesson's own theme, both written years ago for somebody else's screen. The second one holds the whole of this lesson's opening in eight words, and the phrase « j'y pense » is published beside them as a card of its own.
cards.head: and the corpus said so first
cards.label: published, by somebody not teaching this

cards.fr: Nous y allons ensemble.
cards.sub: Elle y va tous les jours.
cards.body: [noo zee ah-LOHⁿ ahⁿ-SAHⁿBL] then [ehl ee VAH too lay ZHOOR] The word does not agree with anything, does not change for anything, and sits in the same place every time. Lesson 1 in A2 owns the nous form and this borrows it.
cards.head: and the subject makes no difference
cards.label: nous · elle

cards.fr: Tu y vas souvent ?
cards.body: [tü ee VAH soo-VAHⁿ] then [eel ee PAHⁿSS] The pronoun does not move for a question, which lesson 22 in A1 owns. And pensent sounds exactly like pense, which is lesson 1 in A2's business rather than this lesson's.
cards.head: a question, and a plural subject
cards.label: tu · ils

sections.title: Not Always There

sections.say: Four lines. The ear can tell you whether the word is there at all, which is the thing that matters most. The two ens are one sound, so no listening question in this lesson ever asks you which is which.

lines.en: I am going.
lines.fr: J'y vais.

lines.en: I talk about it.
lines.fr: J'en parle.

lines.en: She talks about it.
lines.fr: Elle en parle.

lines.en: She lives in France.
lines.fr: Elle habite en France.

sections.title: One Sound Apart

questions.q: « J'y vais » against « Je vais ». What separates them?
questions.why: Zhee against zhuh. One vowel, and the second sentence is missing the word this lesson is about. That difference is genuinely audible, which is more than can be said for the one below.
opts: One sound, and it is the whole meaning

questions.q: « Elle en parle » against « Elle habite en France ». What separates the two ens?
questions.why: Before a thing it is a little word. Before a verb it is the pronoun. Nothing else separates them. The two ens are one sound, so no listening question in this lesson ever asks you which is which.

sections.say: De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it. « Un is one of them. Du is some of it. » is lesson 8 in A1's line and you have had du, de la and des since then. En takes all three of them away, and the noun with them.
sections.title: The Other Little Word

examples.en: I talk about my work.
examples.fr: Je parle de mon travail.
examples.note: [zhuh PARL duh mohⁿ trah-VAHY] de, on its own, in front of a thing.

examples.en: I talk about it.
examples.fr: J'en parle.
examples.note: [zhahⁿ PARL] And the de is gone with it. Same verb lesson 22 in A2 used, and a different little word.

examples.en: I drink coffee.
examples.fr: Je bois du café.
examples.note: Published at a1, in the kitchen theme, by somebody teaching food. The word du is de plus le, and the de inside it counts.

examples.en: Do you drink coffee?
examples.fr: Tu bois du café ?
examples.note: [tü BWAH dü ka-FAY] The same du, as a question.

examples.en: I drink some.
examples.fr: J'en bois.
examples.note: [zhahⁿ BWAH] And du café is gone. The English needs « some » and the French needs nothing at all.

examples.en: some coffee
examples.fr: du café
examples.note: [dü ka-FAY] lesson 8 in A1's own card, and the thing en stands in for. It is not re-taught here.

examples.en: Do you want some coffee? Yes, I'd like some.
examples.fr: Tu veux du café ? Oui, j'en veux bien.
examples.note: Published, in this theme, and it is a question and an answer with the whole rule in it.

examples.en: She has three brothers; she talks about them often.
examples.fr: Elle a trois frères ; elle en parle souvent.
examples.note: Also published, also here, and the subject is not je. Three brothers are named and then they are not.

sections.say: French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence. This is the half of the lesson English gives you no help with at all.
sections.hint: Read the second line and then try to finish it.

cards.fr: Oui, j'en ai.
cards.body: [wee, zhahⁿ NAY] for the first line. French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence. English says « Yes, I do. » and none of it stands for the sugar.
cards.head: the answer, and the one that is not one
cards.label: a sentence · and two words that stop

cards.fr: Tu as du sucre ?
cards.body: [tü AH dü SÜKR] then [wee, zhahⁿ NAY] du sucre in the question, and nothing at all in the answer except the word that stands for it.
cards.head: and the question it answers
cards.label: the sugar is named · and then it is not

cards.fr: Tu prends du sucre ?
cards.body: [tü PRAHⁿ dü SÜKR] then [wee, zhahⁿ PRAHⁿ] The English answer is the same three words again. It is a fact about English rather than about avoir.
cards.head: a second verb, and the same gap
cards.label: prendre · and English still says nothing

cards.fr: Tu vas au bureau ?
cards.body: [tü VAH oh bü-ROH] then [wee, zhee VEH] English drops the word here and French keeps it. J'y vais is I am going. « Oui, je vais. » is not a sentence either.
cards.head: and the other word does it too
cards.label: the office is named · and then it is not

sections.title: You Cannot Drop It

sections.say: The thing you already said goes, and the amount stays behind. That shape has no equivalent in English at all: « I have three » says nothing about what three of.
sections.title: How Many, Not What

examples.en: Do you have children?
examples.fr: Tu as des enfants ?
examples.note: [tü AH day zahⁿ-FAHⁿ] des, which lesson 8 in A1 owns.

examples.en: Yes, I have three.
examples.fr: Oui, j'en ai trois.
examples.note: [wee, zhahⁿ nay TRWAH] The number stayed and des enfants went. Nothing in the French says children any more and a French speaker still knows.

examples.en: I have a lot.
examples.fr: J'en ai beaucoup.
examples.note: [zhahⁿ nay boh-KOO] beaucoup de, and the de went inside en along with the noun.

examples.en: I want a little.
examples.fr: J'en veux un peu.
examples.note: [zhahⁿ VUH uhⁿ PUH] un peu de, and the same disappearance.

examples.en: I have enough.
examples.fr: J'en ai assez.
examples.note: [zhahⁿ nay ah-SAY] assez de. Four quantity words and one behaviour between them.

examples.en: a lot of, many, much
examples.fr: beaucoup de
examples.note: [boh-koo duh] lesson 8 in A1's own card. The de on the end of it is the de that goes inside.

examples.en: I want some
examples.fr: j'en veux
examples.note: [zhahⁿ VUH] Published in this theme as a card of its own, and this build repairs its respelling: the nasal was written with a plain n.

examples.en: We take some.
examples.fr: Nous en prenons.
examples.note: [noo zahⁿ pruh-NOHⁿ] A different subject, and the z you hear is a liaison you never write.

examples.en: Do you want some?
examples.fr: Vous en voulez ?
examples.note: [voo zahⁿ voo-LAY] And as a question, with the same two words in the same place.

sections.say: Four things this lesson never showed you. The rule is about the little word in front of the thing, so it does not care which verb put the little word there.
sections.title: Verbs Not Listed Here

check.q: « Il rêve de cette maison. » Replace the house.
check.why: Rêver DE, so it is en. English says « dreams ABOUT it » and points at the wrong little word. The little word is already inside the pronoun, so saying it again says it twice.
opts: Il en rêve de cette maison.

items.en: He dreams about it.

items.en: I need it.

check.q: « Nous revenons de Paris. » Replace the city.
check.why: THE CASE THAT CATCHES EVERYBODY. Paris is a place, and the answer is still en, because revenir takes de and the little word decides rather than the meaning. A learner holding « y is there and en is some » gets this one wrong every time.

items.en: She answers it.

sections.title: One Word, Three Jobs

sections.say: Four cards and then six to prove it. The first card is a sentence nobody says, and it is the one the rule you just learned will build for you if you stop halfway.

rule.body: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice. The little word is already inside the pronoun, so saying it again says it twice. Look for it: if you can still see it, the pronoun should not be there.
rule.title: It is already in there

cards.fr: J'y vais à Paris.
cards.ipa: /ʒi vɛ a pa.ʁi/
cards.tip: The little word is already inside the pronoun, so saying it again says it twice. The sentence sounds like it is finishing something and it is repeating something. Nothing in the sound will stop you.
cards.promptSound: J'y vais à Paris.

cards.fr: J'y vais.
cards.ipa: /ʒi vɛ/
cards.tip: Paris and the à both went into one letter. There is nothing missing from this sentence.
cards.promptLabel: and the whole of it, in two words
cards.promptSound: J'y vais.

cards.fr: J'en veux du café.
cards.ipa: /ʒɑ̃ vø dy ka.fe/
cards.tip: The du is de plus le, so the de is in this sentence twice. Once inside en and once out loud.
cards.promptLabel: and the same mistake on the other word
cards.promptSound: J'en veux du café.

cards.fr: J'en bois.
cards.ipa: /ʒɑ̃ bwa/
cards.tip: Two words, and one of them is doing the work of three.
cards.promptLabel: and the right one, which is shorter
cards.promptSound: J'en bois.

sections.title: Said Twice

sections.say: Il y a is three words that arrived together, and they do not come apart. You have been reading this y since your first month and nobody told you what it was.
sections.hint: Look at the middle word.

cards.fr: Il y a du pain.
cards.sub: [eel ee ah dü PEHⁿ] There is bread.
cards.body: Il y a is three words that arrived together, and they do not come apart. Lesson 14 in A2 owns both of its jobs and neither is re-taught here. What is new is that your own word is in the middle of it.
cards.head: it has been there all along
cards.label: three words · and the middle one is yours

cards.fr: il y a trois jours
cards.body: [EEL EE AH trwah ZHOOR] then [EEL EE AH ÜN UHR] Both are lesson 14's own cards, spelled its way. « Il en a. » is what taking the phrase to pieces gives you: real French, and it means he has some.
cards.head: and the phrase does not come apart
cards.label: Lesson 14 in A2 owns both of its jobs

cards.fr: Il y en a.
cards.sub: [eel ee ahⁿ NAH] There is some.
cards.body: When both turn up, y comes first. Il y en a. It still does not come apart; a second word goes in behind the first. Two of these small words in one sentence is a further question, and it is not answered here.
cards.head: and there is one thing it does take
cards.label: y first · en second

cards.fr: Il y en a trois.
cards.sub: Il y en a un à quatorze heures, quai trois.
cards.body: [eel ee ahⁿ nah TRWAH] The second line is published at a2 in the travel theme, and its own note says out loud that it is « il y a » with this lesson's word added. Nobody wrote it to teach you that.
cards.head: and a number goes after both
cards.label: published, by somebody selling train tickets

sections.title: The Y You Knew

sections.title: What Goes Wrong

errors.why: French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence. This is the error the scene ends on, and it is not carelessness: English closes the sentence with two words and there is nothing in it to translate.
errors.right: Oui, j'en ai.
errors.wrong: Oui, j'ai.

errors.why: The little word is already inside the pronoun, so saying it again says it twice. The rule was applied and then applied again, which is what happens when you build the English sentence first and repair it afterwards.
errors.right: J'y vais.
errors.wrong: J'y vais à Paris.

errors.why: The same thing on the other word. The du is de plus le, so the de is in that sentence twice: once inside en and once out loud.
errors.right: J'en bois.
errors.wrong: J'en veux du café.

errors.why: A person went into y, and a person never does. That is lesson 22 in A2's word, and this one only takes a thing or a place. Lesson 22 in A2 spent itself on which verbs put a person behind à.
errors.right: Je lui parle.
errors.wrong: J'y parle.

sections.say: One negation rule, seven lessons old, and this adds nothing to it. « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. »

cards.fr: J'y vais.
cards.body: [zhee VEH] then [zhuh nee VEH PAH] « Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. » from lesson 21 in A1, and « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » from lesson 15 in A2. One verb, so neither arises.
cards.head: both inside
cards.label: ne · y vais · pas

cards.fr: J'en parle.
cards.body: [zhahⁿ PARL] then [zhuh nahⁿ VUH PAH] The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together. That sentence is lesson 21's, word for word, and lesson 22 in A2 quoted it unchanged one lesson ago. Three lessons, one sentence.
cards.head: and the other word is no different
cards.label: ne · en veux · pas

cards.fr: Il n'y pense pas.
cards.body: [eel nee PAHⁿSS PAH] then [noo nahⁿ par-LOHⁿ PAH] Nothing about the wrap responds to either of them.
cards.head: a different subject, and a different verb
cards.label: il · nous

cards.fr: J'en ai parlé.
cards.body: [zhahⁿ nay par-LAY] then [zhuh nahⁿ nay pah par-LAY] The pronoun goes in front of BOTH halves, which is lesson 21's rule on lesson 16's tense, and the second word takes nothing at all, which is lesson 22's. Neither is new here.
cards.head: and with two words of verb
cards.label: ne · word · first word · pas · second word

sections.setting: The same Saturday, an hour later, at the stall on the corner. Every answer here is about something that has already been named, which is the only situation these two words are for.

cards.say: J'y vais.
cards.back: The preposition goes inside the pronoun, so it does not get said twice. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it. De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it.
cards.front: What is inside these two words?

cards.say: J'y vais.
cards.back: J'y vais. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it.
cards.front: « Je vais à Paris » Say it without the city.

cards.say: J'en parle.
cards.back: J'en parle. De plus a thing becomes en, and the de disappears with it.
cards.front: « Je parle de mon travail » Say it without the work.

cards.say: Oui, j'en ai.
cards.back: Oui, j'en ai. French will not let you leave it out. « Oui, j'ai. » is not a sentence.
cards.front: Do you have any sugar? Answer yes.

cards.say: J'y vais.
cards.back: The pronoun goes in front of the verb, not after it. Lesson 21's line, unchanged, for the third lesson.

cards.say: Je n'en veux pas.
cards.back: Je n'en veux pas. The wrap goes round the pronoun and the verb together.

cards.say: Je lui parle.
cards.back: Lui, and lesson 22 in A2 owns it. À plus a person becomes lui or leur, and the à disappears with it. À plus a thing becomes y, and the à disappears with it.
cards.front: A person is behind à. Which word?

cards.say: Elle habite en France.
cards.back: The little word, because a country comes next. Before a thing it is a little word. Before a verb it is the pronoun. Nothing else separates them.
cards.front: Which en is « Elle habite en France »?

cards.say: Il y a du pain.
cards.back: Il y a is three words that arrived together, and they do not come apart. « Il en a. » is real French and means he has some.
cards.front: Does « il y a » come apart?

cards.say: Il y en a.
cards.back: When both turn up, y comes first. Il y en a. Two of these small words in one sentence is a further question, and it is not answered here.
cards.front: Both words in one sentence. Which order?

cards.say: J'y ai pensé.
cards.back: Nothing, and lesson 22 in A2 settled that one lesson ago.
cards.front: And in the past, does anything go on the end?
